title: Clique immersion conjecture
open: Must every graph of chromatic number \(t\) contain the complete graph \(K_t\) as a weak immersion — that is, \(t\) distinct branch vertices joined pairwise by edge-disjoint paths?
status: Open since the late twentieth century. Fox–Pach–Suk (2025) establish the conclusion when the graph has at most \((1.64-o(1))t\) vertices ([*Immersions and Albertson's conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.05893)); the general conjecture remains unresolved.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given for all \(t\)-chromatic graphs; the current partial result covers graphs with at most \((1.64-o(1))t\) vertices, so a full resolution must handle graphs of arbitrarily many vertices relative to \(t\).
why: It would force complete communication patterns — an immersed clique — out of chromatic complexity alone, giving a structural certificate for high chromatic number.
key_works: Fox–Pach–Suk (2025), [*Immersions and Albertson’s conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.05893).

title: Thomassen’s large-girth, large-minimum-degree conjecture
open: For every choice of \(k\) and \(g\), is there a constant \(D(k,g)\) such that every graph of minimum degree at least \(D(k,g)\) contains a subgraph with minimum degree at least \(k\) and girth at least \(g\)? In other words, can arbitrarily high minimum degree force the existence of a highly connected subgraph that is locally sparse?
status: The conjecture was proposed by Thomassen in 1983. Important bounded-girth cases have been resolved, but the general statement remains open. A recent extension of the conjecture to directed graphs has been studied by Christoph–Janzer–Petrova–Steiner (2025), [*Extending Thomassen’s conjecture to directed graphs*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.11311).
solved_when: For every pair of positive integers \(k\) and \(g\), an explicit (or even existence) bound \(D(k,g)\) is established such that every graph of minimum degree at least \(D(k,g)\) contains a subgraph of minimum degree at least \(k\) and girth at least \(g\).
why: A solution would show that dense graphs always contain subgraphs that are simultaneously well-connected and locally sparse, providing a fundamental tool for extracting sparse structure from high connectivity.
key_works: Christoph–Janzer–Petrova–Steiner (2025), [*Extending Thomassen’s conjecture to directed graphs*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.11311).

title: Reed’s chromatic-number conjecture
open: Is the chromatic number of every graph bounded above by the average of its two classical obstructions — the clique number plus one and the maximum degree plus one? Formally, does \(\chi(G)\le\lceil(\Delta(G)+1+\omega(G))/2\rceil\) hold for every graph \(G\)?
status: The conjecture was proposed by Reed in 1998. Weaker universal interpolation bounds are known, and the inequality has been verified exactly in many special cases.
solved_when: The inequality \(\chi(G)\le\lceil(\Delta(G)+1+\omega(G))/2\rceil\) is proven for all graphs, or a counterexample graph is exhibited.
why: It would give a sharp interpolation between the two fundamental bounds \(\chi\le\Delta+1\) and \(\chi\le\omega+1\) (up to rounding), showing that degree-based and clique-based obstructions to coloring cannot conspire to force more colors than their midpoint.
key_works: Reed (1998), [*ω, Δ, and χ*](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/%28SICI%291097-0118%28199804%2927%3A4%3C177%3A%3AAID-JGT1%3E3.0.CO%3B2-K).

title: Total coloring conjecture
open: Can every simple graph have its vertices and edges colored simultaneously with at most \(\Delta+2\) colors, so that any two adjacent or incident elements receive distinct colors?
status: Proposed independently in the 1960s (the Behzad–Vizing conjecture). Numerous classes are settled, and dense-graph results — e.g. Henderschedt–McDonald–Shan (2025), [*Total coloring graphs with large minimum degree*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.05548) — do not cover the unrestricted case.
solved_when: A proof (or construction refuting it) that every simple graph of maximum degree \(\Delta\) admits a total coloring with at most \(\Delta+2\) colors.
why: It gives the fundamental simultaneous bound for scheduling nodes and links under all adjacency and incidence conflicts.
key_works: Henderschedt–McDonald–Shan (2025), [*Total coloring graphs with large minimum degree*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.05548).

title: Equitable list-coloring conjecture
open: If every vertex of a graph \(G\) has maximum degree at most \(r-1\), must any assignment of lists of \(r\) colors admit a proper coloring in which no color is used more than \(\lceil |V(G)|/r\rceil\) times? In other words, does the classical equitable-coloring guarantee extend from a shared palette of \(r\) colors to arbitrary lists of \(r\) colors per vertex?
status: The conjecture was proposed in 2003 by Kostochka–Pelsmajer–West in [*A list analogue of equitable coloring*](https://doi.org/10.1002/jgt.10137). Ordinary equitable coloring is settled; the unrestricted list version remains open.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) that for every graph with \(\Delta(G)\le r-1\), every assignment of lists of size \(r\) admits a proper list-coloring with each color class of size at most \(\lceil |V(G)|/r\rceil\).
why: It asks whether each vertex choosing from its own available colors is still compatible with keeping the color classes balanced — combining individual eligibility with equitable workloads across the palette.
key_works: Kostochka–Pelsmajer–West (2003), [*A list analogue of equitable coloring*](https://doi.org/10.1002/jgt.10137).

title: Cereceda’s quadratic recoloring conjecture
open: Can any two proper \((d+2)\)-colorings of an \(n\)-vertex \(d\)-degenerate graph be connected by a sequence of \(O_d(n^2)\) single-vertex recolorings, each maintaining a proper coloring? Equivalently, is the diameter of the \((d+2)\)-coloring reconfiguration graph bounded quadratically for \(d\)-degenerate graphs?
status: Open since 2007. A general \(O(n^{d+1})\) bound is known, and quadratic bounds have been established under additional slack or restrictions; see Bousquet–Heinrich (2019), [*A polynomial version of Cereceda's conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.05619).
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) that every pair of proper \((d+2)\)-colorings of any \(n\)-vertex \(d\)-degenerate graph is connected by at most \(O_d(n^2)\) valid single-vertex recolorings.
why: The bound measures the worst-case cost of moving between feasible configurations of a coloring solution space, with direct ties to the behavior of recoloring-based algorithms and rapid mixing of coloring Glauber dynamics.
key_works: Bousquet–Heinrich (2019), [*A polynomial version of Cereceda’s conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.05619).

title: Fan–Raspaud conjecture
subfield: Flows, perfect matchings, and cycle covers
open: Does every bridgeless cubic graph admit three perfect matchings whose common intersection is empty? Equivalently, must there exist perfect matchings $M_1, M_2, M_3$ with $M_1 \cap M_2 \cap M_3 = \emptyset$?
status: Proposed in 1994; it is implied by the Berge–Fulkerson conjecture, and numerous special cases are known. Recent work includes Karabáš–Máčajová–Nedela–Škoviera (2026), [*Regular colouring defect of a cubic graph and the conjectures of Fan–Raspaud and Fulkerson*](https://doi.org/10.26493/1855-3974.3291.A20).
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given for the statement that every bridgeless cubic graph has three perfect matchings with empty common intersection.
why: The conjecture isolates a weaker matching-compatibility obstruction than the full Berge–Fulkerson conjecture, so resolving it clarifies how far matching structure in bridgeless cubic graphs can be pushed without settling the stronger statement.
key_works: Karabáš–Máčajová–Nedela–Škoviera (2026), [*Regular colouring defect of a cubic graph and the conjectures of Fan–Raspaud and Fulkerson*](https://doi.org/10.26493/1855-3974.3291.A20).

title: Barnette’s conjecture
open: Does every 3-connected cubic bipartite planar graph contain a Hamiltonian cycle? In other words, do planarity, 3-regularity, bipartiteness, and 3-connectivity alone force a spanning tour?
status: Proposed in 1969. Special face-size cases and strong approximate Hamiltonian structures are known; see Bekos–Kaufmann–Pfister (2025), [*Approximating Barnette’s Conjecture*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.GD.2025.6).
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given for Hamiltonicity in every 3-connected cubic bipartite planar graph.
why: It would show that spanning tours follow purely from planarity, regularity, and connectivity, resolving a long-standing link between these structural conditions and Hamiltonicity.
key_works: Bekos–Kaufmann–Pfister (2025), [*Approximating Barnette’s Conjecture*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.GD.2025.6).

title: Sheehan’s conjecture
open: Can a finite simple 4-regular graph have exactly one Hamiltonian cycle? Sheehan's conjecture asserts that the answer is no, and asks for a proof of this impossibility.
status: The conjecture was proposed in 1975. Odd-degree parity arguments rule out unique Hamiltonicity in odd-degree settings, and extensive searches have failed to find a counterexample, but the 4-regular case remains open. Key works: Sheehan (1977), "Graphs with exactly one hamiltonian circuit" (https://doi.org/10.1002/jgt.3190010110); Brinkmann–De Pauw (2024), "Uniquely hamiltonian graphs for many sets of degrees" (https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.08946).
solved_when: A proof that no finite simple 4-regular graph has exactly one Hamiltonian cycle; alternatively, a counterexample exhibiting such a graph.
why: It would force multiple spanning tours from modest uniform redundancy, showing that even a small amount of regular structure guarantees non-uniqueness of Hamiltonian cycles.
key_works: Sheehan (1977), [*Graphs with exactly one hamiltonian circuit*](https://doi.org/10.1002/jgt.3190010110); Brinkmann–De Pauw (2024), [*Uniquely hamiltonian graphs for many sets of degrees*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.08946).

title: Chvátal’s toughness conjecture
open: Is there a universal constant \(t\) such that every \(t\)-tough graph is Hamiltonian? Here a graph is \(t\)-tough if, for every cutset \(S\) with \(c(G-S)>1\), one has \(|S| \ge t\,c(G-S)\), where \(c\) counts the components of \(G-S\).
status: Open since 1973. Numerous forbidden-induced-subgraph classes are known to admit sufficient toughness constants; e.g. Shan (2025), [*Hamiltonian cycles in tough \((P_4\cup P_1)\)-free graphs*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.08936).
solved_when: A constant \(t\) is exhibited such that every \(t\)-tough graph contains a Hamiltonian cycle — or, equivalently, the conjecture is refuted by constructing, for every \(t\), a non-Hamiltonian \(t\)-tough graph.
why: It asks whether a bounded strengthening of the standard separation obstruction to Hamiltonicity fully captures it, making toughness a clean sufficient condition for Hamiltonicity.
key_works: Shan (2025), [*Hamiltonian cycles in tough \((P_4\cup P_1)\)-free graphs*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.08936).

title: Matthews–Sumner conjecture
open: Is every 4-connected claw-free graph Hamiltonian? Equivalently (as Thomassen conjectured in the line-graph formulation), does every 4-connected line graph contain a Hamiltonian cycle?
status: Proposed in 1984. It is known that every 7-connected claw-free graph is Hamilton-connected (Ryjáček–Vrána 2011, [Line graphs of multigraphs and Hamilton-connectedness of claw-free graphs](https://doi.org/10.1002/jgt.20498)); the case of connectivity four remains open.
solved_when: A proof, or counterexample, is given for Hamiltonicity of every 4-connected claw-free graph.
why: It would turn a local branching prohibition (no induced claw) into a sharp spanning-cycle guarantee, unifying connectivity and Hamiltonicity at the natural threshold of four.
key_works: Ryjáček–Vrána (2011), [*Line graphs of multigraphs and Hamilton-connectedness of claw-free graphs*](https://doi.org/10.1002/jgt.20498).
aliases: Equivalent to Thomassen’s 4-connected line-graph Hamiltonicity conjecture.

title: Classification of 2-factor-Hamiltonian cubic bipartite braces
open: Are \(K_{3,3}\) and the Heawood graph the only cubic bipartite braces in which every 2-factor is Hamiltonian?
status: The Pfaffian case was settled in 2025 by Gorsky–Johanni–Wiederrecht ([*A note on the 2-Factor Hamiltonicity Conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.08128)); the non-Pfaffian braces remain open.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given that determines exactly which cubic bipartite braces have all 2-factors Hamiltonian, covering both the Pfaffian and the non-Pfaffian cases.
why: It would complete the classification of graphs in which every spanning degree-two structure is connected.
key_works: Gorsky–Johanni–Wiederrecht (2025), [*A note on the 2-Factor Hamiltonicity Conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.08128).

title: Graceful tree conjecture
open: Can every tree on \(n\) vertices be gracefully labeled — that is, labeled bijectively with \(0,\ldots,n-1\) so that the edge differences are exactly \(1,\ldots,n-1\)?
status: The conjecture is due to Rosa (1967), also known as the Ringel–Kotzig conjecture. Many families of trees are settled, and recent work on the gracesize of trees by Letzter–Pokrovskiy–Williams (2025–2026), [*On the gracesize of trees*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.11331), obtains almost all of the required differences.
solved_when: A proof (or construction) that every finite tree admits a graceful labeling; equivalently, for each \(n\)-vertex tree, a bijection to \(0,\ldots,n-1\) whose \(n-1\) edge differences are precisely \(1,\ldots,n-1\).
why: A graceful labeling yields structured cyclic decompositions of complete graphs with no repeated differences, turning a labeling question into a decomposition tool.
key_works: Letzter–Pokrovskiy–Williams (2025–2026), [*On the gracesize of trees*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.11331).

title: Tree packing conjecture
open: Can every sequence of trees \(T_1,\dots,T_n\), where \(T_i\) has exactly \(i\) vertices, be packed edge-disjointly into the complete graph \(K_n\)? Equivalently, is there a decomposition of \(K_n\)'s edges into copies of the trees \(T_i\) with \(|V(T_i)|=i\) for \(1\le i\le n\)?
status: The conjecture was proposed in 1976. It is known for trees of almost-linear maximum degree (Allen et al., [*The tree packing conjecture for trees of almost linear maximum degree*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.11720)). An unrestricted claimed proof by Chalise–Clark–Gnang ([withdrawn proof](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13840)) was withdrawn in September 2026.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given for packing arbitrary trees \(T_i\) with \(|V(T_i)|=i\), \(1\le i\le n\), edge-disjointly into \(K_n\).
why: It would show that the orders of the trees alone suffice for a complete coordinated packing into \(K_n\), with no further structural restrictions.
key_works: Allen et al., [*The tree packing conjecture for trees of almost linear maximum degree*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.11720); Chalise–Clark–Gnang, [withdrawn proof](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13840).

title: Gallai’s path decomposition conjecture
open: Can the edge set of every connected \(n\)-vertex graph be partitioned into at most \(\lceil n/2\rceil\) simple paths?
status: Open since the 1960s. The conjecture has been settled for planar graphs, graphs of maximum degree at most five, and further classes; see Chu–Fan–Zhou (2026), [*Gallai’s conjecture and the path number of odd semi-cliques*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.disc.2025.114725).
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) establishing whether every connected \(n\)-vertex graph admits a decomposition of its edges into at most \(\lceil n/2\rceil\) simple paths.
why: It would give an optimal universal bound on how few nonrepeating routes are needed to cover any graph, a fundamental measure of graph structure.
key_works: Chu–Fan–Zhou (2026), [*Gallai’s conjecture and the path number of odd semi-cliques*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.disc.2025.114725).

title: Codegree threshold for a tetrahedron
open: Does a minimum pair-codegree above \((1/2+\varepsilon)n\) force a copy of the complete 3-uniform tetrahedron \(K_4^{(3)}\) in every sufficiently large 3-uniform hypergraph? Formally, is \(t_3(n, K_4^{(3)}) \leq (1/2+\varepsilon)n\) for large enough \(n\)?
status: Matching lower constructions exist, so the conjectured threshold cannot be improved. The analogous codegree threshold for the tetrahedron minus an edge, \(K_4^{(3)-}\), is settled by Falgas-Ravry–Pikhurko–Vaughan–Volec (2023), [*The codegree threshold of \(K_4^-\)*](https://doi.org/10.1112/jlms.12722); the complete tetrahedron case remains open.
solved_when: A proof shows that every sufficiently large 3-uniform hypergraph with minimum codegree greater than \((1/2+\varepsilon)n\) contains \(K_4^{(3)}\), or a counterexample disproves it.
why: It measures how local abundance of pairs forces global structural consistency — a basic test case for the general relationship between codegree conditions and clique appearance.
key_works: Falgas-Ravry–Pikhurko–Vaughan–Volec (2023), [*The codegree threshold of \(K_4^-\)*](https://doi.org/10.1112/jlms.12722).

title: Brown–Erdős–Sós sparse-configuration conjecture
open: Must every 3-uniform hypergraph with \(\varepsilon n^2\) edges contain \(k\) edges spanning at most \(k+3\) vertices, for each \(k\ge3\)?
status: Proposed in 1973 by Brown–Erdős–Sós. The \(k=3\) case is exactly the Ruzsa–Szemerédi theorem; the first unresolved case is four edges on seven vertices.
solved_when: For every \(k\ge3\), it is proved that any 3-uniform hypergraph on \(n\) vertices with \(\varepsilon n^2\) edges contains such a configuration of \(k\) edges on at most \(k+3\) vertices.
why: It connects sparse hypergraphs to removal lemmas and recurrence phenomena in additive combinatorics; the \(k=3\) case already underlies the Ruzsa–Szemerédi theorem and sharp arithmetic removal bounds.
key_works: Brown–Erdős–Sós (1973), *On the existence of triangulated spheres in 3-graphs, and related problems*; [Erdős’ problem archive](https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/TripleSystems.html).

title: Erdős’ girth conjecture
open: For every fixed \(k\ge2\), do there exist arbitrarily large graphs of girth greater than \(2k\) with \(\Omega(n^{1+1/k})\) edges? Equivalently, can the extremal density for graphs with no cycles of length at most \(2k\) be achieved up to a constant factor by explicit constructions?
status: The upper exponent follows from breadth-first expansion. Matching constructions are known for selected parameters, including \(k=2,3,5\); see Parter (2014), [*Bypassing Erdős’ Girth Conjecture: Hybrid Stretch and Sourcewise Spanners*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1404.6835).
solved_when: For every fixed \(k\ge2\), a construction is given of graphs on \(n\) vertices with girth greater than \(2k\) and \(\Omega(n^{1+1/k})\) edges.
why: A solution would determine the optimal density of graphs without short cycles, which in turn pins down optimal size–stretch tradeoffs for graph spanners.
key_works: Parter (2014), [*Bypassing Erdős’ Girth Conjecture: Hybrid Stretch and Sourcewise Spanners*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1404.6835).

title: Meyniel’s cop-number conjecture
subfield: Graph parameters and topological graph theory
open: Do \(O(\sqrt n)\) cops always suffice to capture a single robber on every connected \(n\)-vertex graph in the standard perfect-information pursuit game? Formally, the conjecture asserts a universal bound of \(c(G) = O(\sqrt n)\) on the cop number.
status: The conjecture was proposed in the 1980s. The \(\sqrt n\) scale is necessary, and random graphs satisfy the conjecture (Prałat–Wormald 2016, [Meyniel's conjecture holds for random graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/1301.2841)), but the universal bound remains open.
solved_when: There exist constants \(C\) and \(n_0\) such that every connected graph \(G\) on \(n \ge n_0\) vertices has cop number at most \(C\sqrt n\).
why: It would pin down the sharp universal pursuit resource requirement: the \(\sqrt n\) scale cannot be improved in general, so the conjecture gives the correct order of cops needed in the worst case.
key_works: Prałat–Wormald (2016), [*Meyniel’s conjecture holds for random graphs*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1301.2841).

title: Harary–Hill crossing-number conjecture
subfield: Graph parameters and topological graph theory
open: What is the minimum number of crossings required to draw the complete graph on \(n\) vertices in the plane? The Harary–Hill conjecture asserts that \(\operatorname{cr}(K_n)=\frac14\lfloor n/2\rfloor\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor\lfloor(n-2)/2\rfloor\lfloor(n-3)/2\rfloor\).
status: Proposed in the 1960s, the conjecture remains open. Drawings of \(K_n\) achieving the conjectured number of crossings are known, so the formula gives an upper bound, and the matching lower bound has been established for substantial restricted drawing classes, including shellable drawings (Ábrego–Aichholzer–Fernández-Merchant–Ramos–Salazar 2013, [*Shellable drawings and the cylindrical crossing number of \(K_n\)*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1309.3665)).
solved_when: The formula \(\frac14\lfloor n/2\rfloor\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor\lfloor(n-2)/2\rfloor\lfloor(n-3)/2\rfloor\) is proved to equal \(\operatorname{cr}(K_n)\) for all \(n\), or a counterexample drawing with fewer crossings is exhibited.
why: It pins down the unavoidable crossings in complete interconnection networks, the exact baseline against which drawing and VLSI-type crossing questions are measured.
key_works: Ábrego–Aichholzer–Fernández-Merchant–Ramos–Salazar (2013), [*Shellable drawings and the cylindrical crossing number of \(K_n\)*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1309.3665).

title: Leading constant in \(R(3,t)\)
open: Does the Ramsey number \(R(3,t)\) grow asymptotically as \(c\,t^2/\log t\), and if so, what is the leading constant \(c\)?
status: The order of magnitude was settled in 1995. A 2025–2026 preprint of Hefty–Horn–King–Pfender, [*Improving \(R(3,k)\) in just two bites*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.19718), raises the lower constant to \(1/2\); the upper constant remains one.
solved_when: The asymptotic \(R(3,t)\sim c\,t^2/\log t\) is established and the constant \(c\) is determined.
why: It would precisely quantify how large a triangle-free graph with bounded independence number can be, sharpening the 1995 order-of-magnitude result to an exact leading term.
key_works: Hefty–Horn–King–Pfender, [*Improving \(R(3,k)\) in just two bites*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.19718).

title: Polynomial superlinearity for bounded-degree size-Ramsey numbers
open: Does there exist, for fixed \(\Delta\) and \(\varepsilon>0\), an \(n\)-vertex graph of maximum degree \(\Delta\) whose size-Ramsey number is at least \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\)? Formally: can bounded local complexity force a polynomial overhead beyond the trivial linear lower bound in the size-Ramsey setting?
status: Linear growth is false: known subcubic constructions achieve size-Ramsey numbers \(n\exp(c\sqrt{\log n})\), which is superlinear but still subpolynomial. See Tikhomirov (2024), [*On bounded degree graphs with large size-Ramsey numbers*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.05818).
solved_when: For some fixed \(\Delta\ge 1\) and \(\varepsilon>0\), an explicit or probabilistic construction of \(n\)-vertex graphs with maximum degree \(\Delta\) and size-Ramsey number at least \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\) is given (or the question is resolved negatively for all such \(\Delta,\varepsilon\)).
why: It tests whether bounded local complexity can force polynomial hosting overhead, separating polynomial from merely superlinear growth in size-Ramsey numbers.
key_works: Tikhomirov (2024), [*On bounded degree graphs with large size-Ramsey numbers*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.05818).

bib.title: Polynomial superlinearity for bounded-degree size-Ramsey numbers

title: Ramsey multiplicity constant of \(K_4\)
open: What is the minimum asymptotic proportion of monochromatic \(K_4\)'s in any red–blue coloring of the edges of the complete graph? Equivalently, determine the Ramsey multiplicity constant \(c_4 = \lim_{n\to\infty} \min_{\text{colorings of } K_n} k_4(K_n)/\binom{n}{4}\).
status: Thomason refuted the natural random-coloring value \(1/32\) in 1989; current constructions and lower bounds do not coincide. Recent progress appears in Parczyk–Pokutta–Spiegel–Szabó (2025), [*New Ramsey Multiplicity Bounds and Search Heuristics*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.04036).
solved_when: The value of \(c_4\) is determined, i.e., a matching construction and lower bound are proved.
why: It measures how abundant monochromatic cliques must be beyond mere Ramsey existence, sharpening quantitative Ramsey theory at its first open case.
key_works: Parczyk–Pokutta–Spiegel–Szabó (2025), [*New Ramsey Multiplicity Bounds and Search Heuristics*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.04036).

title: Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture
open: Must every \(n\)-vertex digraph of minimum outdegree at least \(r\) contain a directed cycle of length at most \(\lceil n/r\rceil\)? Equivalently, is the Caccetta–Häggkvist bound tight: no digraph on \(n\) vertices with minimum outdegree \(r\) can avoid all directed cycles of length \(\lceil n/r\rceil\) or shorter?
status: Proposed in 1978, the conjecture remains open; even the exact triangle threshold near \(n/3\) is unresolved. A related line of attack appears in Aharoni–Berger–Chudnovsky–Guo–Zerbib (2021), [*Non-uniform degrees and rainbow versions of the Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.11183).
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given for the statement above for all \(n\) and \(r\); in particular, resolving the special case \(r = \lfloor n/3\rfloor\), i.e. whether minimum outdegree near \(n/3\) forces a directed triangle, would settle the long-standing central case.
why: It would let one infer short feedback loops from one-sided expansion: a minimum-outdegree condition alone would guarantee a directed cycle of the corresponding short length.
key_works: Aharoni–Berger–Chudnovsky–Guo–Zerbib (2021), [*Non-uniform degrees and rainbow versions of the Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.11183).

title: Hoàng–Reed directed cactus conjecture
open: Must every digraph of minimum outdegree \(d\) contain directed cycles \(C_1,\ldots,C_d\) such that each \(C_i\) meets the union of its predecessors in at most one vertex?
status: The conjecture was proposed in the 1980s and remains open in general; the cases through \(d=3\) are known, the case \(\delta^+=3\) being settled by Welhan (2010), [*The Hoàng–Reed Conjecture for \(\delta^+=3\)*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.disc.2010.03.001).
solved_when: A proof, for every \(d\), that every digraph with minimum outdegree \(d\) contains such a sequence \(C_1,\ldots,C_d\), or a counterexample for some \(d\).
why: A positive answer would guarantee tightly controlled, cactus-like branching arrangements of directed cycles in any digraph of large outdegree, giving structural leverage where general digraphs offer little.
key_works: Welhan (2010), [*The Hoàng–Reed Conjecture for \(\delta^+=3\)*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.disc.2010.03.001).

title: Neumann-Lara’s planar dichromatic conjecture
open: Can every oriented planar graph have its vertex set partitioned into two parts, each inducing an acyclic digraph?
status: The conjecture was proposed in 1985. Many girth-restricted cases are settled, but the statement for arbitrary planar orientations remains open. See Steiner (2019), [*A Note on Graphs of Dichromatic Number 2*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.00351).
solved_when: A proof, or disproof by counterexample, of the statement that every oriented planar graph has dichromatic number at most 2.
why: It would bound the directed cyclic complexity of planar graphs by two layers, giving a directed analogue of planar graph bipartiteness-type structure results.
key_works: Steiner (2019), [*A Note on Graphs of Dichromatic Number 2*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.00351).

title: Erdős–Turán additive-basis conjecture
open: Can an additive basis be too efficient? If every sufficiently large integer is a sum \(a+b\) with \(a,b\) from a set \(A\subseteq\mathbb N_0\), must the number of ordered representations of \(n\) as \(a+b\) grow without bound as \(n\to\infty\)? Formally, is it impossible for the ordered representation function \(r_{A+A}(n)\) to stay bounded?
status: Conjectured by Erdős and Turán in 1941 and open since. Known fixed lower bounds on representation counts, including the bound of eight, do not establish unboundedness. See Borwein–Choi–Chu (2006), [*An old conjecture of Erdős–Turán on additive bases*](https://www.sfu.ca/~schoia/paper/erdos.pdf). A historical Erdős prize of US$500 was attached; current administration is unverified. The question connects to Hardy–Littlewood's binary Goldbach asymptotic formula.
solved_when: A proof that for every \(A\subseteq\mathbb N_0\) such that every sufficiently large integer lies in \(A+A\), the ordered representation counts \(r_{A+A}(n)\) are unbounded (or, disproof: a construction of such a basis with bounded representation counts).
why: It would rule out the possibility of an additive basis with uniformly sparse representations, settling whether a basis must be "redundant" at large values.
key_works: Borwein–Choi–Chu (2006), [*An old conjecture of Erdős–Turán on additive bases*](https://www.sfu.ca/~schoia/paper/erdos.pdf).
prize: Historical Erdős offer: US$500; current administration unverified.

title: Sharp four-term progression bounds
open: How large can a subset of the integers up to \(N\) be before it must contain a nontrivial four-term arithmetic progression? Formally, determine the asymptotic scale of \(r_4(N)\).
status: Density convergence for four-term progressions was proved in 1969. The best verified quantitative benchmark is \(r_4(N)\ll N(\log N)^{-c}\), due to Green–Tao (2017), [*New bounds for Szemerédi’s theorem, III: A polylogarithmic bound for \(r_4(N)\)*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.01703), which remains far from the known constructions.
solved_when: The asymptotic order of \(r_4(N)\) is determined up to constants (in particular, closing the gap between the known upper bound \(r_4(N)\ll N(\log N)^{-c}\) and the known constructions).
why: It isolates the first major quantitative gap in Szemerédi-type bounds where quadratic structure governs the answer, so a sharp result would reveal how higher-order Fourier behavior truly constrains progressions.
key_works: Green–Tao (2017), [*New bounds for Szemerédi’s theorem, III: A polylogarithmic bound for \(r_4(N)\)*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.01703).

title: Sharp Szemerédi bounds for longer progressions
open: What is the true asymptotic size of \(r_k(N)\), the largest density avoiding \(k\)-term arithmetic progressions, for each fixed \(k\ge5\)? In other words, determine the correct asymptotic scale of \(r_k(N)\) for fixed \(k\ge5\).
status: Existence of such progressions in dense sets was settled in 1975 (Szemerédi's theorem). The best quantitative bounds are due to Leng–Sah–Sawhney (2024), [*Improved Bounds for Szemerédi's Theorem*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17995), who give \(r_k(N)\) bounded above by \(N\exp[-(\log\log N)^{c_k}]\); a large gap remains between this and the conjectured truth.
solved_when: For each fixed \(k\ge5\), the asymptotic order of \(r_k(N)\) is determined up to constants in the exponent, closing the large gap between the current upper bound \(N\exp[-(\log\log N)^{c_k}]\) and known lower bounds.
why: A solution would make higher-order Fourier analysis quantitatively predictive, yielding usable numerical bounds for the density of sets lacking long arithmetic progressions.
key_works: Leng–Sah–Sawhney (2024), [*Improved Bounds for Szemerédi’s Theorem*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17995).

bib.title: Sharp Szemerédi bounds for longer progressions

title: Sharp corners bounds
open: How large can a subset of the \(N\times N\) grid be if it contains no corner, i.e., no triple \((x,y),(x+d,y),(x,y+d)\) with \(d\ne0\)? Determine the maximum size of \(A\subset[N]^2\) avoiding such configurations.
status: The corners theorem originates with Ajtai–Szemerédi (1974). A 2025 theorem of Jaber–Liu–Lovett–Ostuni–Sawhney, [*Quasipolynomial bounds for the corners theorem*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.07006), gives density at most \(\exp[-(\log N)^{\Omega(1)}]\).
solved_when: The maximum size of a corner-free set \(A\subset[N]^2\) is determined up to constant factors in the exponent; in particular, matching the current upper bound density \(\exp[-(\log N)^{\Omega(1)}]\) with a construction of the same shape.
why: The corners problem is the basic multidimensional Szemerédi-type avoidance question, and its bounds directly govern the three-party Number-on-Forehead communication complexity of Exactly-N, so sharp bounds transfer between combinatorics and communication complexity.
key_works: Jaber–Liu–Lovett–Ostuni–Sawhney (2025), [*Quasipolynomial bounds for the corners theorem*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.07006).

title: Quantitative density Hales–Jewett
open: How large must the dimension be before every density-\(\delta\) subset of \([k]^N\) is forced to contain a combinatorial line? Formally, determine the least dimension \(N(k,\delta)\) with this guarantee.
status: Existence of such a dimension was proved in 1991. For three letters, the D. H. J. Polymath project (2009/2012, [*A new proof of the density Hales–Jewett theorem*](https://arxiv.org/abs/0910.3926)) gives a tower of height \(O(\delta^{-3})\); matching scales remain remote.
solved_when: An explicit value, or tight upper and lower bounds, for the least dimension \(N(k,\delta)\) forcing a combinatorial line in every density-\(\delta\) subset of \([k]^N\).
why: It quantifies a foundational density and recurrence principle, turning a qualitative existence statement into a usable finite bound.
key_works: D. H. J. Polymath (2009/2012), [*A new proof of the density Hales–Jewett theorem*](https://arxiv.org/abs/0910.3926).

title: Hindman’s mixed sum–product quadruple
open: Must every finite coloring of the natural numbers contain two distinct numbers x and y such that x, y, x+y, and xy all share the same color? The challenge is to prove this for arbitrary finite colorings, where the required monochromatic configuration mixes additive and multiplicative structure simultaneously.
status: Posed in 1979. The two-color case and rational-number analogues are settled; arbitrary finite colorings of the natural numbers remain open. Related recent work includes Richter (2025/2026), *Sums and products in sets of positive density* (https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.00515).
solved_when: A proof that for every finite coloring of \(\mathbb{N}\) there exist distinct \(x, y\) with \(x\), \(y\), \(x+y\), and \(xy\) all the same color; equivalently, a counterexample coloring for some finite number of colors refuting the statement.
why: The configuration demands simultaneous additive and multiplicative recurrence, the two structures that current Ramsey-theoretic tools typically handle separately; a solution would advance understanding of colorings that mix both.
key_works: Richter (2025/2026), [*Sums and products in sets of positive density*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.00515).

title: Arbitrarily large finite sums-and-products configurations
open: For every finite coloring of the natural numbers and every \(k\), must there exist \(k\) distinct numbers such that all nonempty subset sums and all subset products formed from them share a single color? This asks whether Hindman's theorem can be strengthened to control two algebraic operations simultaneously.
status: Hindman's theorem (1979) settles the additive side with one infinite set; the rational analogue of this problem is proved (Alweiss, *Monochromatic Sums and Products over \(\mathbb Q\)*), but the version demanding one infinite set of numbers is false. A density approach is pursued by Richter.
solved_when: For every finite coloring of \(\mathbb N\) and every positive integer \(k\), one exhibits \(k\) distinct natural numbers whose nonempty subset sums and products are monochromatic.
why: It probes how far the additive and multiplicative structures of \(\mathbb N\) can be forced to be compatible under a single coloring, a central tension in arithmetic combinatorics.
key_works: Alweiss (2023/2026), [*Monochromatic Sums and Products over \(\mathbb Q\)*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.08901); Richter, [density approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.00515).

title: Chvátal’s hereditary-family conjecture
open: In every finite hereditary family of sets containing a nonempty set, must some maximum-size intersecting subfamily form a star — that is, consist of sets all sharing a common element?
status: Proposed by Chvátal in 1974. Many structured hereditary families are settled, including the uniform case treated by Kupavskii (2023, [uniform hereditary families](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.02246)), building on Chvátal's original paper *Intersecting families of edges in hypergraphs having the hereditary property*; the unrestricted nonuniform case remains open.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given for the unrestricted, nonuniform case: every finite hereditary family containing a nonempty set has a maximum intersecting subfamily that is a star.
why: It would extend the Erdős–Ko–Rado theorem beyond uniform set systems to arbitrary down-sets, giving a universal star-maximality principle for intersecting families.
key_works: Chvátal (1974), *Intersecting families of edges in hypergraphs having the hereditary property*; Kupavskii (2023), [uniform hereditary families](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.02246).

title: Additive-square avoidance
open: Does there exist an infinite word over a finite integer alphabet that contains no additive square — that is, no pair of consecutive blocks of equal length and equal sum? In other words, can additive-square avoidance be achieved over some finite integer alphabet?
status: The problem was posed around 2000 and remains open in the one-dimensional square case. Additive cubes can be avoided, and a two-dimensional alphabet analogue of the problem is settled; only the one-dimensional additive squares remain unresolved. A Lebesgue variant of the additive square problem is treated by Vukusic (2025), [*A Lebesgue variant of the additive square problem*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.21200).
solved_when: An explicit (or existence proof of an) infinite word over a finite integer alphabet in which no two consecutive blocks of the same length have the same sum is given; the problem is resolved negatively if such avoidance is shown impossible over every finite integer alphabet.
why: It separates arithmetic repetition from exact repetition and anagram repetition, testing whether the usual hierarchy of repetition avoidance survives when equality of blocks is replaced by equality of sums.
key_works: Vukusic (2025), [*A Lebesgue variant of the additive square problem*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.21200).

title: Mäkelä’s ternary abelian-square conjecture
open: Does there exist an infinite word over a ternary alphabet whose only abelian-square factors are 00, 11, and 22 — or is every infinite ternary word forced to contain some other abelian square?
status: Open for decades. Avoidance of all sufficiently long abelian squares over ternary alphabets is known, but this sharp restriction is not settled. The problem is stated as Conjecture 20 in Fici–Puzynina (2023), [*Abelian Combinatorics on Words: a Survey*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.09937).
solved_when: An explicit construction of an infinite ternary word whose abelian-square factors are exactly \(00,11,22\), or a proof that no such word exists.
why: It pins down an exact boundary between alphabet size and unavoidable abelian repetition, sharpening what is known about avoidance of repeated structure in words.
key_works: Fici–Puzynina (2023), [*Abelian Combinatorics on Words: a Survey*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.09937), Conjecture 20.

title: Additive cubes on \(\{0,1,2,3\}\)
open: Does there exist an infinite word over the alphabet \(\{0,1,2,3\}\) containing no three consecutive blocks of equal length whose sums of letters are all equal? Formally, is the additive cube avoidable over this four-letter alphabet?
status: Explicitly open as of 2025. For other four-element integer alphabets outside the arithmetic-progression equivalence class, avoiding constructions are known. See Andrade–Mol (2025), [*Avoiding abelian and additive powers in rich words*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.15390).
solved_when: An explicit infinite word on \(\{0,1,2,3\}\) avoiding additive cubes is constructed, or a proof is given that no such word exists.
why: It completes the classification of additive-cube avoidability for four-letter integer alphabets, which is otherwise settled.
key_works: Andrade–Mol (2025), [*Avoiding abelian and additive powers in rich words*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.15390).

title: Kolakoski density
open: Does the symbol 1 occur with limiting frequency 1/2 in the Kolakoski sequence, the self-run-length sequence beginning \(122112122\ldots\)? That is, does the natural density of positions holding a 1 converge to \(1/2\)?
status: The problem dates to Oldenburger (1939) and was popularized by Kolakoski (1965). Even the existence of the limit is unproved, though liminf and limsup are tightly constrained. Chvátal (1993/1994), *Notes on the Kolakoski Sequence* ([link](https://archive.dimacs.rutgers.edu/TechnicalReports/abstracts/1993/93-84.html)), is a key reference; related work concerns unique ergodicity of the Kolakoski symbolic system.
solved_when: The limiting frequency of the symbol 1 in the Kolakoski sequence is proved to exist and equal \(1/2\).
why: It tests whether a simple self-referential process obeys the statistical regularity one expects, despite the sequence being defined by its own run lengths.
key_works: Chvátal (1993/1994), [*Notes on the Kolakoski Sequence*](https://archive.dimacs.rutgers.edu/TechnicalReports/abstracts/1993/93-84.html).

title: Long even Barker sequences
open: Can a binary Barker sequence have even length greater than four — that is, can a \(\pm 1\) sequence of such length have all its nonzero-shift aperiodic autocorrelations lying in \(\{-1,0,1\}\)? Equivalently, does an ideal binary pulse-compression sequence of even length beyond four exist?
status: Barker introduced these sequences in 1953. Odd lengths beyond thirteen have been excluded, and severe restrictions are known for the even case, but the even-length question remains open; see Willms (2021), [*A note on Barker sequences of even length*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.00502).
solved_when: An explicit binary sequence of even length greater than four whose aperiodic autocorrelations at every nonzero shift lie in \(\{-1,0,1\}\) is exhibited, or a proof is given that no such sequence exists.
why: It decides whether ideal binary pulse-compression sequences — used where sidelobe suppression matters — can be made arbitrarily or substantially longer, or whether length four is an inherent ceiling for the even case.
key_works: Willms (2021), [*A note on Barker sequences of even length*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.00502).

title: Asymptotic binary merit factor
open: What is the largest asymptotic merit factor achievable by binary sequences — that is, what is the value of \(\limsup_n \max_a n^2/(2\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}C_k(a)^2)\) over binary sequences \(a\) with aperiodic autocorrelations \(C_k\)?
status: This is the Littlewood–Golay problem, studied since the 1960s. Known constructions achieve merit factor approximately 6.34206, and even the finiteness of the optimum remains open; see Jedwab–Katz–Schmidt (2013), [*Littlewood Polynomials with Small \(L^4\) Norm*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1205.0260). The problem is related to the Bernasconi-model ground-state energy.
solved_when: The value of this limsup is determined; in particular, it would settle whether the optimum is finite and whether it exceeds the approximately 6.34206 attained by current constructions.
why: It sets the ultimate limit on aggregate sidelobe suppression for long binary signals, governing how well binary sequences can perform in radar and communications applications.
key_works: Jedwab–Katz–Schmidt (2013), [*Littlewood Polynomials with Small \(L^4\) Norm*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1205.0260).

title: Eventual periodicity of finite octal games
open: Does every impartial take-and-break game given by a finite octal code have an eventually periodic Sprague–Grundy sequence? Equivalently, is there, for every finite octal code, a preperiod and period after which the Grundy values of heap positions repeat forever?
status: A longstanding problem of Guy. Many individual octal codes have certified eventual periods, but the universal statement remains open; see Guy–Nowakowski, [*Unsolved problems in combinatorial games*](https://library.slmath.org/books/Book71/files/GONC6-04.pdf), and Dailly–Duchêne–Larsson–Paris (2020), [*Partition games*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.02621).
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given for the universal statement: for every finite octal game, there exist preperiod length $N$ and period $p$ such that $g(n+p) = g(n)$ for all $n \geq N$.
why: Eventual periodicity would collapse the infinitely many heap positions of any finite octal game into a finite strategy table, making optimal play computable from finite data; a counterexample would reveal structurally new behavior in take-and-break games.
key_works: Dailly–Duchêne–Larsson–Paris (2020), [*Partition games*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.02621); Guy–Nowakowski, [*Unsolved problems in combinatorial games*](https://library.slmath.org/books/Book71/files/GONC6-04.pdf) (edition year verify).

title: Infinite three-dimensional Chomp
open: Who wins the game of three-dimensional Chomp played from the infinite box \(\mathbb N_0^3\) with a poisoned origin, where a move deletes a chosen point together with every coordinatewise larger point? Determine, with proof, the winning player and a winning strategy from \(\mathbb N_0^3\).
status: Gale's question remains unresolved; the strategy-stealing argument that settles finite boards does not decide this infinite position. The problem appears as D1 in Guy–Nowakowski's list of open game problems. Gale's historical offer of US$300 stands, though its current administration is unverified.
solved_when: A proof identifies the first or second player as the winner from \(\mathbb N_0^3\) (poisoned origin, moves deleting a chosen point and all coordinatewise larger points) and supplies the corresponding winning strategy.
why: It tests whether winning strategies can be extracted from the well-founded structure of an infinite position, a setting where the classical finite-board strategy-stealing argument does not decide the outcome.
key_works: Gale (1974), *A curious Nim-type game*; Guy–Nowakowski, [open game problems](https://library.slmath.org/books/Book71/files/GONC6-04.pdf), D1.
prize: Historical Gale offer: US$300; current administration unverified.

title: Exact logical strength of Hindman’s theorem
open: How much set-existence strength does Hindman's finite-sums theorem actually require? Formally, determine its reverse-mathematical strength over \(\mathsf{RCA}_0\), and in particular whether \(\mathsf{ACA}_0\) suffices to prove it.
status: Blass–Hirst–Simpson (1987), in *Logical analysis of some theorems of combinatorics and topological dynamics*, placed Hindman's theorem strictly between \(\mathsf{ACA}_0\) and \(\mathsf{ACA}_0^+\) in strength, and this gap remains open; Carlucci et al. (2020) have studied restricted Hindman principles ([arXiv:1701.06095](https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.06095)).
solved_when: The theorem is proven (or refuted) in \(\mathsf{ACA}_0\), or otherwise shown equivalent to a known subsystem, closing the gap between \(\mathsf{ACA}_0\) and \(\mathsf{ACA}_0^+\).
why: A precise calibration identifies exactly which infinitary resources this fundamental theorem of infinitary combinatorics needs, sharpening the boundary between constructive and stronger set-existence principles.
key_works: Blass–Hirst–Simpson (1987), *Logical analysis of some theorems of combinatorics and topological dynamics*; Carlucci et al. (2020), [restricted Hindman principles](https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.06095).

title: Positive combinatorial rule for Kronecker coefficients
open: Is there a uniform combinatorial rule that computes every symmetric-group Kronecker coefficient \(g_{\lambda\mu\nu}\) as the count of explicitly defined finite objects? In other words, a positive formula — no alternating signs or cancellations — valid for arbitrary partitions \(\lambda, \mu, \nu\).
status: The problem has been open for decades. Combinatorial rules are known only for special families of partitions; recent results covering two-row and rectangular shapes do not extend to arbitrary partitions.
solved_when: A rule is given that, for all partitions \(\lambda, \mu, \nu\), produces a finite set of explicitly constructed combinatorial objects whose cardinality equals \(g_{\lambda\mu\nu}\), with the construction uniform across all shapes.
why: It would explain tensor-product multiplicities of symmetric-group representations by direct counting, eliminating the cancellations inherent in current character-based computations.
key_works: Pak–Panova–Swanson (2025), [*A combinatorial interpretation for certain plethysm and Kronecker coefficients*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.02312).

bib.title: Positive combinatorial rule for Kronecker coefficients

title: Positive combinatorial rule for plethysm
open: Is there a general positive combinatorial rule for the Schur coefficients in the plethysm \(s_\lambda[s_\mu]\)? That is, a formula expressing each coefficient as the number of combinatorial objects of a prescribed shape, valid for all partitions \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\).
status: A longstanding open problem; the available rules all impose restrictions on the outer partition, the inner partition, or the target partition. Recent work includes Pak–Panova–Swanson (2025), [*A combinatorial interpretation for certain plethysm and Kronecker coefficients*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.02312); the problem is related to orbit-closure equations in geometric complexity theory.
solved_when: A positive combinatorial formula for the Schur expansion of \(s_\lambda[s_\mu]\) is given that holds for arbitrary outer and inner partitions and arbitrary target partition, without restriction.
why: It would make multiplicities of composed symmetric-group and GL representations structurally understandable rather than computable only by recursion or symmetric-function identities.
key_works: Pak–Panova–Swanson (2025), [*A combinatorial interpretation for certain plethysm and Kronecker coefficients*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.02312).

title: Stanley’s Jack Littlewood–Richardson positivity
open: Do Jack symmetric functions yield a positive Littlewood–Richardson rule? Specifically, is the scalar product \(\langle J_\mu^{(\alpha)}J_\nu^{(\alpha)},J_\lambda^{(\alpha)}\rangle_\alpha\) a polynomial in \(\alpha\) with nonnegative integer coefficients, under the integral Jack normalization with \(\langle p_\rho,p_\sigma\rangle_\alpha=\delta_{\rho\sigma}z_\rho\alpha^{\ell(\rho)}\)?
status: Proposed by Stanley in 1989. Special parameters and particular families of partitions are understood, but the general positivity statement remains open in the 2026 literature; recent work includes Cuenca–Dołęga's Jack generating functions. Key works: Stanley (1989), [*Some combinatorial properties of Jack symmetric functions*](https://doi.org/10.1016/0001-8708(89)90015-7); Cuenca–Dołęga, [Jack generating functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.13098).
solved_when: A proof (or disproof, via an explicit negative coefficient) of nonnegative integrality of the polynomial \(\langle J_\mu^{(\alpha)}J_\nu^{(\alpha)},J_\lambda^{(\alpha)}\rangle_\alpha\) is given for all partitions \(\mu,\nu,\lambda\).
why: A positive formula would give a deformed Littlewood–Richardson rule — positive multiplication and convolution laws at the Jack level, extending the classical story for Schur functions.
key_works: Stanley (1989), [*Some combinatorial properties of Jack symmetric functions*](https://doi.org/10.1016/0001-8708(89)90015-7); Cuenca–Dołęga, [Jack generating functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.13098).

title: Combinatorial Schur expansion of modified Macdonald polynomials
open: Is there an explicit combinatorial rule that computes every coefficient \(\widetilde K_{\lambda\mu}(q,t)\) in the Schur expansion of the modified Macdonald polynomial \(\widetilde H_\mu\) as a positive weighted sum over discrete objects?
status: Haiman proved positivity geometrically in 2001 via Hilbert schemes and polygraphs, resolving the Macdonald positivity conjecture; a general positive combinatorial rule remains missing. Assaf (2018), [*Toward the Schur Expansion of Macdonald Polynomials*](https://doi.org/10.37236/7419), represents progress toward such a rule.
solved_when: A general positive combinatorial formula is given for all \(\widetilde K_{\lambda\mu}(q,t)\), valid for every pair of partitions \(\lambda, \mu\), with each coefficient realized as a generating function over explicitly described structures.
why: It would explain the two-parameter multiplicities appearing in the Schur expansion through concrete discrete objects, turning Haiman's geometric positivity into an effective, structural counting rule.
key_works: Haiman (2001), *Hilbert schemes, polygraphs and the Macdonald positivity conjecture*; Assaf (2018), [*Toward the Schur Expansion of Macdonald Polynomials*](https://doi.org/10.37236/7419).

title: Exact type-\(B\) diagonal-coinvariant dimensions
open: What is the dimension and bigraded character of the diagonal coinvariant ring for the type-\(B\) Weyl group, \(\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_n,y_1,\ldots,y_n]/\langle\mathbb C[x,y]^{B_n}_+\rangle\)? In other words, can one give an exact formula for this ring, refining the known lower bounds into a full dimension and character computation?
status: The problem has been studied since the 1990s. The familiar \((2n+1)^n\) lower bound is not exact in general, and existing improved lower bounds lack matching dimension formulas. Recent work includes Ajila–Griffeth (2024), [*Representation theory and the diagonal coinvariant ring of the type B Weyl group*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.03077).
solved_when: An exact formula for the dimension of the ring (as a function of \(n\)), together with its full bigraded character, is established.
why: It is a sharp test of how the well-understood type-\(A\) diagonal coinvariant phenomena extend to other reflection groups, and exact dimensions would anchor the combinatorics of type-\(B\) harmonic analysis.
key_works: Ajila–Griffeth (2024), [*Representation theory and the diagonal coinvariant ring of the type B Weyl group*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.03077).

title: General positive Schubert multiplication rule
open: Is there a uniform combinatorial rule that counts, by explicit discrete objects, every Schubert structure constant \(c_{uv}^w\) for the cohomology ring of the complete flag variety? A positive formula should apply to all triples of permutations at once, not case by case.
status: Open for decades despite the geometric nonnegativity of the constants; many special descent and permutation classes already have positive rules, e.g. Gao–Zhu (2024/2025) on Boolean Schubert structure coefficients and Pak–Robichaux (2025) on signed interpretations, but no rule covers the general case.
solved_when: A single rule, valid for all permutations \(u, v, w\), exhibits \(c_{uv}^w\) as the cardinality of an explicitly described finite set of combinatorial objects.
why: It would turn the calculation of intersection multiplicities in the complete flag variety into direct counting, replacing indirect algebraic or geometric computation with concrete discrete objects.
key_works: Gao–Zhu (2024/2025), [*Boolean Schubert Structure Coefficients*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.05527); Pak–Robichaux (2025), [signed interpretations](https://doi.org/10.5802/alco.413).

title: BBDVW recurrence for arbitrary Bruhat intervals
open: Does the BBDVW recurrence — the hypercube decomposition — hold for the Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials of arbitrary Bruhat intervals in symmetric groups? In other words, can the recurrence established for lower intervals \([e,v]\) be extended to intervals \([u,v]\) with arbitrary lower endpoint?
status: The problem was introduced in 2021. The recurrence is settled for lower intervals \([e,v]\) by Barkley–Gaetz (2026), [*The BBDVW Conjecture for Kazhdan–Lusztig Polynomials of Lower Intervals*](https://doi.org/10.1093/imrn/rnag022); intervals with arbitrary lower endpoints remain open.
solved_when: The hypercube-decomposition recurrence for Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials is proved for every Bruhat interval \([u,v]\) in a symmetric group, with no restriction on the lower endpoint.
why: It would give a concrete recursive route toward combinatorial invariance of Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials for the symmetric groups.
key_works: Barkley–Gaetz (2026), [*The BBDVW Conjecture for Kazhdan–Lusztig Polynomials of Lower Intervals*](https://doi.org/10.1093/imrn/rnag022).

title: Exact enumeration of \(1324\)-avoiders
open: Is there a usable exact formula — a generating function or structural recurrence — for the number of permutations avoiding the pattern 1324 of each length? This is the last length-four single pattern whose enumeration remains out of reach.
status: The outstanding length-four single-pattern enumeration problem. Recent inversion-refined formulas by Linusson–Verkama (2025), [*Enumerating 1324-Avoiders with Few Inversions*](https://doi.org/10.37236/13387), cover only part of the parameter range.
solved_when: An exact generating function, or a structural recurrence computing the count of 1324-avoiding permutations of every length, is established for the full parameter range, not just part of it.
why: It would settle the outstanding length-four enumeration problem and test the limits of permutation-class decomposition, since none of the existing techniques extends across the whole range.
key_works: Linusson–Verkama (2025), [*Enumerating 1324-Avoiders with Few Inversions*](https://doi.org/10.37236/13387).

title: \(1324\) Stanley–Wilf limit
open: What is the exact value of the Stanley–Wilf limit for the pattern \(1324\), the last of the length-four patterns whose growth constant remains unknown? Formally, determine \(L(1324)=\lim_n|\operatorname{Av}_n(1324)|^{1/n}\).
status: The existence of the limit is proved. The best verified bounds as of 2025 are \(10.271<L(1324)<13.5\); key works include Bevan (2015), *Permutations avoiding 1324 and patterns in Łukasiewicz paths* (arXiv:1406.2890), and Linusson–Verkama (2025), inversion-refined enumeration (doi:10.37236/13387).
solved_when: An exact value, or arbitrarily tight bounds, for \(L(1324)\) is established, improving on the verified interval \(10.271<L(1324)<13.5\) reported in 2025.
why: It supplies a concrete unresolved entropy constant for pattern-avoiding permutations, and its resolution would likely require new techniques for lower bounds that could transfer to other permutation classes.
key_works: Bevan (2015), [*Permutations avoiding 1324 and patterns in Łukasiewicz paths*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.2890); Linusson–Verkama (2025), [inversion-refined enumeration](https://doi.org/10.37236/13387).

title: Inversion-refined monotonicity for \(1324\)-avoiders
open: Is the number of \(1324\)-avoiding permutations on \(n\) letters with exactly \(k\) inversions always at most the corresponding number on \(n+1\) letters with the same inversion count — that is, does \(\operatorname{av}_n^k(1324)\le\operatorname{av}_{n+1}^k(1324)\) hold for all \(n\) and \(k\)?
status: Proposed in 2012 by Claesson–Jelínek–Steingrímsson (*Upper bounds for the Stanley–Wilf limit of 1324 and other layered patterns*); the inequality is verified in the region \(n\ge(k+7)/2\), with recent progress due to Linusson–Verkama (2025), [recent progress](https://doi.org/10.37236/13387).
solved_when: The inequality \(\operatorname{av}_n^k(1324)\le\operatorname{av}_{n+1}^k(1324)\) is proved for every \(n,k\), or a counterexample is exhibited; a full proof would yield an improved growth upper bound of approximately \(13.002\).
why: A proof converts this refined monotonicity into a global improvement of the enumeration-based upper bound for the Stanley–Wilf limit of \(1324\).
key_works: Claesson–Jelínek–Steingrímsson (2012), *Upper bounds for the Stanley–Wilf limit of 1324 and other layered patterns*; Linusson–Verkama (2025), [recent progress](https://doi.org/10.37236/13387).

title: Rank-unimodality of permutation-pattern intervals
open: In the poset of permutations ordered by (classical) pattern containment, do the rank numbers of every finite interval always form a unimodal sequence? Formally, if the interval [σ, π] has exactly r_k elements of rank k, must r_0 ≤ r_1 ≤ ⋯ ≤ r_m ≤ ⋯ hold up to a peak and then decrease?
status: McNamara–Steingrímsson (2015), [*On the topology of the permutation pattern poset*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcta.2015.02.009). The analogue for consecutive pattern containment is known to hold; the ordinary containment case remains unresolved.
solved_when: A proof that for every pair of permutations σ ≤ π, the rank-generating sequence of the interval [σ, π] is unimodal, or an explicit counterexample interval whose rank sequence fails to be unimodal.
why: The intervals of this poset can have complicated, irregular topology, and a positive answer would show that a strong numerical regularity persists through that complexity, constraining how wild such intervals can be.
key_works: McNamara–Steingrímsson (2015), [*On the topology of the permutation pattern poset*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcta.2015.02.009).

title: Two unrestricted stacks in series
open: Can we count the permutations sortable by passing through two stacks in series, where each stack may be operated freely at any time? A generating function, or even the asymptotic growth rate of this class of permutations, would answer the question.
status: Studied since Tarjan's 1972 work on sorting with networks of queues and stacks. The problem remains distinct from the solved enumeration for two iterations of West's deterministic stack-sorting map, which imposes a fixed operating discipline rather than unrestricted choices.
solved_when: The generating function (or asymptotic enumeration) for permutations sortable by some sequence of operations through two unrestricted stacks in series is determined.
why: It measures the power of a minimal compositional storage model — two elementary buffers composed in series — which is a basic benchmark for what restricted storage can sort.
key_works: Tarjan (1972), *Sorting Using Networks of Queues and Stacks*; [*Permutations sortable by two stacks in series*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1510.08663).

title: Real-rooted Durfee polynomials
open: Is the Durfee polynomial \(D_n(z)=\sum_d p(n,d)z^d\) — where \(p(n,d)\) counts partitions of \(n\) with Durfee-square side \(d\) — real-rooted for every \(n\)?
status: Conjectured in 1998 by Canfield–Corteel–Savage in [*Durfee Polynomials*](https://doi.org/10.37236/1370). Asymptotic normality and extensive numerical evidence support the conjecture but do not establish real-rootedness.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof with explicit counterexample) that all roots of \(D_n(z)\) are real for every \(n\).
why: Real-rootedness would impose strong regularity on the full Durfee-size distribution, beyond what asymptotic normality alone provides.
key_works: Canfield–Corteel–Savage (1998), [*Durfee Polynomials*](https://doi.org/10.37236/1370).

title: Gabow’s serial symmetric exchange conjecture
open: Given two disjoint bases of a matroid, can the elements be ordered so that swapping the two bases element-by-element in tandem keeps every intermediate pair a pair of bases? Formally, is there a sequence of symmetric exchanges realizing a serial exchange between the two bases?
status: Conjectured by Gabow in 1976 ("Decomposing symmetric exchanges in matroid bases"). The regular-matroid case is settled, per Bérczi–Mátravölgyi–Schwarcz (2026), ["Reconfiguration of basis pairs in regular matroids"](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jctb.2025.10.009). The general statement remains open and survives recent counterexamples to stronger exchange properties.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) for arbitrary matroids of the existence of such an ordering; the regular-matroid case is already done, so the criterion is settling the general statement.
why: A positive answer would yield exceptionally short feasible reconfiguration paths between basis pairs.
key_works: Gabow (1976), *Decomposing symmetric exchanges in matroid bases*; Bérczi–Mátravölgyi–Schwarcz (2026), [*Reconfiguration of basis pairs in regular matroids*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jctb.2025.10.009).

title: Cyclic orderability of uniformly dense matroids
open: When must a matroid's ground set admit a cyclic ordering in which every window of \(r(E)\) consecutive elements is a basis? Specifically, if a matroid on \(E\) is uniformly dense — \(|E|\,r(X)\ge r(E)\,|X|\) for all \(X\subseteq E\) — is its ground set always cyclically orderable this way?
status: The problem dates to Kajitani–Ueno–Miyano in the 1980s. Cyclic orderability is known for coprime size/rank, sparse-paving matroids, and further special cases; see Bérczi–Jánosik–Mátravölgyi (2026), [*Cyclic Ordering of Split Matroids*](https://doi.org/10.37236/13537).
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) that every matroid satisfying \(|E|\,r(X)\ge r(E)\,|X|\) for all \(X\subseteq E\) admits a cyclic ordering of \(E\) in which every \(r(E)\) consecutive elements form a basis.
why: It would turn a fractional density condition into a concrete sliding-window independence structure, giving bases uniformly along the ordering rather than merely on average.
key_works: Bérczi–Jánosik–Mátravölgyi (2026), [*Cyclic Ordering of Split Matroids*](https://doi.org/10.37236/13537).

title: Infinite matroid intersection
open: Does every pair of matroids on a common ground set, possibly infinite, admit a common independent set whose natural closures cover the ground set? Formally, for arbitrary matroids \(M,N\) on possibly infinite \(E\), must there exist a common independent \(I=I_M\sqcup I_N\) with \(\operatorname{cl}_M(I_M)\cup\operatorname{cl}_N(I_N)=E\)?
status: The problem traces to Nash-Williams, around 1990. Significant special cases have been proved and new augmentation tools developed, but the unrestricted statement remains open; see Bowler (2018, [survey](https://matroidunion.org/?p=2374)) and Joó (2025, [*Hindrance from a wasteful common independent set*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.04342)).
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) of the unrestricted statement for arbitrary — possibly infinite — matroids \(M,N\) on a common ground set \(E\).
why: It would extend min–max duality beyond arguments that rely on finite cardinality, opening intersection-type dualities to the infinite setting.
key_works: Bowler (2018), [survey](https://matroidunion.org/?p=2374); Joó (2025), [*Hindrance from a wasteful common independent set*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.04342).

title: Almost all matroids are sparse paving
open: Do almost all matroids have a sparse paving structure? Formally, prove that \(s_n/m_n\to1\), where \(s_n\) counts labelled sparse paving matroids on \(n\) elements and \(m_n\) all labelled matroids on \(n\) elements.
status: The conjecture was formalized in 2011. So far only the weaker logarithmic equivalence \(\log s_n/\log m_n\to1\) is established, due to Pendavingh–van der Pol (2015), [*On the number of matroids compared to the number of sparse paving matroids*](https://research.tue.nl/en/publications/on-the-number-of-matroids-compared-to-the-number-of-sparse-paving-2/). Related to exact asymptotic constant-weight code rates.
solved_when: The limit \(s_n/m_n\to1\) is proved; that is, the labelled sparse paving matroids are shown to make up asymptotically all labelled matroids.
why: A proof would identify the typical finite independence system, making asymptotic questions about matroids tractable by reducing them to the well-understood sparse paving class.
key_works: Pendavingh–van der Pol (2015), [*On the number of matroids compared to the number of sparse paving matroids*](https://research.tue.nl/en/publications/on-the-number-of-matroids-compared-to-the-number-of-sparse-paving-2/).

title: Leading constant in matroid enumeration
open: What is the true asymptotic number \(m_n\) of matroids on \(n\) elements? More precisely, determine \(\log_2 m_n\) to relative error \(1+o(1)\), especially the coefficient of \(n^{-1}\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\) in it.
status: Knuth's lower construction and later upper bounds leave the coefficient between one and \(2+o(1)\); key works are Knuth (1974), *The asymptotic number of geometries*, and Bansal–Pendavingh–van der Pol (2013/2015), [*On the number of matroids*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1206.6270).
solved_when: \(\log_2 m_n\) is known up to relative error \(1+o(1)\), pinning down the leading coefficient of \(n^{-1}\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\).
why: It determines the entropy of finite matroids.
key_works: Knuth (1974), *The asymptotic number of geometries*; Bansal–Pendavingh–van der Pol (2013/2015), [*On the number of matroids*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1206.6270).

title: Hadamard existence conjecture
open: Does a Hadamard matrix exist for every order \(4m\) — that is, for every positive integer \(m\), a \(\{\pm1\}\)-matrix \(H\) of order \(4m\) with \(HH^{\mathsf T}=4mI\)?
status: Usually dated to Paley, 1933. Extensive infinite constructions and finite databases — including the Cati–Pasechnik (2024/2025) database of constructions of Hadamard matrices ([arXiv:2411.18897](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.18897)) — do not establish every admissible order.
solved_when: For every positive integer \(m\), an explicit construction (or existence proof) of a sign matrix \(H\) of order \(4m\) satisfying \(HH^{\mathsf T}=4mI\).
why: Hadamard matrices yield optimal orthogonal signals and optimal determinant bounds, underpinning designs and codes where they exist; the general case remains the central gap.
key_works: Paley (1933), *On orthogonal matrices*; Cati–Pasechnik (2024/2025), [*A database of constructions of Hadamard matrices*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.18897).

title: Skew-Hadamard existence
open: Does there exist, for every order \(4m\), a Hadamard matrix \(H\) that is skew in the sense that \(H+H^{\mathsf T}=2I\)? That is, can the famous Hadamard existence conjecture be strengthened to demand a skew-type representative at every admissible order?

title: Circulant Hadamard conjecture
open: Can a circulant Hadamard matrix exist at any order greater than four, or is four the largest possible order? Equivalently, prove that no circulant Hadamard matrix of order exceeding four exists.
status: The conjecture dates to Ryser in the 1960s and remains open. Arithmetic and field-descent restrictions, developed in work such as Leung–Schmidt (2012), [*New restrictions on possible orders of circulant Hadamard matrices*](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10623-011-9493-1), and Borwein–Mossinghoff (2013), [*Wieferich pairs and Barker sequences, II*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1306.0045), exclude enormous ranges of orders, but universal nonexistence is unproven.
solved_when: A proof that no circulant Hadamard matrix of any order greater than four exists (or, conversely, an explicit construction at some larger order).
why: It would establish a sharp limit on perfectly orthogonal periodic binary signals, settling which cyclic binary sequences can achieve ideal autocorrelation.

title: Ryser’s odd-order transversal conjecture
open: Does every Latin square of odd order contain a full transversal — a set of cells meeting each row, each column, and each symbol exactly once?
status: Conjectured in 1967. Near-transversals and almost-everywhere transversal decompositions do not settle every odd-order square. Key works: Montgomery (2024), [*Transversals in Latin Squares*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.19873); Bowtell–Montgomery (2025), [almost-everywhere decomposition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.05438).
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given for the existence of a full transversal in every Latin square of odd order.
why: A transversal guarantees simultaneous distinctness across rows, columns, and symbols, settling the central structural question about odd-order Latin squares.
key_works: Montgomery (2024), [*Transversals in Latin Squares*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.19873); Bowtell–Montgomery (2025), [almost-everywhere decomposition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.05438).

title: Alon–Tarsi Latin-square parity conjecture
open: Is the signed count of Latin squares of order \(n\) nonzero for every even \(n\)? Equivalently, is the coefficient \([\prod_{ij}x_{ij}](\det X)^n\) nonzero for all even \(n\)?
status: Proposed in 1992 by Alon and Tarsi (*Colorings and orientations of graphs*). The conjecture is currently established for orders \(p-1\) and \(p+1\), where \(p\) is an odd prime. A Weingarten-calculus formulation appears in Xu (2026).
solved_when: A proof (or disproof, via an even \(n\) with vanishing signed sum) is given; the conjecture is confirmed when \([\prod_{ij}x_{ij}](\det X)^n\ne0\) is established for every even \(n\).
why: The conjecture supplies powerful algebraic certificates for the existence of decompositions, turning a combinatorial existence question into a nonzero-coefficient computation.
key_works: Alon–Tarsi (1992), *Colorings and orientations of graphs*; Xu (2026), [Weingarten-calculus formulation](https://escholarship.org/uc/item/6g574562).

title: Minimum critical sets in Latin squares
open: How few entries of a Latin square of order \(n\) can suffice to determine it uniquely? Formally, prove — or disprove — that the smallest minimal uniquely completable partial Latin square of order \(n\) has exactly \(\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor\) entries.
status: The conjecture has stood since 1979. The best known lower bound is a positive constant times \(n^2\), still far from the conjectured coefficient \(1/4\). The problem connects to teaching dimension versus VC dimension, as studied by Hatami–Qian (2016), [*Teaching dimension, VC dimension, and critical sets in Latin squares*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.00032).
solved_when: The minimum size of a minimal uniquely completable partial Latin square of order \(n\) is determined to equal \(\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor\) (or a counterexample establishes a different value).
why: A solution identifies exactly the least information needed to uniquely specify a Latin square, the natural measure of a critical set's true size.
key_works: Hatami–Qian (2016), [*Teaching dimension, VC dimension, and critical sets in Latin squares*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.00032).

title: Finiteness of biplanes
open: Are there only finitely many nontrivial symmetric \(2\)-\((v,k,2)\) designs (biplanes), or do infinitely many exist? Formally, does there exist a constant \(V\) such that no nontrivial biplane has more than \(V\) points?
status: A longstanding fixed-\(\lambda\) design problem. Known examples and symmetry classifications — such as Kaski–Östergård (2008), [There are exactly five biplanes with \(k=11\)](https://doi.org/10.1002/jcd.20145), and the double Hall graph approach of Chen et al. (2025/2026), [arXiv:2502.10903](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.10903) — do not yield any universal bound on \(v\).
solved_when: Either a universal bound on \(v\) for nontrivial symmetric \(2\)-\((v,k,2)\) designs is proved, or an infinite family of such designs is constructed.
why: It would separate the behavior of repeated-pair symmetric designs from the known abundance of projective planes, settling a longstanding fixed-\(\lambda\) question in design theory.
key_works: Kaski–Östergård (2008), [*There are exactly five biplanes with \(k=11\)*](https://doi.org/10.1002/jcd.20145); Chen et al. (2025/2026), [double Hall graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.10903).

title: Existence of \(S(3,5,41)\)
open: Does a Steiner system \(S(3,5,41)\) exist — 1,066 five-element blocks on 41 points with every triple of points contained in exactly one block? Either an explicit construction or a proof of impossibility settles it.
status: The parameter set is a longstanding admissible gap retained in the 2025–2026 construction table; it remains listed as unresolved in Kiermaier–Krčadinac–Wassermann, [*Steiner 3-designs as extensions*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.23483), and the [maintained table](https://web.math.pmf.unizg.hr/~krcko/results/steiner3.html).
solved_when: An explicit set of 1,066 blocks on a 41-point ground set in which every 3-subset appears in exactly one block is exhibited, or a proof that no such system exists is given.
why: It fills one of the earliest unresolved small cases in the census of Steiner 3-designs, directly extending the maintained classification table.
key_works: Kiermaier–Krčadinac–Wassermann, [*Steiner 3-designs as extensions*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.23483); [maintained table](https://web.math.pmf.unizg.hr/~krcko/results/steiner3.html).

title: Prime-power order conjecture
open: Must every finite projective plane have prime-power order, or does a plane of some other order exist?
status: Open for decades. Order ten is excluded (Lam, 1991, *The search for a finite projective plane of order 10*); order twelve remains unresolved despite strong automorphism restrictions (Akiyama–Suetake–Tanaga 2023, [order-twelve restrictions](https://doi.org/10.1002/jcd.21869)).
solved_when: Either a proof shows that every finite projective plane has prime-power order, or an explicit counterexample — a plane of non-prime-power order — is constructed.
why: It asks whether finite-field arithmetic controls the entire existence spectrum of projective planes, so a counterexample would reveal planes arising from a fundamentally different structure.
key_works: Lam (1991), *The search for a finite projective plane of order 10*; Akiyama–Suetake–Tanaka (2023), [order-twelve restrictions](https://doi.org/10.1002/jcd.21869).

title: Uniqueness of prime-order projective planes
open: Is every projective plane of prime order \(p\) isomorphic to the Desarguesian plane \(\mathrm{PG}(2,p)\)? Formally, prove uniqueness at prime orders, or produce a non-Desarguesian plane of prime order.
status: This is a longstanding conjecture. Bagchi (2019), [*A coding theoretic approach to the uniqueness conjecture for projective planes of prime order*](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10623-019-00623-y), obtained coding-theoretic uniqueness results, but these hold only under extra weight-enumerator hypotheses and do not settle the unrestricted statement.
solved_when: Either a proof shows every plane of prime order \(p\) is isomorphic to \(\mathrm{PG}(2,p)\), or an explicit non-Desarguesian example of prime order is constructed.
why: A proof would establish rigidity of finite projective planes at prime orders, showing the Desarguesian plane is the only possibility there.
key_works: Bagchi (2019), [*A coding theoretic approach to the uniqueness conjecture for projective planes of prime order*](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10623-019-00623-y).
