title: Linearity of small minimal blocking sets
open: Must every small minimal \(k\)-blocking set in \(\mathrm{PG}(n,q)\) — one of size below \(3(q^k+1)/2\) — be a linear set over a subfield? In other words, does the smallness of a minimal blocking set force it to arise from the subfield structure of the ambient projective space?
status: Cases built on cubic fields and higher-dimensional reductions are established, but the general statement for arbitrary prime-power \(q\) remains open. Key works include Van de Voorde (2010) on higher-dimensional reductions and Lavrauw–Storme–Van de Voorde (2011) on the cubic-field theorem.
solved_when: It is proved that every minimal \(k\)-blocking set in \(\mathrm{PG}(n,q)\) of size below \(3(q^k+1)/2\) is a linear set over a subfield of \(\mathbb{F}_q\), for all prime powers \(q\).
why: It would show that a purely incidence-geometric condition — being small and minimal — forces a rich algebraic structure, giving subfield linear sets a characterization and a sharp structural dichotomy in finite projective spaces.
key_works: Van de Voorde (2010), [higher-dimensional reductions](https://biblio.ugent.be/publication/2917400); Lavrauw–Storme–Van de Voorde (2011), [cubic-field theorem](https://biblio.ugent.be/publication/1261642).

title: Exact binary rate–distance tradeoff
open: What is the true largest size of a binary error-correcting code? Formally, determine the asymptotic rate \(R_2(\delta)=\limsup_n n^{-1}\log_2 A_2(n,\lceil\delta n\rceil)\) exactly, for every relative distance \(\delta\).
status: The Gilbert–Varshamov lower bounds and linear-programming upper bounds still leave exponential gaps. Coregliano–Jeronimo–Jones–Linial–Loyfer (2026), [*Higher-Order Delsarte Dual LPs: Lifting, Constructions and Completeness*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ITCS.2026.44).
solved_when: A closed-form (or otherwise exact) determination of \(R_2(\delta)\) as a function of \(\delta\), pinning down the exponential growth rate of \(A_2(n,\lceil\delta n\rceil)\) with no exponential gap remaining between upper and lower bounds.
why: It establishes the packing capacity of binary Hamming space — the fundamental limit on how densely binary codes can be — and settles the basic extremal question underlying coding theory.
key_works: Coregliano–Jeronimo–Jones–Linial–Loyfer (2026), [*Higher-Order Delsarte Dual LPs: Lifting, Constructions and Completeness*](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ITCS.2026.44).

title: Extremal binary self-dual code of length 72
open: Does there exist a doubly even self-dual binary code of length 72 with minimum distance 16? Equivalently, construct an extremal self-dual \([72,36,16]\) code or prove that no such code exists.
status: The problem was posed by Sloane in 1973 (Sloane (1973), [*Is there a \((72,36)\), \(d=16\) self-dual code?*](https://doi.org/10.1109/TIT.1973.1054975)). Known examples reach minimum distance 12, and extensive symmetry restrictions have not ruled out distance 16; recent work of Hannusch–Major (2025) on [small automorphism groups](https://www.preprints.org/manuscript/202506.2100) continues this line.
solved_when: Either an explicit \([72,36,16]\) doubly even self-dual binary code is constructed, or a proof is given that no such code exists.
why: It settles a central finite parameter in coding theory whose resolution carries consequences for associated designs and for extremal even unimodular lattices in dimension 72.
key_works: Sloane (1973), [*Is there a \((72,36)\), \(d=16\) self-dual code?*](https://doi.org/10.1109/TIT.1973.1054975); Hannusch–Major (2025), [small automorphism groups](https://www.preprints.org/manuscript/202506.2100).

title: Sharp Erdős distinct-distance bound
open: Does every set of \(n\) points in the plane determine at least on the order of \(n/\sqrt{\log n}\) distinct pairwise distances? Equivalently, is the Erdős distinct-distances conjecture true: the number of distinct distances is \(\Omega(n/\sqrt{\log n})\)?
status: Posed by Erdős in 1946. Guth–Katz (2015), [*On the Erdős distinct distance problem in the plane*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1011.4105), prove an \(\Omega(n/\log n)\) lower bound, while lattice constructions give the conjectured upper scale. Related to Falconer's distance-set conjecture.
solved_when: A proof that any \(n\)-point planar set determines \(\Omega(n/\sqrt{\log n})\) distinct distances, matching the scale achieved by lattice constructions up to constants.
why: It would close the remaining logarithmic gap in planar distance diversity between the known lower bound and the conjectured truth, completing Erdős's founding problem of discrete geometry.
key_works: Guth–Katz (2015), [*On the Erdős distinct distance problem in the plane*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1011.4105).

title: Hadwiger–Nelson problem
open: Determine the chromatic number of the plane when points one unit apart must have different colors.
status: The current interval is five to seven; de Grey established the lower bound five in 2018.
why: Connects finite coloring obstructions to Euclidean geometry.
key_works: de Grey (2018), [*The chromatic number of the plane is at least 5*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.02385).

title: Exact Erdős–Szekeres convex-polygon numbers
open: Does every set of \(2^{k-2}+1\) points in the plane in general position contain \(k\) points in convex position? Formally, is the Erdős–Szekeres conjecture true, i.e., is the exact threshold for forcing a convex \(k\)-gon equal to \(2^{k-2}+1\)?
status: Proposed in 1935. The exact values are known through \(k=6\), and asymptotic bounds of \(2^{k+o(k)}\) are known, but the cases \(k\ge7\) remain open. Key works include Suk (2017), [*On the Erdős–Szekeres convex polygon problem*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.08657), and Holmsen–Mojarrad–Pach–Tardos (2020), [*Two extensions of the Erdős–Szekeres problem*](https://ems.press/journals/jems/articles/17088).
solved_when: For some \(k\ge7\), it is proved that any \(2^{k-2}+1\) planar points in general position contain \(k\) points in convex position (or a counterexample is exhibited); ideally for all \(k\).
why: It pins down the exact unavoidable convex structure in planar point sets, completing the quantitative answer to the founding question of combinatorial geometry.
key_works: Suk (2017), [*On the Erdős–Szekeres convex polygon problem*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.08657); Holmsen–Mojarrad–Pach–Tardos (2020), [*Two extensions of the Erdős–Szekeres problem*](https://ems.press/journals/jems/articles/17088).

title: Planar \(k\)-set complexity
open: How many \(k\)-element subsets of an \(n\)-point set in the plane can be cut off from the rest by a single line? Equivalently, what is the maximum number of \(k\)-sets attainable by a planar point set?
status: A decades-old gap persists: Dey (1998), *Improved bounds on planar k-sets and related problems*, gives the upper bound \(O(nk^{1/3})\), while known lower constructions are substantially smaller; see also The Open Problems Project, problem 7.
solved_when: Matching upper and lower bounds are established for the maximum number of \(k\)-sets of an \(n\)-point planar set, up to constant factors, for all \(k \le n\); this must improve on the current gap between Dey's \(O(nk^{1/3})\) upper bound and the substantially smaller known lower-bound constructions.
why: The count of \(k\)-sets governs the complexity of levels in arrangements of lines, so tight bounds would settle geometric selection complexity and a decades-old question in discrete geometry.
key_works: Dey (1998), *Improved bounds on planar k-sets and related problems*; [The Open Problems Project, problem 7](https://topp.openproblem.net/p7).

title: Danzer’s finite-density hitting set
open: Does there exist a set of finite upper density in \(\mathbb R^d\), \(d\ge2\), that intersects every convex body of volume one? Formally, can one hit all unit-volume convex sets while keeping the upper density of the point set finite?
status: Open since the 1960s. Dense forests and weaker visibility constructions do not solve Danzer's condition. Key work: Adiceam (2020), [*Around the Danzer Problem and the Construction of Dense Forests*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.06756).
solved_when: A set \(S\subset\mathbb R^d\) with finite upper density is constructed (or shown not to exist) such that \(S\cap K\neq\varnothing\) for every convex body \(K\) of volume one, for some \(d\ge2\).
why: A positive answer would give a sparse universal geometric sampling set; a negative answer shows no such sparse hitting structure can exist.
key_works: Adiceam (2020), [*Around the Danzer Problem and the Construction of Dense Forests*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.06756).

title: Complex illumination conjecture
open: Can every unit ball of a complex norm on \(\mathbb C^d\) be illuminated by at most \(2^{d+1}-1\) directions? Equivalently, does the complex analogue of the classical illumination bound hold with this sharply smaller constant in place of the real one?
status: The conjecture was proposed in 2024 and published in 2026. Complex zonoids and various other special cases are already settled. Key work: Rotem–Schejter–Slomka (2026), [*The complex Illumination problem*](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00493-025-00195-7).
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that the unit ball of every complex norm on \(\mathbb C^d\) admits illumination by at most \(2^{d+1}-1\) directions.
why: It isolates precisely how complex symmetry reduces covering complexity, giving a sharp dividing line between real and complex normed geometry.
key_works: Rotem–Schejter–Slomka (2026), [*The complex Illumination problem*](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00493-025-00195-7).

title: Lebesgue’s universal covering constant
open: What is the smallest area of a convex planar set that contains an isometric copy of every diameter-one planar set? Formally, determine the exact value of Lebesgue's universal covering constant.
status: Open since 1914. The constant is known to lie between approximately 0.832 and 0.8440935944. Key works include Gibbs (2018), [*An Upper Bound for Lebesgue's Covering Problem*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.10089), and Arman et al. (2025), [covering bounds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.04023).
solved_when: The exact minimum area is determined, closing the gap between the known bounds of approximately 0.832 and 0.8440935944.
why: It identifies the smallest universal geometric container for all diameter-one planar sets, a foundational constant in discrete and computational geometry.
key_works: Gibbs (2018), [*An Upper Bound for Lebesgue’s Covering Problem*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.10089); Arman et al. (2025), [covering bounds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.04023).

title: Shortest opaque barrier for a square

title: Geometric tetrahedral flip connectivity
open: Are the geometric triangulations of every finite point set in \(\mathbb R^3\) connected through valid bistellar flips? That is, can any tetrahedral mesh on such a point set be transformed into any other by a sequence of local flip operations?
status: Open even for important restricted configurations; known disconnected examples in higher dimensions do not settle the three-dimensional case. See the Open Problems Project, problem 28, and Wagner–Welzl (2022), a triangulation study.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that for every finite point set in \(\mathbb R^3\), the graph of geometric triangulations — with edges given by valid bistellar flips — is connected.
why: It determines whether local retriangulation can explore every tetrahedral mesh, which underpins whether flip-based algorithms can reach an arbitrary target mesh or optimize over all triangulations.
key_works: [The Open Problems Project, problem 28](https://topp.openproblem.net/p28); Wagner–Welzl (2022), [triangulation study](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00454-022-00436-2).

title: Voronoi diagrams of lines in three dimensions
open: What is the maximum number of faces in the Euclidean Voronoi diagram of \(n\) lines in \(\mathbb R^3\)? Formally, determine the worst-case combinatorial complexity of the Voronoi diagram of \(n\) lines in three-dimensional space.
status: Quadratic lower bounds and essentially cubic upper bounds remain separated; near-quadratic growth is conjectured. See Sharir (1994) and relevant envelope bounds; the problem is also listed as problem 3 of [The Open Problems Project](https://topp.openproblem.net/p3).
solved_when: The asymptotic growth of the maximum combinatorial complexity is determined, closing the gap between the known quadratic lower bounds and the essentially cubic upper bounds; in particular, either a proof of the conjectured near-quadratic bound or a construction with superquadratic complexity.
why: The answer controls basic proximity computation for spatial line structures — how efficiently nearest-line queries and distance relationships among lines in 3D can be processed.
key_works: Sharir (1994), relevant envelope bounds; [The Open Problems Project, problem 3](https://topp.openproblem.net/p3).

title: Polynomial-time sum-of-square-roots comparison
open: Can the sign of an expression of the form √a₁ + ⋯ + √aₘ − √b₁ − ⋯ − √bₙ, where the aᵢ and bᵢ are binary-encoded integers, always be decided in time polynomial in the input length? This is the classic sum-of-square-roots problem, a special case of comparing algebraic numbers given succinctly.
status: The problem has been studied since at least the 1980s and the exact arithmetic complexity remains unresolved. Burnikel–Fleischer–Mehlhorn–Schirra (2000) gave separation bounds, and it is listed as problem 33 of The Open Problems Project; a related question is whether PosSLP is in polynomial time.
solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm (in the number of input bits) is given that correctly decides the sign of any such difference of sums of square roots of binary-encoded integers, or a proof that no such algorithm exists under a standard complexity assumption.
why: The problem is a foundational bottleneck in exact geometric optimization, since many geometric predicates reduce to comparing sums of square roots; a solution would make exact algebraic decision work routine in computational geometry.
key_works: Burnikel–Fleischer–Mehlhorn–Schirra (2000), separation bounds; [The Open Problems Project, problem 33](https://topp.openproblem.net/p33).

title: Uniform quadratic-time sorting of \(X+Y\)
open: Can the Minkowski sum \(X+Y\) of two \(n\)-element sets of real numbers — that is, all \(n^2\) pairwise sums — be sorted in uniform quadratic time? Formally, is there a single algorithm that sorts all \(n^2\) sums in \(O(n^2)\) time for every input?
status: Fredman (1976) showed via a comparison-tree argument that the information-theoretic bound for this task is quadratic; however, no uniform algorithm achieving quadratic time is known. See Fredman, *How good is the information theory bound in sorting?*, and The Open Problems Project, problem 41.
solved_when: A uniform algorithm sorts all \(n^2\) pairwise sums of two \(n\)-element real sets in \(O(n^2)\) time, matching Fredman's comparison-tree bound.
why: It would close the gap between the information-theoretic comparison complexity of the problem and the complexity of an actually executable algorithm, showing the bound is tight constructively.
key_works: Fredman (1976), *How good is the information theory bound in sorting?*; [The Open Problems Project, problem 41](https://topp.openproblem.net/p41).

title: Polynomial Hirsch conjecture
open: Is there a polynomial \(p\), independent of the dimension \(d\), such that the graph of every \(d\)-polytope with \(n\) facets has diameter at most \(p(n)\)? In other words, can the linear Hirsch bound be replaced by any uniform polynomial bound in the number of facets?
status: The original linear Hirsch conjecture is false: Santos (2012), [A counterexample to the Hirsch conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/1006.2814), disproved it. The best known result toward the polynomial version is the quasi-polynomial diameter bound of Kalai–Kleitman (1992), *A quasi-polynomial bound for the diameter of graphs of polyhedra*; a general polynomial bound remains unproved.
solved_when: Explicit constants \(C, k\) are given, with proof, such that every \(d\)-polytope with \(n\) facets has graph diameter at most \(C n^k\); the bound must be uniform in \(d\).
why: A polynomial bound would constrain the combinatorial difficulty of navigating linear programs, where vertex-to-vertex paths along the polytope's graph model simplex-type pivoting steps.
key_works: Kalai–Kleitman (1992), *A quasi-polynomial bound for the diameter of graphs of polyhedra*; Santos (2012), [*A counterexample to the Hirsch conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1006.2814).

title: Oda’s integer-decomposition conjecture
open: Does every smooth lattice polytope have the integer-decomposition property — that is, can every lattice point of a dilation \(kP\) always be written as a sum of \(k\) lattice points of \(P\)?
status: The conjecture was posed in 1997. Numerous classes of smooth lattice polytopes and various low-dimensional cases are known to satisfy the integer-decomposition property, but the general question remains open; see Hofscheier–Kasprzyk (2025), [*Is there a smooth lattice polytope which does not have the integer decomposition property?*](https://doi.org/10.14760/SNAP-2025-008-EN).
solved_when: A proof that every smooth lattice polytope \(P\) has the integer-decomposition property, or a counterexample: a smooth lattice polytope and some \(k\) with a lattice point of \(kP\) not expressible as a sum of \(k\) lattice points of \(P\).
why: It would show that a purely local condition — smoothness of the polytope — forces a global integral decomposability property, a bridge between the geometry of the polytope and the arithmetic of its lattice points.
key_works: Hofscheier–Kasprzyk (2025), [*Is there a smooth lattice polytope which does not have the integer decomposition property?*](https://doi.org/10.14760/SNAP-2025-008-EN).

title: Koszulness of smooth lattice polytopes
open: Is the lattice-point semigroup algebra of every smooth lattice polytope a Koszul algebra? In other words, does smoothness of the polytope force the quadratic relations of its toric coordinate ring to admit a linear free resolution?
status: This is Bøgvad's longstanding conjecture. Extensive results for special families of polytopes are known — see Beck–Delgado–Gubeladze–Michałek (2015), [Very ample and Koszul segmental fibrations](https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.7422) — but the general case remains open.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) that for every smooth lattice polytope the associated semigroup algebra is Koszul.
why: A positive answer would tightly control the syzygies of smooth toric embeddings, giving uniform homological control over this entire class of toric varieties.
key_works: Beck–Delgado–Gubeladze–Michałek (2015), [*Very ample and Koszul segmental fibrations*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.7422).

title: Unimodular triangulations of smooth polytopes
open: Does every smooth lattice polytope admit a triangulation all of whose simplices are unimodular? Equivalently, can the smoothness condition alone guarantee a full unimodular triangulation of the polytope itself?
status: Unimodular triangulations are known to exist for many classes of smooth polytopes, following Haase–Paffenholz–Piechnik–Santos (2021), [*Existence of unimodular triangulations—positive results*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1405.1687); however, general dilation theorems do not supply a unimodular triangulation of the original polytope, so the general question remains open.
solved_when: A proof that every smooth lattice polytope admits a unimodular triangulation, or an explicit smooth lattice polytope admitting none.
why: A positive answer would yield exact lattice decompositions of smooth polytopes and squarefree algebraic degenerations, with direct consequences for the algebraic side of the theory.
key_works: Haase–Paffenholz–Piechnik–Santos (2021), [*Existence of unimodular triangulations—positive results*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1405.1687).

title: Gal’s gamma-nonnegativity conjecture
open: Is the gamma-vector of every flag homology sphere nonnegative? Equivalently, does the cd-index refinement of the flag f-vector of such a sphere always carry nonnegative coefficients?
status: Proposed by Gal in 2005 after the stronger real-rootedness statement failed for five and higher dimensional spheres [Gal (2005), *Real Root Conjecture fails for five and higher dimensional spheres*](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0501046); many low-dimensional and structured cases have since been settled.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that the gamma-vector is nonnegative for every flag homology sphere.
why: It would reveal hidden positivity in the face enumeration of flag spheres, extending the combinatorial shadow of the Charney–Davis and Gal conjectures.
key_works: Gal (2005), [*Real Root Conjecture fails for five and higher dimensional spheres*](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0501046).

title: Charney–Davis conjecture
open: For every flag homology \((2d-1)\)-sphere, prove \((-1)^d h(-1)\ge0\).
status: Proposed in 1995 by Charney–Davis ([*The Euler characteristic of a nonpositively curved, piecewise Euclidean manifold*](https://people.math.osu.edu/davis.12/old_papers/euler95.pdf)). Low-dimensional cases are known; higher-dimensional generality remains open.
solved_when: Every flag homology \((2d-1)\)-sphere satisfies \((-1)^d h(-1)\ge0\).
why: It connects face enumeration to curvature and Euler-characteristic signs, serving as a combinatorial counterpart to conjectures like Hopf's on the sign of Euler characteristic.
key_works: Charney–Davis (1995), [*The Euler characteristic of a nonpositively curved, piecewise Euclidean manifold*](https://people.math.osu.edu/davis.12/old_papers/euler95.pdf).

title: Nevo–Petersen realization of gamma-vectors
open: Can the gamma-vector of every flag homology sphere be realized as the face vector of some simplicial complex? Ideally, can this always be done with a balanced complex?
status: Proposed in the late 2000s. Realizations are established for barycentric subdivisions and certain other classes; the general case remains open. See Nevo–Petersen (2011), [*On gamma-vectors satisfying the Kruskal–Katona inequalities*](https://arxiv.org/abs/0909.0694) and [balanced realizations](https://arxiv.org/abs/1003.2544).
solved_when: For every flag homology sphere, a simplicial complex (ideally balanced) is constructed whose face vector equals the sphere's gamma-vector.
why: It would convert gamma-positivity from a numerical property into an explicit combinatorial realization, giving concrete objects behind the gamma-entries.
key_works: Nevo–Petersen (2011), [*On gamma-vectors satisfying the Kruskal–Katona inequalities*](https://arxiv.org/abs/0909.0694); [balanced realizations](https://arxiv.org/abs/1003.2544).

title: Beck–Fiala in the remaining sparse regime
open: Does every set system in which each element lies in at most \(t\) sets admit a coloring with discrepancy \(O(\sqrt t)\)? This is the Beck–Fiala conjecture in the sparse regime not yet covered by current techniques.
status: The problem was proposed in 1981. Recent work of Bansal–Jiang (2025/2026), [*Decoupling via Affine Spectral-Independence: Beck–Fiala and Komlós Bounds Beyond Banaszczyk*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.03961), resolves the case \(t \ge \log^2 n\); the full sparse regime remains open.
solved_when: A proof (explicit or randomized) that any set system of maximum element degree \(t\) has discrepancy bounded by \(C\sqrt t\) for an absolute constant \(C\), covering the full sparse regime below the currently resolved threshold \(t \ge \log^2 n\).
why: It would make discrepancy depend optimally on column sparsity, replacing the general \(t\)-dependent bounds with the conjectured correct order of magnitude.
key_works: Bansal–Jiang (2025/2026), [*Decoupling via Affine Spectral-Independence: Beck–Fiala and Komlós Bounds Beyond Banaszczyk*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.03961).

title: Strongly polynomial linear programming
open: Is there an algorithm that solves any linear program over rational data in a number of arithmetic operations bounded by a polynomial in the number of variables and constraints alone, with no dependence on the bit lengths of the input coefficients?
status: The problem has been open for decades; existing weakly polynomial algorithms do not meet the requirement. It is listed as problem 8 in The Open Problems Project and appears in Smale (1998), *Mathematical problems for the next century*.
solved_when: A single algorithm achieves, for every rational linear program, an arithmetic operation count that is polynomial in the dimensions (numbers of variables and constraints) and independent of the coefficient bit lengths.
why: This is Smale's ninth problem and a central open complexity question in optimization: it would settle whether linear programming admits a strongly polynomial-time algorithm, a property that all known weakly polynomial methods fail to provide.
key_works: Smale (1998), *Mathematical problems for the next century*; [The Open Problems Project, problem 8](https://topp.openproblem.net/p8).

title: FPRAS for perfect matchings in general graphs
open: Is there an FPRAS for the number of perfect matchings of an arbitrary graph, without any bipartiteness assumption? Equivalently, can we approximately count perfect matchings in general nonbipartite graphs in randomized polynomial time?

See Štefankovič–Vigoda–Wilmes (2017), [*On Counting Perfect Matchings in General Graphs*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.07504).
solved_when: A randomized polynomial-time algorithm produces, for every graph, an estimate of its number of perfect matchings within the FPRAS guarantee (arbitrarily small relative error with high probability).
why: It would extend efficient approximation counting to general dimer systems, where the bipartite restriction is not available.

title: Four-thirds subtour-LP conjecture
open: Is the integrality gap of the subtour linear programming relaxation at most \(4/3\) for the metric symmetric traveling salesman problem? That is, does the standard subtour LP always admit a tour of cost at most four-thirds of its fractional optimum?
status: Lower-bound examples approach \(4/3\), while the best general upper bound, due to Karlin–Klein–Oveis Gharan (2021) [*A (Slightly) Improved Bound on the Integrality Gap of the Subtour LP for TSP*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.10043), is below \(3/2\) but remains larger than \(4/3\).
solved_when: A proof that the subtour LP's integrality gap for metric symmetric TSP is at most \(4/3\); equivalently, every instance has a tour costing no more than \(4/3\) times the LP optimum.
why: It would expose the exact strength of the standard TSP relaxation and is closely tied to the goal of a polynomial-time \(4/3\)-approximation for metric TSP.
key_works: Karlin–Klein–Oveis Gharan (2021), [*A (Slightly) Improved Bound on the Integrality Gap of the Subtour LP for TSP*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.10043).

title: Constant additive gap for bin packing
open: Is there an absolute constant \(C\) such that the optimal number of bins differs from the configuration-LP optimum by at most \(C\), for every bin packing instance? Equivalently, can the additive integrality gap of the configuration LP be bounded by a constant independent of the instance?
status: The best known general additive bound is \(O(\log \mathrm{OPT})\), due to Hoberg–Rothvoss (2017), [*A Logarithmic Additive Integrality Gap for Bin Packing*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.08796); whether the loss can be reduced to a constant remains open. A related question is the modified integer round-up conjecture.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) that the additive gap \(\mathrm{OPT} - \mathrm{LP}\) is bounded by an absolute constant, with an explicit value of that constant, for all bin packing instances.
why: A constant gap would nearly eliminate rounding waste when passing from the LP relaxation to an actual packing, directly improving guarantees for packing and cutting stock applications.
key_works: Hoberg–Rothvoss (2017), [*A Logarithmic Additive Integrality Gap for Bin Packing*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.08796).

title: Zigzag fluctuations of random-graph chromatic number
open: How irregularly does the chromatic number of a random graph fluctuate as the number of vertices grows? Determine the fluctuation scale and limiting distributions of \(\chi(G(n,1/2))\) for all \(n\), including the predicted oscillating behavior of this scale.
status: Large fluctuations along subsequences of \(n\) are proved, by Heckel–Riordan (2021/2023) in [*How does the chromatic number of a random graph vary?*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.14014), but a complete all-\(n\) law is still missing.
solved_when: A complete description of the fluctuations of \(\chi(G(n,1/2))\) holds for every \(n\), not just along subsequences — that is, the fluctuation scale, including its predicted oscillation, is determined together with the limiting distributions.
why: It characterizes the irregular uncertainty of one of the most basic random optimization parameters, telling us precisely when and why its variance behaves non-monotonically.
key_works: Heckel–Riordan (2021/2023), [*How does the chromatic number of a random graph vary?*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.14014).

title: Rapid mixing of colorings at \(q\ge\Delta+2\)
open: Does single-site Glauber dynamics for proper \(q\)-colorings mix in polynomial time on every graph of maximum degree \(\Delta\) whenever \(q\ge\Delta+2\)?
status: Decades of work have steadily lowered the number of colors sufficient for rapid mixing, but the best general results remain around \(1.809\Delta\), still well above the conjectured \(\Delta+2\) threshold; Carlson–Vigoda (2024), [*Flip Dynamics for Sampling Colorings: Improving \((11/6-\varepsilon)\) Using a Simple Metric*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.04870), represent the current frontier.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) of polynomial-time mixing of Glauber dynamics for all graphs of maximum degree \(\Delta\) at every \(q\ge\Delta+2\).
why: It would give efficient sampling and counting of colorings at essentially the minimum number of colors where the state space is nontrivially connected, closing the gap to the conjectured threshold.
key_works: Carlson–Vigoda (2024), [*Flip Dynamics for Sampling Colorings: Improving \((11/6-\varepsilon)\) Using a Simple Metric*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.04870).

title: Planar SAW counting exponent \(43/32\)
subfield: Lattice paths, growth models, and statistical mechanics
open: Does the number of \(n\)-step planar self-avoiding walks grow as \(c_n = \mu^n n^{\gamma-1+o(1)}\) with the exponent \(\gamma = 43/32\) predicted by physics? The task is to rigorously pin down this polynomial correction to the exponential growth rate.
status: The exponent \(\gamma = 43/32\) was predicted by Nienhuis in 1982 (Exact critical point and critical exponents of O(n) models in two dimensions). Rigorous results establish only the exponential growth rate (see Grimmett–Li, [Self-avoiding walks and connective constants](https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.05884)), which does not determine the polynomial correction.
solved_when: A proof that \(c_n = \mu^n n^{\gamma-1+o(1)}\) with \(\gamma = 43/32\) for planar self-avoiding walks.
why: It would validate a central prediction of two-dimensional universality, confirming that planar self-avoiding walks lie in the dilute \(O(n)\)-model universality class.
key_works: Nienhuis (1982), *Exact critical point and critical exponents of O(n) models in two dimensions*; Grimmett–Li, [*Self-avoiding walks and connective constants*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.05884).

title: Planar SAW displacement exponent \(3/4\)
subfield: Lattice paths, growth models, and statistical mechanics
open: Does a typical \(n\)-step self-avoiding walk in the plane travel a distance on the order of \(n^{3/4}\)? Formally, prove that the characteristic displacement of an \(n\)-step planar self-avoiding walk scales as \(n^{3/4+o(1)}\).
status: The exponent \(3/4\) is strongly supported by physics heuristics and numerical computation, but rigorous results are far weaker: sub-ballisticity — the fact that displacement grows strictly slower than linearly in \(n\) — is known (Duminil-Copin–Hammond 2013, [*Self-avoiding walk is sub-ballistic*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1205.0401)) and is the state of the art.
solved_when: A rigorous proof establishes that the characteristic displacement of an \(n\)-step planar self-avoiding walk scales as \(n^{3/4+o(1)}\).
why: This exponent governs universal polymer swelling: it fixes how excluded-volume interactions stretch a long chain, a hallmark prediction of the polymer model that self-avoiding walks encode.
key_works: Duminil-Copin–Hammond (2013), [*Self-avoiding walk is sub-ballistic*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1205.0401).

title: SAW convergence to \(\mathrm{SLE}_{8/3}\)
subfield: Lattice paths, growth models, and statistical mechanics
open: Does the planar lattice self-avoiding walk, rescaled appropriately, converge to \(\mathrm{SLE}_{8/3}\)? More precisely, does the scaling limit of suitably rescaled self-avoiding walks on the planar lattice exist and coincide with chordal \(\mathrm{SLE}_{8/3}\)?
status: The convergence was predicted in the early 2000s, and extensive numerical agreement supports it, but this does not establish the scaling limit. Lawler–Schramm–Werner (2004) provide the relevant SLE characterization; Kennedy (2002), [*Monte Carlo Tests of SLE Predictions for the 2D Self-Avoiding Walk*](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0112246), documents the numerical evidence.
solved_when: A proof that suitably rescaled planar lattice self-avoiding walks converge in the scaling limit to \(\mathrm{SLE}_{8/3}\).
why: It would connect the discrete geometry of polymers to conformal probability, grounding the long-predicted SLE description of the self-avoiding walk in rigorous theory.
key_works: Lawler–Schramm–Werner (2004), relevant SLE characterization; Kennedy (2002), [*Monte Carlo Tests of SLE Predictions for the 2D Self-Avoiding Walk*](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0112246).

title: Four-dimensional strict-SAW logarithmic corrections
subfield: Lattice paths, growth models, and statistical mechanics
open: Does the strict self-avoiding walk on \(\mathbb{Z}^4\) exhibit the predicted logarithmic corrections to scaling, with the \(1/4\) exponent? A proof establishing these corrections for the strict (as opposed to weakly) self-avoiding model is the goal.
status: Rigorous results exist for weakly self-avoiding walk (Bauerschmidt–Brydges–Slade, 2014) but do not settle the strict model; simulations, including a four-dimensional numerical study by Fang–Deng–Zhou (2021), support the predicted corrections.
solved_when: The logarithmic corrections at the upper critical dimension four are rigorously proved for strict self-avoiding walk on \(\mathbb{Z}^4\), including the \(1/4\) exponent.
why: It settles the behavior of strict self-avoiding walk exactly at the upper critical dimension, where mean-field exponents acquire logarithmic corrections.
key_works: Bauerschmidt–Brydges–Slade (2014), weak-model analysis; Fang–Deng–Zhou (2021), [four-dimensional numerical study](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevE.104.064108).

title: Conformal invariance of square-lattice bond percolation
subfield: Lattice paths, growth models, and statistical mechanics
open: Does critical bond percolation on the square lattice have the same conformally invariant scaling limit as its triangular cousin — specifically, do its exploration interfaces converge to SLE₆? This is the last missing step in extending the rigorous SLE₆ picture from the triangular-site model to the square lattice.
status: The triangular-site model is settled; transferring this universality to the square-bond model remains open. See Duminil-Copin (2018), [*Sixty years of percolation*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.04651).
solved_when: The percolation interfaces of critical square-lattice bond percolation are shown to converge, in the scaling limit, to \(\mathrm{SLE}_6\), establishing conformal invariance for the model.
why: It would establish that critical percolation geometry is lattice-independent, cementing universality of two-dimensional critical scaling limits.
key_works: Duminil-Copin (2018), [*Sixty years of percolation*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.04651).

subfield: Lattice paths, growth models, and statistical mechanics
open: Is the limit shape of planar first-passage percolation — say, with independent exponential edge weights — strictly convex and differentiable everywhere on its boundary?

why: It would give control over directional passage times and the geometry of geodesics.

title: KPZ exponents for ordinary first-passage percolation
subfield: Lattice paths, growth models, and statistical mechanics
open: Does ordinary planar first-passage percolation exhibit the KPZ-predicted scaling exponents — a passage-time fluctuation exponent of \(1/3\) and a geodesic wandering exponent of \(2/3\)? More precisely, are these exponents realized for standard planar first-passage percolation with nonintegrable weights?
status: Solvable last-passage models exhibit these exponents; ordinary FPP remains unresolved. See Auffinger–Damron–Hanson, [*50 years of first passage percolation*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.03262), and a [recent primary discussion](https://doi.org/10.1093/imrn/rnae168).
solved_when: The passage-time fluctuation exponent \(1/3\) and the geodesic wandering exponent \(2/3\) are rigorously established for standard planar first-passage percolation.
why: It would confirm KPZ universality outside the integrable models where the exponents are currently provable, a key test of whether the KPZ scaling picture is genuinely universal.
key_works: Auffinger–Damron–Hanson, [*50 years of first passage percolation*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.03262); [recent primary discussion](https://doi.org/10.1093/imrn/rnae168).

title: Absence of planar FPP bigeodesics
subfield: Lattice paths, growth models, and statistical mechanics
open: Prove that, almost surely, planar first-passage percolation with a standard continuous independent weight law admits no doubly infinite geodesic — that is, no bi-infinite path whose every finite segment is optimal.
status: Directional and conditional nonexistence results are known, notably Damron–Hanson (2017), [*Bigeodesics in first-passage percolation*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.00804); unrestricted all-direction nonexistence remains open.
solved_when: An almost-sure proof of nonexistence of doubly infinite geodesics is established for planar FPP with a standard continuous independent weight law, with no restriction on direction.
why: It would classify the global structure of optimal paths, determining how geodesics can extend indefinitely through the disordered environment.
key_works: Damron–Hanson (2017), [*Bigeodesics in first-passage percolation*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.00804).

title: BKS midpoint problem in dimension three
subfield: Lattice paths, growth models, and statistical mechanics
open: In standard first-passage percolation on \(\mathbb{Z}^3\), does the probability that the origin lies on a geodesic between \(-ne_1\) and \(ne_1\) tend to zero as \(n \to \infty\)? Formally, show \(\mathbb{P}(0 \in \gamma(-ne_1, ne_1)) \to 0\).
status: The planar version has quantitative solutions (Dembin–Elboim–Peled 2022, *Coalescence of geodesics and the BKS midpoint problem in planar first-passage percolation*, arXiv:2204.02332); dimensions three and higher remain unresolved.
solved_when: A proof, in standard FPP on \(\mathbb{Z}^3\), that this midpoint probability tends to zero as \(n \to \infty\).
why: It measures delocalization of long optimal paths: a positive answer shows that geodesics between distant points typically wander away from any fixed midpoint, a basic signature of fluctuation behavior in higher dimensions.
key_works: Dembin–Elboim–Peled (2022), [*Coalescence of geodesics and the BKS midpoint problem in planar first-passage percolation*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.02332).

title: Exact square-lattice hard-core critical activity
subfield: Lattice paths, growth models, and statistical mechanics
open: What is the exact value of the critical activity \(\lambda_c\) at which the hard-core model on \(\mathbb{Z}^2\) transitions from uniqueness to nonuniqueness of Gibbs measures? Formally, determine the uniqueness-to-nonuniqueness threshold activity for independent sets on the square lattice.
status: Rigorous upper and lower thresholds for the transition remain separated, while the numerical prediction places \(\lambda_c\) at approximately 3.796 (Vera–Vigoda–Yang 2013, [Improved Bounds on the Phase Transition for the Hard-Core Model in 2-Dimensions](https://arxiv.org/abs/1306.0431)); the transition is expected to lie in the Ising universality class.
solved_when: The exact value of \(\lambda_c\) is determined, matching (or replacing) the numerical prediction of approximately 3.796 with a rigorous derivation.
why: It would establish a basic nonintegrable lattice-gas critical point, giving an exactly solvable threshold in a model where standard integrability techniques do not apply.
key_works: Vera–Vigoda–Yang (2013), [*Improved Bounds on the Phase Transition for the Hard-Core Model in 2-Dimensions*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1306.0431).

title: Golomb–Welch perfect Lee-code conjecture
open: Is it impossible, in three or more dimensions, to perfectly cover the integer lattice by copies of the Lee ball? Formally: prove that for every dimension \(n\ge3\) and integer radius \(r\ge2\), \(\mathbb Z^n\) cannot be partitioned into translates of the Lee ball \(\{x\in\mathbb Z^n:\sum_i|x_i|\le r\}\).
status: Open since 1968. Several low-dimensional and large-radius cases are settled. Leung–Zhou exclude lattice tilings by radius-two Lee balls in every dimension at least three, but arbitrary translational tilings need not be lattice tilings, so the general conjecture remains unresolved.
solved_when: A proof exists that no tiling of \(\mathbb Z^n\) by translates of the Lee ball of radius \(r\ge2\) exists for any \(n\ge3\); equivalently, the impossibility holds for all dimension–radius pairs with \(n\ge3\), \(r\ge2\).
why: It determines where perfect error correction in the Manhattan (Lee) metric becomes impossible, marking the boundary of achievable perfect codes.
key_works: Peter Horak and Dongryul Kim (2018), [*50 Years of the Golomb–Welch Conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03589); Ka Hin Leung and Yue Zhou (2020), [*No lattice tiling of \(\mathbb Z^n\) by Lee sphere of radius 2*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcta.2019.105157).

title: Binary adversarial-deletion zero-rate threshold
open: Up to what fraction of adversarially deleted bits can a binary code of positive asymptotic rate still uniquely correct? Formally, determine the supremum \(\delta_*\) of deletion fractions \(\delta\) for which binary codes exist at positive asymptotic rate that correct every pattern of \(\lfloor\delta n\rfloor\) deletions.
status: Explicit constructions correct deletion fractions approaching \(\sqrt2-1\approx0.4142\). Guruswami–He–Li prove that \(\delta_*<1/2\) by an absolute amount, disproving the former conjectural threshold \(1/2\). The exact threshold remains open.
solved_when: The exact value of \(\delta_*\) is determined, closing the gap between the best known constructions (which achieve \(\delta\) approaching \(\sqrt2-1\approx0.4142\)) and the upper bound of \(1/2\) minus an absolute constant.
why: It sets the maximum resilience of positive-rate binary communication against adversarial loss of synchronization, the fundamental limit for deletion-correcting codes.
key_works: Boris Bukh, Venkatesan Guruswami and Johan Håstad (2017), [*An improved bound on the fraction of correctable deletions*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2015/117/); Venkatesan Guruswami, Xiaoyu He and Ray Li (2021), [*The zero-rate threshold for adversarial bit-deletions is less than \(1/2\)*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.05250).

title: Maximum nonlinearity of a nine-variable Boolean function
open: What is the maximum possible nonlinearity of a Boolean function on nine variables — that is, the largest distance from any such function to the nearest affine function? Equivalently, what is the covering radius of the first-order Reed–Muller code \(RM(1,9)\)?
status: Kavut–Yücel constructed functions of nonlinearity \(242\) in 2008 (within the generalized rotation class), and the best known upper bound is \(244\). No function attaining \(243\) or \(244\) is known, and no impossibility proof closing the gap exists.
solved_when: The exact value of \(\max_f\min_{\ell\text{ affine}}d_H(f,\ell)\) for \(f:\mathbb F_2^9\to\mathbb F_2\) is determined — either by exhibiting a function of nonlinearity \(243\) or \(244\), or by proving the maximum is \(242\), thereby closing the gap with the known upper bound of \(244\).
why: It determines the strongest possible resistance to affine approximation at a small but computationally challenging truth-table size (512 bits).
key_works: Selçuk Kavut and Melek D. Yücel (2008/2010), [*9-variable Boolean Functions with Nonlinearity 242 in the Generalized Rotation Class*](https://arxiv.org/abs/0808.0684); Claude Carlet (2021), *Boolean Functions for Cryptography and Coding Theory*.
aliases: Covering radius of the first-order Reed–Muller code of length \(512\).

title: Complete census of quadratic APN functions in dimension eight
open: Can we produce a complete census of quadratic APN functions from \(\mathbb F_2^8\) to itself, listed up to CCZ-equivalence? That is, enumerate every CCZ-equivalence class of such maps, with canonical representatives and a checkable completeness certificate, where CCZ equivalence means an invertible affine map of \(\mathbb F_2^{16}\) sends one function's graph onto the other's.
status: A 2025 construction supplies \(3{,}775{,}599\) inequivalent examples and estimates roughly six million classes; the catalogue and estimate do not constitute a complete classification. See Christof Beierle, Philippe Langevin, Gregor Leander, Alexandr Polujan and Shahram Rasoolzadeh (2025), [*Millions of inequivalent quadratic APN functions in eight variables*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.04644).
solved_when: A catalogue exists that contains a canonical representative of every CCZ-equivalence class of quadratic APN maps \(\mathbb F_2^8\to\mathbb F_2^8\), together with a certificate proving no class is missing — in particular, covering all classes beyond the \(3{,}775{,}599\) inequivalent examples currently known and confirming or refuting the estimate of roughly six million classes.
why: It would provide an exhaustive small-dimensional search space for nonlinear functions, associated codes, and exceptional cryptographic constructions, allowing questions about quadratic APN functions in eight variables to be settled by inspection rather than search.
key_works: Christof Beierle, Philippe Langevin, Gregor Leander, Alexandr Polujan and Shahram Rasoolzadeh (2025), [*Millions of inequivalent quadratic APN functions in eight variables*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.04644).

title: Curling-number termination conjecture
open: For a nonempty finite integer sequence \(S\), let \(k(S)\) be the largest \(k\) for which \(S=XY^k\) with \(Y\ne\varnothing\); if one repeatedly appends \(k(S)\) to the current sequence, must a \(1\) eventually appear for every starting sequence?
status: The conjecture was formulated in the 2000s and remains open even for starting sequences consisting only of \(2\)'s and \(3\)'s. Published exhaustive searches cover initial lengths through \(48\); some conclusions about longer sequences rely on conjectural reductions. See Benjamin Chaffin and N. J. A. Sloane (2009), [*Curling Numbers*](https://arxiv.org/abs/0912.2382); Benjamin Chaffin, J. P. Linderman, N. J. A. Sloane and A. R. Wilks (2013), [*On Curling Numbers of Integer Sequences*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1212.6102).
solved_when: A proof is given that, for every nonempty finite starting sequence, the iteration that repeatedly appends the curling number \(k(S)\) eventually produces a \(1\).
why: It would establish universal termination for a simple string-rewriting rule whose dependence on its entire history makes conventional induction difficult.
key_works: Benjamin Chaffin and N. J. A. Sloane (2009), [*Curling Numbers*](https://arxiv.org/abs/0912.2382); Benjamin Chaffin, J. P. Linderman, N. J. A. Sloane and A. R. Wilks (2013), [*On Curling Numbers of Integer Sequences*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1212.6102).

title: Recurrence of the Kolakoski sequence
open: Does every finite factor of the self-run-length-encoding sequence \(122112122\ldots\) occur infinitely often? In other words, is the Kolakoski sequence recurrent?
status: The sequence appears in Oldenburger's 1939 work and Kolakoski's 1965 rediscovery. Nonperiodicity is known; recurrence remains open and would imply reversal invariance.
solved_when: Every finite block that appears somewhere in the sequence is shown to appear infinitely often.
why: It determines whether every pattern that appears once must persist throughout the infinite word, and a proof would imply reversal invariance of the sequence.
key_works: Alessandro Della Corte (2020), [*Kolakoski Sequence: Links between Recurrence, Symmetry and Limit Density*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.08306).

title: Complement symmetry of the Kolakoski language
open: Whenever a finite word \(w\) occurs in the Kolakoski sequence, must the word obtained by exchanging every \(1\) and \(2\) also occur? Equivalently, is the Kolakoski language closed under the complement morphism \(1 \leftrightarrow 2\)?
status: Open despite extensive finite evidence. Complement symmetry implies recurrence and is a separate assertion from reversal symmetry or equality of digit densities. Relevant works include F. Michel Dekking (1997), *What is the Long Range Order in the Kolakoski Sequence?*; Alessandro Della Corte (2020), [*Kolakoski Sequence: Links between Recurrence, Symmetry and Limit Density*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.08306).
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that for every finite factor \(w\) of the Kolakoski sequence, the complemented word \(\bar{w}\) obtained by swapping \(1\) and \(2\) is also a factor.
why: It would establish a global symmetry of the sequence that is not apparent from its asymmetric initial condition, and would establish recurrence.
key_works: F. Michel Dekking (1997), *What is the Long Range Order in the Kolakoski Sequence?*; Alessandro Della Corte (2020), [*Kolakoski Sequence: Links between Recurrence, Symmetry and Limit Density*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.08306).

title: Irreducible unimodular Pisot substitution conjecture
open: Does every primitive substitution whose incidence matrix has irreducible characteristic polynomial, determinant \(\pm1\), and Pisot Perron eigenvalue generate a dynamical system with pure discrete spectrum? In other words, must the substitutive system's spectral measure be purely atomic in this setting?
status: A longstanding conjecture from the 1980s. Many classes are settled, including Pisot \(\beta\)-substitutions (Barge 2015, *The Pisot Conjecture for \(\beta\)-substitutions*, https://arxiv.org/abs/1505.04408); arbitrary irreducible unimodular Pisot substitutions remain outside those results.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) showing that every primitive substitution with irreducible unimodular Pisot incidence matrix has pure discrete spectrum.
why: It would connect a purely algebraic property of a finite substitution rule to quasiperiodic spectral order, explaining pure-point spectrum through the matrix data alone.
key_works: Marcy Barge (2015), [*The Pisot Conjecture for \(\beta\)-substitutions*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1505.04408); Valérie Berthé and Michel Rigo, editors (2016), *Combinatorics, Words and Symbolic Dynamics*.

title: Eventual periodicity of Grundy’s unequal-splitting game
status: Open since the classical development of impartial games. Flammenkamp reports computations through heap size \(284{,}944{,}236{,}543\), without an established eventual period; observed sparse-value behavior gives conditional approaches.
why: Tests whether a very elementary splitting rule can produce permanently nonperiodic game values.
key_works: Patrick M. Grundy (1939), *Mathematics and games*; Achim Flammenkamp, [*Grundy’s Game*](https://wwwhomes.uni-bielefeld.de/achim/grundy.html), computational tables and commentary.

title: Complete misère analysis of Dawson’s chess
open: Can one give a complete description of the misère quotient \((Q,P)\) of Dawson’s chess — its monoid operation, its losing subset \(P\), and the heap-class map \(\Phi(n)\) for arbitrary \(n\) — yielding a uniform determination of outcomes and winning moves in arbitrary finite sums of positions?
status: Open since Dawson’s 1935 formulation. For the equivalent heap game \(0.07\), the quotient restricted to heaps of size at most \(33\) has \(638\) elements; a full description remains unknown. Key works: Thane E. Plambeck and Aaron N. Siegel (2008), [Misère quotients for impartial games](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0609825); Richard J. Nowakowski (2025), [Unsolved problems in combinatorial games](https://library.slmath.org/books/Book71/files/GONC6-04.pdf), problem A15.
solved_when: A full description of the misère quotient of Dawson’s chess (equivalently the octal game \(0.07\)) is published, specifying the monoid \(Q\), the subset \(P\), and \(\Phi(n)\) for all heap sizes \(n\), sufficient to decide outcomes and winning moves of any finite disjunctive sum. (A US$500 prize offered by Plambeck, reported in the 2025 survey, accompanies the problem, though its present administration has not been independently confirmed.)
why: It would extend practical misère algebra to one of its oldest major test cases, giving a workable computational tool for a game that has resisted analysis since 1935.
key_works: Thane E. Plambeck and Aaron N. Siegel (2008), [*Misère quotients for impartial games*](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0609825); Richard J. Nowakowski (2025), [*Unsolved problems in combinatorial games*](https://library.slmath.org/books/Book71/files/GONC6-04.pdf), problem A15.
prize: US$500 offered by Plambeck, reported in the 2025 survey; present administration has not been independently confirmed.

title: The wild quaternary game \(0.3102\)
open: Can one give a complete description of the misère quotient of the wild quaternary game \(0.3102\), in which a move removes one token freely, removes two only if that empties the heap, or removes four while leaving a nonempty heap? In particular, what are the quotient monoid, its losing classes, and the map assigning each heap size to its class?
status: The problem is retained in the 2025 problem list (Nowakowski, *Unsolved problems in combinatorial games*, A15). Only a partial quotient, computed through heap size \(11\), is known, and it already has \(74\) elements; no complete description of the quotient exists. Plambeck and Siegel (2008), *Misère quotients for impartial games*, Appendix A.4, treats the game. A US$200 prize is offered by Plambeck per the 2025 survey, though its present administration has not been independently confirmed.
solved_when: The misère quotient (monoid, losing ideal, and heap-class map for all heap sizes) of the game \(0.3102\) is fully determined; this would go beyond the known partial quotient through heap size \(11\), which has \(74\) elements.
why: The game exhibits genuinely difficult misère behavior despite not allowing heaps to split, so a complete description would illuminate how wild misère quotients can arise even under severe restrictions on the moves.
key_works: Thane E. Plambeck and Aaron N. Siegel (2008), [*Misère quotients for impartial games*](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0609825), Appendix A.4; Richard J. Nowakowski (2025), [*Unsolved problems in combinatorial games*](https://library.slmath.org/books/Book71/files/GONC6-04.pdf), A15.
prize: US$200 offered by Plambeck, reported in the 2025 survey; present administration has not been independently confirmed.

title: Recognizing infinite misère quotients
open: Given a finite, explicitly represented collection of finite impartial games, is there an algorithm that decides whether the misère quotient of its closure under followers and disjunctive sums is infinite? Formally, either produce a general decision algorithm for this problem or prove that it is undecidable.
status: The problem is listed by Plambeck–Siegel and retained in Nowakowski's 2025 survey. Existing quotient algorithms handle many finite cases but provide no general termination guarantee when the quotient is infinite.
solved_when: A general decision algorithm for infiniteness of the misère quotient is established, or undecidability of the problem is proved; existing quotient algorithms lack any general termination guarantee when the quotient is infinite.
why: A solution determines whether a major failure mode of automated misère game analysis — nontermination on infinite quotients — can be recognized algorithmically.
key_works: Thane E. Plambeck and Aaron N. Siegel (2007), [*Misère quotients for impartial games: Supplementary material*](https://arxiv.org/abs/0705.2404); Richard J. Nowakowski (2025), [*Unsolved problems in combinatorial games*](https://library.slmath.org/books/Book71/files/GONC6-04.pdf).

title: Symmetric Mahler volume-product conjecture
open: Does every origin-symmetric convex body in \(\mathbb R^d\) attain the conjectured sharp lower bound on its volume product with its polar? Formally, is Mahler's symmetric conjecture true in all dimensions, with the extremal bodies understood?
status: The problem originates in Mahler's 1930s work. Iriyeh–Shibata (2020, [arXiv:1706.01749](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.01749)) prove the three-dimensional symmetric case, including equality. Unconditional bodies and other structured classes are known; Bourgain–Milman (1987) give general reverse Santaló inequalities yielding the correct dimensional scale without the sharp constant.
solved_when: The sharp reverse Santaló inequality for origin-symmetric convex bodies is proved in every dimension \(d\), with an equality characterization.
why: It would determine the smallest possible volume product of a norm ball and its dual, the fundamental constant in the duality between a normed space and its dual.
key_works: Hiroshi Iriyeh and Masataka Shibata (2020), [*Symmetric Mahler’s conjecture for the volume product in the three dimensional case*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.01749); Jean Bourgain and Vitali Milman (1987), *New volume ratio properties for convex symmetric bodies in \(\mathbb R^n\)*.

title: Ulam’s least-dense-packing conjecture
open: Is the sphere the worst shape to pack in three dimensions? Prove that every three-dimensional convex body admits a packing by congruent copies — arbitrary rotations allowed — of density at least \(\pi/\sqrt{18}\), the optimal sphere-packing density.
status: The conjecture was recorded by Ulam in the 1970s. Kallus (2014, [*The 3-ball is a local pessimum for packing*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1212.2551)) proves that the ball is a local pessimum among origin-symmetric convex bodies, covering sufficiently small symmetric deformations; the general case of arbitrary convex shapes remains unresolved. The relevant sphere-packing constant follows from Hales's 2005 proof of the Kepler conjecture.
solved_when: Every three-dimensional convex body is shown to admit a congruent-copy packing of density at least \(\pi/\sqrt{18}\).
why: It would establish a universal lower bound on packing efficiency for convex particles and identify the ball as the global worst case for packing.
key_works: Yoav Kallus (2014), [*The 3-ball is a local pessimum for packing*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1212.2551); Thomas Hales (2005), *A proof of the Kepler conjecture*.

title: Optimal packing density of regular tetrahedra
open: What is the densest possible packing of congruent regular tetrahedra in three-dimensional space, with no restriction to periodic arrangements? Formally, determine the supremal packing density over all rotations and configurations — in particular, is the value \(4000/4671\) globally optimal?
status: Chen–Engel–Glotzer (2010) constructed a dimer crystal of density \(4000/4671\approx0.856347\). Rigorous upper bounds remain far from certifying this value: optimization over small periodic cells cannot exclude improvements from larger cells or nonperiodic arrangements.
solved_when: The supremal density of packings of congruent regular tetrahedra in \(\mathbb R^3\) (arbitrary rotations, periodic or nonperiodic) is determined exactly, certifying or refuting that it equals \(4000/4671\approx0.856347\).
why: It would settle a basic packing optimum for nonspherical particles and provide a rigorous benchmark that calibrates computational crystal-structure searches.
key_works: Elizabeth Chen, Michael Engel and Sharon Glotzer (2010), [*Dense crystalline dimer packings of regular tetrahedra*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1001.0586); Simon Gravel, Veit Elser and Yoav Kallus (2011), [*Upper bound on the packing density of regular tetrahedra and octahedra*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1008.2830).

title: Voronoi’s parallelohedron conjecture
open: Is every convex polytope that tiles \(\mathbb R^d\) by translations affinely equivalent to the Dirichlet–Voronoi cell of some lattice?
status: Posed in 1908. Many structural classes are known. Garber's proof for all five-dimensional parallelohedra was published in 2025 (arXiv:1906.05193); earlier, Garber, Gavrilyuk and Magazinov (2014) settled parallelohedra with simply connected \(\delta\)-surface (arXiv:1212.1019). The universal cases in dimensions at least six remain open.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) is given for all dimensions, with the universal cases in dimension at least six settled.
why: It would classify convex translational tiles through the theory of quadratic forms and nearest-lattice-point geometry.
key_works: Alexey Garber (2025), [*Voronoi conjecture for five-dimensional parallelohedra*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.05193); Alexey Garber, Andrey Gavrilyuk and Alexander Magazinov (2014), [*The Voronoi conjecture for parallelohedra with simply connected \(\delta\)-surface*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1212.1019).

title: Gilbert–Pollak Steiner-ratio conjecture
open: How much shorter can a connecting network get if you are allowed to add new junction points? The conjecture says that for every finite planar point set, the Euclidean Steiner minimum tree has length at least \(\sqrt3/2\) times the Euclidean minimum spanning tree length, with equality attained by equilateral triangles.
status: Proposed in 1968 by Gilbert and Pollak. A famous claimed complete proof contains a gap. Ke and collaborators' published 2026 work reports the certified partial lower bound \(0.8559\), below the conjectured \(0.866025\ldots\). Key works: Edgar Gilbert and Henry Pollak (1968), *Steiner minimal trees*; Yisi Ke, Tianyu Huang, Yankai Shu, Di He, Jingchu Gai and Liwei Wang (2026), [*Towards Solving the Gilbert-Pollak Conjecture via Large Language Models*](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v306/ke26a.html).
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that the Steiner ratio \(\inf \operatorname{SMT}/\operatorname{MST}\) over all finite planar point sets equals \(\sqrt3/2 \approx 0.866025\), with equality exactly at equilateral-triangle configurations.
why: It determines the largest possible saving obtainable by introducing additional junctions into a shortest connecting network, a fundamental limit for network design with freely placeable intermediate nodes.
key_works: Edgar Gilbert and Henry Pollak (1968), *Steiner minimal trees*; Yisi Ke, Tianyu Huang, Yankai Shu, Di He, Jingchu Gai and Liwei Wang (2026), [*Towards Solving the Gilbert-Pollak Conjecture via Large Language Models*](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v306/ke26a.html).

title: Unbounded fatness of convex four-polytopes
open: Can the fatness of convex four-dimensional polytopes be made arbitrarily large? Equivalently, is there a constant C such that every convex 4-polytope has fatness at most C?
status: The problem was highlighted by Eppstein–Kuperberg–Ziegler in 2003. Known constructions exceed the bounds available for simple or simplicial polytopes, and strongly regular cell decompositions of the three-sphere can have unbounded fatness — but convex realizability remains the crucial additional constraint.
solved_when: Either an explicit construction of convex 4-polytopes with fatness exceeding any prescribed bound is given, or a universal upper bound on the fatness of convex 4-polytopes is proved.
why: It would settle a major qualitative uncertainty about which face vectors are realizable by convex polytopes in dimension four.
key_works: David Eppstein, Greg Kuperberg and Günter Ziegler (2003), [*Fat 4-polytopes and fatter 3-spheres*](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0204007); Günter Ziegler (2004), *Face numbers of 4-polytopes and 3-spheres*.

title: Optimal size of planar weak epsilon-nets
open: What is the minimum number of points needed to pierce every convex region that contains at least an \(\epsilon\)-fraction of a given finite point set in the plane? Formally, determine the optimal worst-case size \(f_2(\epsilon)\) of a weak \(\epsilon\)-net, where the piercing points may lie outside the input set.
status: The problem has been studied since the early 1990s. The best upper bound is due to Rubin, who showed \(f_2(\epsilon)=O(\epsilon^{-3/2-\gamma})\) for every fixed \(\gamma>0\) (Natan Rubin (2022), *An Improved Bound for Weak Epsilon-Nets in the Plane*, https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.02686). The best lower bound is \(\Omega(\epsilon^{-1}\log(1/\epsilon))\), due to Bukh, Matoušek, and Nivasch (2011) in *Lower bounds for weak epsilon-nets and stair-convexity*, leaving an exponent gap between the two.
solved_when: The exact asymptotic order of \(f_2(\epsilon)\) as \(\epsilon \to 0\) is determined, closing the gap between the upper bound \(O(\epsilon^{-3/2-\gamma})\) for every fixed \(\gamma>0\) and the lower bound \(\Omega(\epsilon^{-1}\log(1/\epsilon))\).
why: It settles how efficiently all large convex ranges over a point set can be represented by a small set of witnesses, a measure central to range-searching and discrepancy applications.
key_works: Natan Rubin (2022), [*An Improved Bound for Weak Epsilon-Nets in the Plane*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.02686); Boris Bukh, Jiří Matoušek and Gabriel Nivasch (2011), *Lower bounds for weak epsilon-nets and stair-convexity*.

bib.title: Optimal size of planar weak epsilon-nets

title: Exact planar Hadwiger–Debrunner \((4,3)\) piercing number
open: What is the smallest number of points that always suffices to pierce a finite family of convex sets in the plane with the property that among any four of the sets, some three have a common point? The conjectured answer is three.
status: A concrete case of the 1957 Hadwiger–Debrunner program; the \((p,q)\) theorem establishes finiteness. Gyárfás, Kleitman and Tóth (2001) studied convex sets in the plane with three of every four meeting. McGinnis (2022) improved the universal upper bound from thirteen to nine (*A family of convex sets in the plane satisfying the (4,3)-property can be pierced by nine points*, arXiv:2010.13195), while known examples require three points, leaving \(3\le h\le 9\).
solved_when: The exact least integer \(h\) is determined; currently the gap is \(3\le h\le 9\), so success means proving \(h=3\) or exhibiting a family requiring four or more piercing points.
why: It would quantify exactly how a local intersection condition on every four sets forces a small global transversal.
key_works: Daniel McGinnis (2022), [*A family of convex sets in the plane satisfying the \((4,3)\)-property can be pierced by nine points*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.13195); András Gyárfás, Daniel Kleitman and Géza Tóth (2001), *Convex sets in the plane with three of every four meeting*.

title: Polynomial-time rotation distance
open: Can the minimum number of rotations needed to transform one ordered rooted binary tree into another with the same ordered leaves be computed exactly in polynomial time? Equivalently, can the exact flip distance between triangulations of a convex polygon be computed in polynomial time?
status: Open since the classical 1980s work on rotation distance. Constant-factor approximation and fixed-parameter algorithms in the distance are known; Cleary–St. John obtain a linear-size kernel. General polynomial-time exact computation remains unresolved. Key works: Sean Cleary and Katherine St. John (2009), [Rotation distance is fixed-parameter tractable](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ipl.2009.04.023); Anoop S. K. M. and Jayalal Sarma (2023), [On Rotation Distance of Rank Bounded Trees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.03985).
solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm is given that outputs the exact rotation distance (equivalently, the exact flip distance between convex-polygon triangulations) for any pair of trees, or the problem is shown to be hard for exact computation.
why: It would settle the complexity of a fundamental local reconfiguration metric used in data structures and associahedron geometry.
key_works: Sean Cleary and Katherine St. John (2009), [*Rotation distance is fixed-parameter tractable*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ipl.2009.04.023); Anoop S. K. M. and Jayalal Sarma (2023), [*On Rotation Distance of Rank Bounded Trees*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.03985).

title: Conway’s thrackle conjecture
open: Can every finite simple graph drawn in the plane so that each pair of distinct edges meets exactly once—either at a shared endpoint or a proper crossing—have at most as many edges as vertices? In Conway's terminology, is every thrackle satisfying the inequality \(m \le n\)?
status: The conjecture was posed in the late 1960s and remains open. Straight-line thrackles are known to satisfy it. Xu's 2021 general improvement gives coefficient \(1.393\) in the corresponding connected bound; unrestricted drawings with curved edges remain unresolved.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that any such drawing of a graph with \(n\) vertices has at most \(n\) edges; in particular, resolving the unrestricted case with curved edges, beyond the known straight-line case and the best known connected bound with coefficient \(1.393\).
why: It probes how strongly an extreme pairwise intersection rule constrains a graph's global size—a natural test case for the interaction between local drawing conditions and global counting.

title: Explicit point sets with optimal linear dimension dependence
open: Can one construct, deterministically and in time polynomial in \(d\) and \(1/\epsilon\), a rational point set \(P\subset[0,1]^d\) of size \(O(d\epsilon^{-2})\) whose star discrepancy is at most \(\epsilon\), uniformly for all \(d\ge1\) and \(0<\epsilon<1\)? Here star discrepancy means the largest error over all axis-parallel boxes anchored at the origin.
status: Heinrich–Novak–Wasilkowski–Woźniakowski (2001) proved by probabilistic methods that such point sets exist. Dick–Pillichshammer's 2025/2026 work obtains almost-optimal dimension dependence using randomly shifted (digitally shifted Korobov polynomial) lattice constructions. A deterministic polynomial-time construction attaining the stated bound remains open.
solved_when: A deterministic algorithm, running in time polynomial in \(d\) and \(1/\epsilon\), outputs rational points \(P\subset[0,1]^d\) with \(|P|=O(d\epsilon^{-2})\) and star discrepancy at most \(\epsilon\), for every \(d\ge1\) and \(0<\epsilon<1\).
why: It would convert optimal high-dimensional integration guarantees into efficiently reproducible deterministic point sets, removing the reliance on probabilistic existence or randomized shifts.
key_works: Stefan Heinrich, Erich Novak, Grzegorz Wasilkowski and Henryk Woźniakowski (2001), *The inverse of the star-discrepancy depends linearly on the dimension*; Josef Dick and Friedrich Pillichshammer (2025/2026), [*The star discrepancy of a union of randomly digitally shifted Korobov polynomial lattice point sets depends polynomially on the dimension*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.15877).

title: Whitehead’s asphericity conjecture
open: Must every connected subcomplex of an aspherical two-dimensional CW complex be aspherical? Here aspherical means that all homotopy groups in dimensions at least two vanish.
status: Open since Whitehead's 1941 work. Diagrammatic methods establish many special classes, including suitable labeled oriented trees; rational and \(p\)-adic analogues have advanced (A. M. Mikhovich, 2025, [Rational and \(p\)-adic analogues of J. H. C. Whitehead's conjecture](https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/im9597)). The original integral conjecture remains open.
solved_when: A proof or counterexample is given for arbitrary connected subcomplexes of aspherical two-dimensional CW complexes over the integers.
why: It would explain when deleting cells preserves the absence of higher homotopy, connecting cell combinatorics with group presentations.
key_works: Stephan Rosebrock (2026), [*Labelled Oriented Trees and the Whitehead Conjecture*](https://www.mathematik.uni-mainz.de/en/2026/01/12/mathematics-colloquium-15-1-26-stephan-rosebrock-karlsruhe-labelled-oriented-trees-and-the-whitehead-conjecture/); A. M. Mikhovich (2025), [*Rational and \(p\)-adic analogues of J. H. C. Whitehead’s conjecture*](https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/im9597).

title: Decidability of embedding two-complexes in four-space
open: Is there an algorithm that, given a finite two-dimensional simplicial complex, decides whether it admits a PL embedding into \(\mathbb R^4\) — or is this problem undecidable? Formally: determine the decidability of PL embeddability of finite 2-complexes in \(\mathbb R^4\).
status: This is a longstanding exceptional case in algorithmic embedding theory. The problem is known to be NP-hard (Matoušek–Tancer–Wagner 2011, *Hardness of embedding simplicial complexes in \(\mathbb R^d\)*), and deleted-product obstructions are incomplete. Georgakopoulos–Winter's 2024 work (*On 2-complexes embeddable in 4-space, and the excluded minors of their underlying graphs*) develops embeddability-preserving operations without settling decidability.
solved_when: A decision algorithm for PL embeddability of finite 2-complexes into \(\mathbb R^4\) is given, or undecidability of the problem is proved.
why: A solution would locate a fundamental limit of finite topological computation in a critical codimension, settling the longstanding exceptional case of algorithmic embedding theory.
key_works: Agelos Georgakopoulos and Martin Winter (2024), [*On 2-complexes embeddable in 4-space, and the excluded minors of their underlying graphs*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.12681); Jiří Matoušek, Martin Tancer and Uli Wagner (2011), *Hardness of embedding simplicial complexes in \(\mathbb R^d\)*.

title: FPRAS for unrestricted integer contingency tables
open: Can we efficiently estimate, with high probability and within relative error \(\epsilon\), the number of nonnegative integer matrices with prescribed row and column sums, when both the number of rows and the number of columns are allowed to grow? Formally, the goal is a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme running in time polynomial in the binary input length and \(1/\epsilon\) for arbitrary margins.
status: The problem has been studied intensively since the 1990s. FPRAS algorithms are known when one dimension is fixed and in sufficiently large-margin regimes, notably in work of Martin Dyer, Ravi Kannan and John Mount (1997), *Sampling contingency tables*, and Mary Cryan, Martin Dyer and Dana Randall (2010), [*Approximately Counting Integral Flows and Cell-Bounded Contingency Tables*](https://doi.org/10.1137/060650544). No known method gives the required uniform guarantee for arbitrary margins and unbounded row and column counts.
solved_when: An FPRAS exists that, for any instance with unbounded numbers of rows and columns and arbitrary row/column sums, outputs an estimate within relative error \(\epsilon\) with high probability, in time polynomial in the binary input length and \(1/\epsilon\).
why: It would enable certified counting, sampling, and exact-margin statistical tests for contingency tables without imposing restrictive assumptions on the table's dimensions or margins.
key_works: Martin Dyer, Ravi Kannan and John Mount (1997), *Sampling contingency tables*; Mary Cryan, Martin Dyer and Dana Randall (2010), [*Approximately Counting Integral Flows and Cell-Bounded Contingency Tables*](https://doi.org/10.1137/060650544).

title: Unique Games conjecture
open: For every \(0<\epsilon<1/2\), is there an alphabet size for which it is NP-hard to distinguish permutation-constraint instances with optimum at least \(1-\epsilon\) from those with optimum at most \(\epsilon\)?
status: Proposed by Khot in 2002 (Khot, *On the power of unique 2-prover 1-round games*, https://doi.org/10.1145/509907.510017). Subexponential algorithms and major hardness theorems for related 2-to-2 games constrain the possibilities (Khot, Minzer, Safra, *Pseudorandom sets in Grassmann graph have near-perfect expansion*, https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2023.198.1.1). The corresponding results with imperfect completeness do not establish the required near-perfect-completeness statement for unique constraints.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) of the above hardness statement for permutation-constraint instances at every \(0<\epsilon<1/2\), with the near-perfect-completeness case settled.
why: Would establish sharp approximation barriers for many combinatorial optimization problems from one constraint-satisfaction hypothesis.
key_works: Subhash Khot (2002), [*On the power of unique 2-prover 1-round games*](https://doi.org/10.1145/509907.510017); Subhash Khot, Dor Minzer and Muli Safra (2023), [*Pseudorandom sets in Grassmann graph have near-perfect expansion*](https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2023.198.1.1).

title: Log-rank conjecture
open: Can two parties always communicate efficiently when their communication matrix has low rank? Formally, is the deterministic communication complexity of every nonzero finite Boolean matrix \(M\) bounded by a fixed polynomial in \(1+\log\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb R}(M)\), with universal constants independent of the matrix dimensions?
status: Formulated by Lovász–Saks in 1988. Sudakov–Tomon improve the general upper bound to \(O(\sqrt{\operatorname{rank}M})\) in work published in 2025. Hambardzumyan–Lovett–Shirley's February 2026 revision gives new equivalent formulations, leaving the polylogarithmic target open.
solved_when: A bound of the form \(D(M) \le (1+\log\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb R}(M))^{O(1)}\) is proved for all nonzero finite Boolean communication matrices, with constants independent of the matrix dimensions.
why: It would connect linear-algebraic simplicity of a communication matrix with efficient two-party communication, showing low rank forces short protocols.
key_works: Benny Sudakov and István Tomon (2025), [*Matrix discrepancy and the log-rank conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.18524); Lianna Hambardzumyan, Shachar Lovett and Morgan Shirley (2026), [*The Log-Rank Conjecture: New Equivalent Formulations*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2025/141/).
