title: Differential transcendence of \(\operatorname{Av}(4123,4231,4312)\)
open: Is the generating function for the permutation class Av(4123, 4231, 4312) differentially transcendental, in the sense that it satisfies no nonzero algebraic differential equation over \(\mathbb{Q}(x)\)?
status: The conjecture was made after 5,000 terms failed extensive differential-equation guessing, and it remains open as of the 2026 survey. See Albert–Homberger–Pantone–Shar–Vatter (2018), [*Generating permutations with restricted containers*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1510.00269).
solved_when: A proof is given that no nonzero algebraic differential equation over \(\mathbb{Q}(x)\) is satisfied by the class's generating function; equivalently, a nonzero such differential equation is exhibited to refute the conjecture.
why: It would establish differential transcendence for an unusually small forbidden basis, a rare and sharp result in the permutation-class setting.
key_works: Albert–Homberger–Pantone–Shar–Vatter (2018), [*Generating permutations with restricted containers*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1510.00269).

title: Are Banff and Louise quivers the same class?
open: Are Banff quivers and Louise quivers exactly the same class? Formally, either prove that every Banff quiver is Louise, or exhibit a counterexample — noting that the Louise recursion imposes an additional condition on deleting both endpoints of a covering pair.
status: The question traces to Bucher–Machacek, OPAC-033 (2021). Ervin–Jackson resolve neighboring OPAC questions but the Banff–Louise equality remains open. Key works: Ervin–Jackson (2024), [*Answering two OPAC problems involving Banff quivers*](https://doi.org/10.5802/alco.352); the same authors (2026), [*A topology on the poset of quiver mutation classes*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.20245).
solved_when: A proof that the two classes coincide, or an explicit quiver that is Banff but not Louise.
why: A positive answer would let simpler Banff certificates be used to unlock tools for Louise cluster varieties.
key_works: Ervin–Jackson (2024), [*Answering two OPAC problems involving Banff quivers*](https://doi.org/10.5802/alco.352); the same authors (2026), [*A topology on the poset of quiver mutation classes*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.20245).

title: Shapiro’s plabic move-and-switch conjecture
open: Must any two plabic graphs whose quivers are mutation-equivalent be connected by the prescribed local moves and switches? Equivalently, is mutation equivalence of quivers exactly matched by equivalence of plabic graphs under these local transformations?
status: The implication from the graph transformations to quiver mutation is established; the converse remains open. See Fomin–Pylyavskyy–Shustin–Thurston (2022), [*Morsifications and mutations*](https://doi.org/10.1112/jlms.12566), Conjecture 6.17, and Fomin (2022), [OPAC slides](https://www.samuelfhopkins.com/OPAC/files/slides/fomin.pdf).
solved_when: The move-and-switch equivalence of plabic graphs is proven to hold exactly when their associated quivers are mutation-equivalent, in particular closing the converse direction (moves from mutation).
why: It would replace an algebraic equivalence relation, quiver mutation, with a hands-on planar geometric calculus of local graph transformations.
key_works: Fomin–Pylyavskyy–Shustin–Thurston (2022), [*Morsifications and mutations*](https://doi.org/10.1112/jlms.12566), Conjecture 6.17; Fomin (2022), [OPAC slides](https://www.samuelfhopkins.com/OPAC/files/slides/fomin.pdf).

title: An exact generating function for solid partitions
open: Is there a usable exact formula, or closed functional characterization, for the generating function of solid partitions \(\sum_{n\ge0}p_3(n)q^n\), where \(p_3(n)\) counts coordinatewise-decreasing three-index arrays of nonnegative integers summing to \(n\)?
status: MacMahon's natural product extension of the plane-partition generating function fails already at \(n=6\). Since then, finite enumeration and simulations have advanced (see the asymptotic work of Balakrishnan–Govindarajan–Prabhakar (2012), [*On the asymptotics of higher-dimensional partitions*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1105.6231), and Destainville–Govindarajan (2015), [*Estimating the asymptotics of solid partitions*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.5605)), but no comparable general formula exists.
solved_when: An exact formula or closed functional characterization of \(\sum_{n\ge0}p_3(n)q^n\) is given, in a form that can actually be used to compute or analyze the coefficients.
why: It would settle the first genuinely higher-dimensional partition enumeration, going beyond the two-dimensional case where exact generating functions are known.
key_works: Balakrishnan–Govindarajan–Prabhakar (2012), [*On the asymptotics of higher-dimensional partitions*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1105.6231); Destainville–Govindarajan (2015), [*Estimating the asymptotics of solid partitions*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.5605).

title: The solid-partition entropy limit and constant
open: Does the sequence \(n^{-3/4}\log p_3(n)\) converge as \(n\to\infty\), and if so, what is its limit? A positive answer would identify the exact entropy constant governing the asymptotic growth of solid partitions.
status: Positive finite lower and upper bounds on \(n^{-3/4}\log p_3(n)\) are proved. Limit existence was incorrectly attributed to earlier work; Dai and collaborators (Dai–Prymak–Shadrin–Tikhonov–Temlyakov, 2023, [*On the cardinality of lower sets and universal discretization*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.02113), §1.2) explicitly correct that claim. Simulations by Destainville–Govindarajan (2015) estimate the limit as \(1.822\pm0.001\).
solved_when: The convergence of \(n^{-3/4}\log p_3(n)\) is proved and its limit is determined (matching the simulated estimate \(1.822\pm0.001\), or refuting it).
why: A solution fixes the leading entropy of solid partitions and quantifies precisely how their growth departs from the exactly understood plane-partition case.
key_works: Dai–Prymak–Shadrin–Temlyakov–Tikhonov (2023), [*On the cardinality of lower sets and universal discretization*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.02113), §1.2; Destainville–Govindarajan (2015), *Estimating the asymptotics of solid partitions*.

title: Davenport’s constant for homocyclic groups of higher rank
open: What is the exact value of Davenport's constant \(D(C_n^r)\) for composite \(n\) and rank \(r\ge4\)? In particular, determine precisely for which pairs \((n,r)\) the constant exceeds the naive bound \(r(n-1)+1\).
status: For prime-power exponents the equality \(D(C_n^r) = r(n-1)+1\) holds. Composite exponents lack any general formula, and recent counterexamples to broader bounds (Geroldinger–Yang, 2026, *On a classical zero-sum invariant*) make the analysis of individual group families essential; the structure of extremal zero-sum free sequences is studied in Geroldinger–Liebmann–Philipp (2010/2012), [*On the Davenport constant and on the structure of extremal zero-sum free sequences*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1009.5835).
solved_when: A general formula for \(D(C_n^r)\) is established for composite \(n\) and all \(r\ge4\), together with a complete characterization of when \(D(C_n^r) > r(n-1)+1\).
why: It quantifies how interactions among the primary components of a group alter zero-sum-free behavior, which is the core phenomenon separating composite from prime-power exponents.
key_works: Geroldinger–Liebmann–Philipp (2010/2012), [*On the Davenport constant and on the structure of extremal zero-sum free sequences*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1009.5835); Geroldinger–Yang (2026), *On a classical zero-sum invariant*.

title: Intermediate-length inverse zero-sum conjecture
open: For \(2\le k\le n-2\), must every length-\(2n-2+k\) sequence in \(C_n^2\) with no nonempty zero-sum subsequence of length at most \(2n-1-k\) take the form \(e_1^{[n-1]}e_2^{[n-1]}(e_1+e_2)^{[k]}\) for some basis \(e_1,e_2\)?
status: Grynkiewicz–Liu reduce the problem to prime moduli; significant prime-power ranges and moduli with no prime factor above seven are established (Grynkiewicz–Liu 2021/2022, [*A Multiplicative Property for Zero-Sums I*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.10300), [*II*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.10309)).
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) covering all \(2\le k\le n-2\) and all \(n\) is given for the stated classification.
why: The conjecture interpolates between the inverse Davenport theorem and short-zero-sum endpoint theorems, so a proof would unify these extreme cases into a single structural picture.
key_works: Grynkiewicz–Liu (2021/2022), [*A Multiplicative Property for Zero-Sums I*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.10300), [*II*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.10309).

title: Gao’s relation between short zero sums and EGZ constants
open: Does Gao's identity \(s(G)=\eta(G)+\exp(G)-1\) hold for every finite abelian group, where \(s(G)\) is the smallest length forcing a zero-sum subsequence of exactly \(\exp(G)\) terms and \(\eta(G)\) the smallest length forcing a zero-sum subsequence of some positive length at most \(\exp(G)\)?
status: The problem was formulated by 2003. The lower bound \(s(G)\ge\eta(G)+\exp(G)-1\) is elementary, and equality is known to hold for groups of rank at most two and for numerous families of higher rank. Key works include Gao (2003), *On zero-sum subsequences of restricted size II*, and Girard–Zotova (2025), [*The Erdős–Ginzburg–Ziv constant of rank-two-like \(p\)-groups*](https://hal.science/hal-05333905v1/document).
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) of the identity \(s(G)=\eta(G)+\exp(G)-1\) for all finite abelian groups \(G\); the natural criterion for this problem type, since no partial quantitative targets are stated.
why: It would reduce the exact-length zero-sum obstruction, governed by \(s(G)\), to the short-subsequence invariant \(\eta(G)\), which is typically easier to control.
key_works: Gao (2003), *On zero-sum subsequences of restricted size II*; Girard–Zotova (2025), [*The Erdős–Ginzburg–Ziv constant of rank-two-like \(p\)-groups*](https://hal.science/hal-05333905v1/document).

title: Exact three-dimensional EGZ constants
open: Is the Erdős–Ginzburg–Ziv constant of the three-dimensional cyclic group exactly linear in \(n\) with a parity-dependent constant — that is, \(s(C_n^3)=8n-7\) when \(n\) is even and \(s(C_n^3)=9n-8\) when \(n\) is odd and at least 3?
status: The stated values are known as construction lower bounds, and equality has been established for powers of two and for important odd families, including \(n=3^a5^b\).
solved_when: The identities \(s(C_n^3)=8n-7\) for all even \(n\) and \(s(C_n^3)=9n-8\) for all odd \(n\ge3\) are proved, or a counterexample to either is exhibited.
why: This is the first dimension beyond the planar case, where the Kemnitz theorem settles the analogous two-dimensional constant, so it is the natural testing ground for whether zero-sum theory extends from the plane to genuine three dimensions.
key_works: Gao–Schmid (2007), [*On short zero-sum subsequences II*](https://www.math.univ-paris13.fr/~schmid/personal/schmid_16.pdf); Edel–Elsholtz–Geroldinger–Kubertin–Rackham (2007), [*Zero-sum problems in finite abelian groups and affine caps*](https://www.yvesedel.de/Papers/EEGKR.pdf).

title: Exact four-dimensional EGZ constants at odd exponents
open: Does the four-dimensional Erdős–Ginzburg–Ziv constant of the cyclic group satisfy \(s(C_n^4)=20n-19\) for every odd \(n\ge3\)? In other words, is the affine-cap lower bound also an upper bound at all odd orders?

See Edel–Elsholtz–Geroldinger–Kubertin–Rackham (2007), [*Zero-sum problems in finite abelian groups and affine caps*](https://www.yvesedel.de/Papers/EEGKR.pdf).
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that \(s(C_n^4)=20n-19\) for every odd \(n\ge3\).
why: It would pin down the exact minimal length guaranteeing a zero-sum subsequence of length \(n\) in \(C_n^4\), tying exact zero-sum constants to the finite-geometric structure of higher-dimensional affine caps.

title: Little cross-number conjecture
open: For a finite abelian group written as a direct sum of cyclic groups of prime-power order, is the largest possible cross number of a zero-sum-free sequence exactly the sum over the cyclic factors of \(1 - p_i^{-a_i}\)? In other words, does the Krause–Zahlten value always give the supremum of \(\sum_{g\in S}1/\operatorname{ord}(g)\) over zero-sum-free sequences \(S\)?
status: The conjecture is known to hold for \(p\)-groups and for many mixed-prime families; arbitrary primary combinations remain open. Key works include Kim (2014/2015), [*The Cross Number of Minimal Zero-sum Sequences in Finite Abelian Groups*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.6867), and Bashir–Schmid (2024), [*Sets of Cross Numbers of Sequences over Finite Abelian Groups*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07138).
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) determines, for every finite abelian group \(G\cong\bigoplus_i C_{p_i^{a_i}}\), whether the maximum of \(\sum_{g\in S}1/\operatorname{ord}(g)\) over zero-sum-free sequences equals \(\sum_i(1-p_i^{-a_i})\).
why: The cross number measures zero-sum complexity in a way that accounts for the orders of the elements involved, so settling it would pin down a fundamental invariant governing the structure of zero-sum-free sequences in finite abelian groups.
key_works: Kim (2014/2015), [*The Cross Number of Minimal Zero-sum Sequences in Finite Abelian Groups*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.6867); Bashir–Schmid (2024), [*Sets of Cross Numbers of Sequences over Finite Abelian Groups*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07138).

title: Large cross-number conjecture
open: Is there a clean formula for the largest possible cross number of a minimal zero-sum sequence over a finite abelian group? Specifically, is the maximum cross number always equal to \(1/\exp(G)+\sum_i(1-p_i^{-a_i})\), where \(G\cong\bigoplus_i C_{p_i^{a_i}}\)?
status: The conjecture is known for \(p\)-groups and substantial mixed-prime families, including \(H_p\oplus C_{q^m}\) and \(C_p\oplus C_q\oplus C_r\) for distinct primes; see Kim (2014/2015), [*The Cross Number of Minimal Zero-sum Sequences in Finite Abelian Groups*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.6867) and Bashir–Schmid (2024), *Sets of Cross Numbers of Sequences over Finite Abelian Groups*.
solved_when: The formula \(1/\exp(G)+\sum_i(1-p_i^{-a_i})\) is proved to give the maximum cross number of a minimal nonempty zero-sum sequence over every finite abelian group \(G\), or a counterexample group is exhibited.
why: It determines the largest weighted size of an indecomposable zero-sum relation, a basic structural invariant in zero-sum theory.
key_works: Kim (2014/2015), [*The Cross Number of Minimal Zero-sum Sequences in Finite Abelian Groups*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.6867); Bashir–Schmid (2024), *Sets of Cross Numbers of Sequences over Finite Abelian Groups*.

title: Girard’s tiny-zero-sum conjecture in rank two
open: Must every rank-two finite abelian group satisfy \(t(G)=\eta(G)\), where \(t(G)\) is the smallest length forcing a nonempty zero-sum subsequence with cross number at most one? Formally, is Girard's conjectured equality between these two invariants true for every \(G\) of rank two?
status: Conjectured in 2012. Additional families were proved in 2022, including certain \(C_n^2\) determined by their smallest prime divisor and number of prime factors; see Gao–Hui–Li–Qin–Yin (2022), [*On tiny zero-sum sequences over finite abelian groups*](https://doi.org/10.4064/cm8607-9-2021). The analogous equality in higher rank is false.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that \(t(G)=\eta(G)\) for every finite abelian group \(G\) of rank two, where \(t(G)\) is the threshold forcing a nonempty zero-sum subsequence with cross number at most one.
why: It asks when a short zero sum can simultaneously be economical in element orders, pinning down the exact interplay between length-based and cross-number-based invariants of zero-sum theory.
key_works: Gao–Hui–Li–Qin–Yin (2022), [*On tiny zero-sum sequences over finite abelian groups*](https://doi.org/10.4064/cm8607-9-2021).

bib.title: Girard’s tiny-zero-sum conjecture in rank two

title: Rodney’s duplex conjecture
open: Must every Latin square of order \(n\ge2\) contain a set of \(2n\) cells with exactly two cells in each row, each column, and each symbol? Equivalently, does every Latin square admit a 2-plex (a duplex)?
status: Open since the 1980s. Every group table is known to have a duplex; the case of arbitrary quasigroups remains unresolved. Key works: Vaughan-Lee–Wanless (2003), [Latin Squares and the Hall–Paige Conjecture](https://doi.org/10.1112/S0024609302001613); Wanless (2007), [Transversals in Latin Squares](https://www.dcs.gla.ac.uk/~pat/cpM/jchoco/latinSquares/papers/transversurveyQRSfin.pdf).
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given for the existence of a duplex in every Latin square of order \(n\ge2\); the conjecture fails if some order admits a Latin square with no 2-plex.
why: It would guarantee a balanced substructure in every Latin square even when no transversal exists, as happens in many group tables.
key_works: Vaughan-Lee–Wanless (2003), [*Latin Squares and the Hall–Paige Conjecture*](https://doi.org/10.1112/S0024609302001613); Wanless (2007), [*Transversals in Latin Squares*](https://www.dcs.gla.ac.uk/~pat/cpM/jchoco/latinSquares/papers/transversurveyQRSfin.pdf).

title: Wanless’s maximum duplex decomposition conjecture
open: Can every Latin square of even order be partitioned entirely into duplexes, and every Latin square of odd order be partitioned into duplexes together with a single transversal?
status: This is a strengthening of Rodney's conjecture. The decomposition is known for all solvable group tables and for small orders; however, merely finding a single duplex does not establish a complete decomposition. Key works: Wanless (2002), *A generalisation of transversals for Latin squares*; Wanless (2007), [*Transversals in Latin Squares*](https://www.dcs.gla.ac.uk/~pat/cpM/jchoco/latinSquares/papers/transversurveyQRSfin.pdf).
solved_when: A proof that such a full decomposition exists for every Latin square of even order, and every Latin square of odd order admits a decomposition into duplexes plus one transversal.
why: It would organize the entire square into balanced experimental blocks, and it strengthens Rodney's conjecture.
key_works: Wanless (2002), *A generalisation of transversals for Latin squares*; Wanless (2007), [*Transversals in Latin Squares*](https://www.dcs.gla.ac.uk/~pat/cpM/jchoco/latinSquares/papers/transversurveyQRSfin.pdf).

title: Van Rees’s maximal 3-subsquare conjecture
open: If an order-\(n\) Latin square contains \(n^2(n-1)/18\) order-three subsquares — the maximum possible — must \(n\) be a power of three? In other words, does attaining the maximal number of 3-subsquares force the order to be a power of 3?
status: The expression \(n^2(n-1)/18\) is a proved upper bound. For \(n>1\), equality requires \(n\equiv3\pmod6\) and corresponds to loops whose every isotope has exponent three; see Kinyon–Wanless (2011), [*Loops with exponent three in all isotopes*](https://cs.du.edu/~mathfiles/preprints/nsm-math-preprint-1104.pdf).
solved_when: It is proved (or disproved by counterexample) that every order-\(n\) Latin square attaining \(n^2(n-1)/18\) order-three subsquares has \(n\) equal to a power of three.
why: It tests whether an abundance of tiny subsquares forces global algebraic structure, since extremal equality corresponds to loops whose every isotope has exponent three.
key_works: Kinyon–Wanless (2011), [*Loops with exponent three in all isotopes*](https://cs.du.edu/~mathfiles/preprints/nsm-math-preprint-1104.pdf).
aliases: Order conjecture for van Rees loops.

title: Exact number of reduced Latin squares of order twelve
open: What is the exact number of Latin squares of order twelve whose first row and column read 1,…,12 — the so-called reduced count R₁₂ — together with an enumeration that others can independently verify?
status: Exact enumeration currently reaches order eleven; order twelve remains uncomputed. See McKay–Wanless (2005), [On the number of Latin squares](https://arxiv.org/abs/0909.2101); Stones (2010), *The many formulae for the number of Latin rectangles*.
solved_when: The exact value of R₁₂ is computed and accompanied by an independently checkable enumeration.
why: It extends a major benchmark for counting highly constrained combinatorial arrays, the natural next step beyond order eleven.
key_works: McKay–Wanless (2005), [*On the number of Latin squares*](https://arxiv.org/abs/0909.2101); Stones (2010), *The many formulae for the number of Latin rectangles*.

title: Rapid mixing of the Jacobson–Matthews Latin-square chain
open: Does the Jacobson–Matthews Markov chain on Latin squares of order \(n\) mix rapidly — that is, provably reach near-stationarity in polynomial time? Formally, establish mixing to total-variation error \(\varepsilon\) in time polynomial in \(n\) and \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\), uniformly over starting states.
status: Ergodicity of the chain has been known since Jacobson–Matthews (1996), [*Generating uniformly distributed random latin squares*](https://doi.org/10.1002/(SICI)1520-6610(1996)4:6%3C405::AID-JCD3%3E3.0.CO;2-J), but no polynomial mixing bound is available. Exact sampling alternatives, such as DeSalvo (2015), [*Exact sampling algorithms for Latin squares and Sudoku matrices via probabilistic divide-and-conquer*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.00235), do not establish any mixing guarantee for this chain.
solved_when: A proof that the chain mixes to total-variation distance at most \(\varepsilon\) from the uniform distribution in time polynomial in \(n\) and \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\), with the bound holding uniformly over all starting states.
why: It would give a quantitative, provable guarantee of efficient uniform random generation of Latin squares, turning a widely used empirical method into a certified algorithm.
key_works: Jacobson–Matthews (1996), [*Generating uniformly distributed random latin squares*](https://doi.org/10.1002/(SICI)1520-6610(1996)4:6%3C405::AID-JCD3%3E3.0.CO;2-J); DeSalvo (2015), [*Exact sampling algorithms for Latin squares and Sudoku matrices via probabilistic divide-and-conquer*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.00235).

bib.title: Rapid mixing of the Jacobson–Matthews Latin-square chain

title: Sharp logarithmic constant for binary strength-three covering arrays
open: What is the true leading constant in the asymptotic size of binary strength-3 covering arrays? Formally, determine \(c_3\) in \(\operatorname{CAN}(3,k,2)=(c_3+o(1))\log_2 k\), or show that no such leading constant exists and find the correct asymptotic formulation.
status: The logarithmic order of \(\operatorname{CAN}(3,k,2)\) in \(k\) is known, but the constants achieved by constructions and by lower bounds do not match, leaving \(c_3\) open. Key works: Kleitman–Spencer (1973), *Families of \(k\)-independent sets*; Sarkar–Colbourn (2016/2017), [Upper bounds on the size of covering arrays](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.07809).
solved_when: The constant \(c_3\) is determined (matching upper and lower bounds on the leading constant), or a proof is given that the leading constant fails to exist together with the correct asymptotic formulation of \(\operatorname{CAN}(3,k,2)\).
why: It fixes the irreducible number of tests needed to cover every binary three-way interaction, the benchmark against which all practical covering-array constructions are measured.
key_works: Kleitman–Spencer (1973), *Families of \(k\)-independent sets*; Sarkar–Colbourn (2016/2017), [*Upper bounds on the size of covering arrays*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.07809).

title: Existence of a projective plane of order twelve
open: Does a projective plane of order twelve exist — that is, can one construct a symmetric \(2\!-\!(157,13,1)\) design, or prove that none exists?
status: Twelve is the smallest unsettled plane order. Akiyama–Suetake–Tanaka's 2023 theorem [Projective planes of order 12 do not have a collineation group of order 4](https://doi.org/10.1002/jcd.21869) restricts a possible collineation group to order one, two, or three.
solved_when: Either an explicit symmetric \(2\!-\!(157,13,1)\) design is given, or it is proved that no such design exists.
why: A construction would disprove the prime-power order conjecture; an exclusion would advance finite-plane classification.
key_works: Akiyama–Suetake–Tanaka (2023), [*Projective planes of order 12 do not have a collineation group of order 4*](https://doi.org/10.1002/jcd.21869).

bib.title: Existence of a projective plane of order twelve

title: Hamada’s minimum-rank conjecture
open: Among all block designs sharing the parameters of a fixed projective- or affine-geometry design over \(\mathbb F_{p^e}\), must the geometric design have the smallest rank of its incidence matrix over \(\mathbb F_p\)?
status: Proposed by Hamada in 1973. Several binary and low-dimensional cases are known. The stronger uniqueness assertion is false; minimum rank itself remains open. Key works include Hamada (1973), *On the \(p\)-rank of the incidence matrix of a balanced or partially balanced incomplete block design and its applications to error correcting codes*, and Tonchev (2011), *Finite geometry designs, codes, and Hamada’s conjecture*.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that the geometric design attains the minimum \(\mathbb F_p\)-rank among all designs with the same parameters, for projective- and affine-geometry designs over \(\mathbb F_{p^e}\).
why: It connects finite geometry to the minimum dimension of incidence-generated codes, giving sharp control over the code dimension these designs produce.
key_works: Hamada (1973), *On the \(p\)-rank of the incidence matrix of a balanced or partially balanced incomplete block design and its applications to error correcting codes*; Tonchev (2011), [*Finite geometry designs, codes, and Hamada’s conjecture*](https://digitalcommons.mtu.edu/math-fp/98/).

title: Exact maximum period of binary orientable sequences
open: Is there a closed-form formula, or unified theory, for M_n — the exact maximum period of a binary orientable sequence of window length n — valid for all n? Here a periodic binary sequence is orientable when no two length-n windows are cyclic shifts of one another up to reversal, so an observer seeing a single window can determine both its position on the cycle and the direction of travel; even a provably tight lower-bound construction family is not known.
status: The notion was introduced by Dai, Martin, and Stinson (around 2001) in the study of sequences for robotic localization on cyclic tracks of markers with unknown orientation; the exact venue (Congressus Numerantium / cryptography-and-coding proceedings) requires verification. Known values of M_n for small n come from explicit constructions and exhaustive/backtracking computations; constructions give good lower bounds, but no exact general formula or unified asymptotic theory is known, and recent computational work may have extended the range of exact values (to be verified). Background context comes from de Bruijn sequences B(2,n) of period 2^n (Fredricksen's SIAM Review 1975 survey of full-length nonlinear shift register cycle algorithms), universal cycles (Chung–Diaconis–Graham 1992), and recent arXiv work on computing/constructing maximum-period orientable sequences (to be verified).
solved_when: An exact expression (or equivalent unified characterization) for M_n is proved for all n, together with, at minimum, a construction family achieving M_n provably; the known exact values currently extend only to small n, obtained by search and explicit construction.
why: A solution settles robot self-localization on cyclic tracks — recovering position and orientation from a single window read — and resolves a de Bruijn-style packing problem under reversal equivalence, where the classic 2^n de Bruijn period is unattainable and the exact achievable period resists general characterization.
key_works: Z.-D. Dai, K. Martin, D. R. Stinson, "Orientable sequences", ~2001 (verify venue: Congressus Numerantium / cryptography-and-coding proceedings); H. Fredricksen, "A survey of full length nonlinear shift register cycle algorithms", SIAM Review 1975 (de Bruijn background); recent arXiv work on computing/constructing maximum-period orientable sequences (verify); related: de Bruijn sequences B(2,n) of period 2^n; universal cycles (Chung–Diaconis–Graham 1992).
aliases: orientable sequence maximum period; M_n for orientable sequences; de Bruijn sequences with reversal constraint.

title: The structural correction in the Ray–West formula
open: Can the statistic \(j(\beta)\) in the Ray–West formula be characterized directly in terms of the structure of \(\beta \in S_m\), without computing it indirectly?
status: The Ray–West formula has been known since 2003 (Ray–West, *Posets of matrices and permutations with forbidden subsequences*), and the structural-statistic problem was posed in 2007; it remains open in the 2026 update (Vatter, *An Assortment of Problems in Permutation Patterns*).
solved_when: An explicit structural description of \(j(\beta)\) as a function of \(\beta \in S_m\) is given, or a proof that no such direct characterization exists.
why: A direct characterization would yield structural tests for Wilf equivalence of permutation classes.
key_works: Ray–West (2003), [*Posets of matrices and permutations with forbidden subsequences*](https://eprints.maths.manchester.ac.uk/609/); Vatter (2026), [*An Assortment of Problems in Permutation Patterns*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16355).

title: APN permutations in even dimensions above six
open: Construct an almost-perfect-nonlinear permutation of \(\mathbb F_2^m\) for some even \(m\ge8\), or prove that none exists in any such dimension. APN means that \(F(x+a)+F(x)=b\) has at most two solutions for every \(a\ne0\) and every \(b\).
status: Dillon's dimension-six construction remains the only known even-dimensional example. Extensive dimension-eight searches and exclusions of substantial algebraic classes leave the unrestricted existence question open. See Christof Beierle, Marcus Brinkmann and Gregor Leander (2020), [*Linearly Self-Equivalent APN Permutations in Small Dimension*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.12006).
solved_when: An APN permutation of \(\mathbb F_2^m\) is exhibited for at least one even \(m\ge8\), or it is proved that no APN permutation exists on \(\mathbb F_2^m\) for any even \(m\ge8\).
why: A construction would yield bijective binary substitution boxes with optimal differential behavior for cryptographic use; an impossibility proof would establish a fundamental obstruction to their existence.
key_works: Christof Beierle, Marcus Brinkmann and Gregor Leander (2020), [*Linearly Self-Equivalent APN Permutations in Small Dimension*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.12006).

bib.title: APN permutations in even dimensions above six

title: Packing-scale binary two-deletion codes
open: Can a binary code of length \(n\) correct two arbitrary deletions with redundancy attaining the packing-bound leading coefficient, that is, \((2+o(1))\log_2 n\) bits? A resolution requires either such a construction or a proof that coefficient two is unattainable.
status: The packing bound gives leading coefficient two. Eyal En Gad's September 2026 preprint claims an existential upper bound \(3\log_2 n+O(\log\log n)\); Guruswami–Håstad's explicit construction has leading coefficient four. The coefficient-two target remains unresolved.
solved_when: Either a binary length-\(n\) two-deletion-correcting code family is constructed with redundancy \((2+o(1))\log_2 n\), or it is proved that no such code can achieve leading coefficient two.
why: It settles the true information cost of correcting even two synchronization errors — the exact constant in front of the redundancy, not just its order.
key_works: Vladimir Levenshtein (1966), *Binary codes capable of correcting deletions, insertions, and reversals*; Venkatesan Guruswami and Johan Håstad (2021), [*Explicit two-deletion codes with redundancy matching the existential bound*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.10592); Eyal En Gad (2026), [*Polynomially larger deletion codes by linear hashing of substring counts*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19493).

title: Optimal universal Komlós constant
open: What is the exact value of the optimal universal Komlós constant \(K_*\) — the smallest constant for which Komlós balancing holds uniformly over all Euclidean-normalized constraint matrices? We know \(K_*\) lies in \([1+\sqrt2,\,6.9013)\), but its precise value remains undetermined.
status: September 2026 proof preprints establish finiteness of \(K_*\). Kunisky's constructions give \(K_*\ge 1+\sqrt2\); Akbas–Sra's revised September/October 2026 preprint reports \(K_*<6.9013\). The exact value remains unknown.
solved_when: The exact value of \(K_*\) is determined — equivalently, when matching upper and lower bounds for \(K_*\) are established, closing the gap between the known bounds \(1+\sqrt2 \le K_* < 6.9013\).
why: Determines the unavoidable cost of balancing Euclidean-normalized constraints and sharpens every reduction through Komlós balancing.
key_works: Dmitriy Kunisky (2023), [*The Discrepancy of Unsatisfiable Matrices and a Lower Bound for the Komlós Conjecture Constant*](https://doi.org/10.1137/22M149819X); Emrullah Akbas and Suvrit Sra (2026), [*Tighter bounds on Komlós discrepancy: existence and algorithmic results*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27172).

title: Six-match football-pool covering number
open: What is the exact value of \(K_3(6,1)\), the smallest number of ternary strings of length six whose radius-one Hamming balls cover all \(3^6=729\) strings? Formally, settle the exact covering number for this instance.
status: The established interval is \(71\le K_3(6,1)\le73\). Recent semidefinite and polyhedral methods improve covering-code bounds, but this small football-pool instance remains unresolved; see Dion Gijswijt and Sven Polak (2025/2026), [*Semidefinite lower bounds for covering codes*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01932); Javier Marenco and Pablo Rey (2026), [*An initial polyhedral study of the football pool problem*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.disopt.2026.100946).
solved_when: The value of \(K_3(6,1)\) is determined exactly — either by a covering construction of fewer than 71 ternary strings of length six, or by a certified lower bound matching a construction, thereby closing the gap within the current interval \(71\le K_3(6,1)\le73\).
why: It provides a compact, difficult benchmark for exact covering, symmetry reduction, and certifiable integer optimization, so a resolution would demonstrate methods that transfer to harder covering instances.
key_works: Dion Gijswijt and Sven Polak (2025/2026), [*Semidefinite lower bounds for covering codes*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01932); Javier Marenco and Pablo Rey (2026), [*An initial polyhedral study of the football pool problem*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.disopt.2026.100946).

title: Exponential growth rate of trifferent codes
open: What is the exponential growth rate of the largest trifferent code — a subset of \(\{0,1,2\}^n\) in which any three distinct codewords show all three symbols in at least one coordinate? Formally, determine the asymptotic behavior of the maximum size of such a \(C\subseteq\{0,1,2\}^n\).
status: The problem originates in work on distinguishable differences and perfect hashing. Bhandari–Khetan improved the upper bound to \(O(n^{-2/5}(3/2)^n)\); constructions still do not match the upper exponential base.
solved_when: The asymptotic exponential growth rate of the maximum code size is determined, with matching upper and lower bounds on the exponential base (closing the gap between the \(O(n^{-2/5}(3/2)^n)\) upper bound and current constructions).
why: It isolates the basic three-object separation problem underlying perfect-hash families, and the growth rate governs what is achievable in related zero-error and hashing settings.
key_works: Siddharth Bhandari and Manik Dhar Khetan (2024), [*Improved Upper Bound for the Size of a Trifferent Code*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.02390); Bishnoi, Kielak, Kovács, Nagy, Somlai, Vizer and Zheng (2026), [*The generalized trifference problem*](https://doi.org/10.1109/TIT.2026.3665439).

bib.title: Exponential growth rate of trifferent codes

title: The true asymptotic diamond-free constant
open: What is the true asymptotic maximum size \(\operatorname{La}(n,Q_2)\) of a family in \(2^{[n]}\) containing no four distinct sets \(A,B,C,D\) with \(A\subset B\subset D\) and \(A\subset C\subset D\)? In particular, determine whether \(\operatorname{La}(n,Q_2)/\binom n{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\) converges and identify its limit, noting that this is weak containment, so \(B,C\) need not be incomparable.
status: The longstanding proposed constant \(2\) was disproved by Tompkins's July 2026 construction, which gives \(2.147908-o(1)\). The published upper bound is \(2.20711+o(1)\).
solved_when: The limit of \(\operatorname{La}(n,Q_2)/\binom n{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\) is proven to exist and its exact value is determined.
why: Tests how far forbidden-poset extremal families can depart from unions of consecutive Boolean levels.
key_works: Dániel Tompkins (2026), [*An Improved Lower Bound for Diamond-Free Families*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09497); Dániel Grósz, Abhishek Methuku and Dániel Tompkins (2018), [*An upper bound on the size of diamond-free families of sets*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.06332).

title: Exact binary deletion-channel capacity
open: Determine the capacity \(C_{\mathrm{del}}(d)\) of the channel that independently deletes each input bit with probability \(d\). A complete solution should characterize capacity-achieving inputs and supply a matching converse.
status: Open since Dobrushin's 1967 framework. Papailiopoulos's September 2026 computer-assisted bounds give a midpoint estimate with error below \(0.0095\) bits uniformly in \(d\); the exact capacity function remains unknown.
solved_when: An exact expression (or provably exact characterization) of \(C_{\mathrm{del}}(d)\) for all deletion probabilities \(d\), together with capacity-achieving input distributions and a matching converse, is obtained.
why: It quantifies the optimal communication rate when the receiver loses symbol alignment, which is the fundamental limit for any synchronization-error channel.
key_works: Roland Dobrushin (1967), *Shannon’s theorems for channels with synchronization errors*; Dimitris Papailiopoulos (2026), [*Binary Deletion Channel Capacity to Within One Hundredth of a Bit*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19412), with [computational certificates](https://github.com/anadim/binary-deletion-channel-capacity).

title: Sharp Matrix Spencer constant
open: What is the smallest universal constant \(C\) such that any \(n\) real symmetric \(n\times n\) matrices of operator norm at most one can be assigned signs making the signed sum have operator norm at most \(C\sqrt n\)? The exact value of this sharp Matrix Spencer constant is unknown.
status: August–September 2026 preprints prove the former Matrix Spencer existence conjecture: Emrullah Akbas and Suvrit Sra (2026), [*A Proof of the Matrix Spencer Conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28816), and Zhao Song and Lichen Zhang (2026), [*Matrix Spencer: Eight Standard Deviations Suffice and an Almost-Linear Time Algorithm for Dense Input*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15025). Song–Zhang give an upper constant below \(7.88\) and examples requiring \((2-o(1))\sqrt n\); their algorithm incurs a larger constant. The sharp universal constant remains unknown.
solved_when: The least universal \(C\) is determined — that is, matching upper and lower bounds are proved for the constant in the \(C\sqrt n\) bound (currently the gap is between \((2-o(1))\sqrt n\) lower examples and an upper constant below \(7.88\)).
why: It pins down the unavoidable spectral imbalance when rounding under noncommuting matrix constraints, and thereby the achievable precision of matrix rounding.
key_works: Emrullah Akbas and Suvrit Sra (2026), [*A Proof of the Matrix Spencer Conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28816); Zhao Song and Lichen Zhang (2026), [*Matrix Spencer: Eight Standard Deviations Suffice and an Almost-Linear Time Algorithm for Dense Input*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15025).

title: Complete enumeration of Costas arrays of order thirty
open: Can we completely enumerate all Costas arrays of order thirty, together with a completeness argument that others can replay and verify?
status: Full enumeration has stopped at order twenty-nine since 2011, and the February 2026 account (Gulec and Abolghasemi, [Universal Costas Matrices: Towards a General Framework for Costas Array Construction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.03407)) confirms that boundary; enumerations of symmetric subclasses at larger orders do not establish completeness for unrestricted order thirty, following Drakakis, Iorio, Rickard and Walsh (2011), *Results of the enumeration of Costas arrays of order 29*.
solved_when: Every order-thirty Costas permutation is listed, including each orbit under the square's rotations and reflections, and an independently replayable argument certifies that no further arrays exist.
why: It would measure how sporadic Costas arrays persist beyond the last settled order and provide a demanding benchmark for exact permutation search methods.
key_works: Konstantinos Drakakis, Francesco Iorio, Scott Rickard and John Walsh (2011), *Results of the enumeration of Costas arrays of order 29*; Gulec and Abolghasemi (2026), [*Universal Costas Matrices: Towards a General Framework for Costas Array Construction*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.03407).

bib.title: Complete enumeration of Costas arrays of order thirty

title: A Costas array of order thirty-two
open: Does there exist a Costas array of order thirty-two — that is, a permutation \(\pi\) of \(\{0,\ldots,31\}\) whose displacement vectors \((j-i,\pi(j)-\pi(i))\), for \(i<j\), are all distinct? Either exhibit such a permutation or certify that none exists.
status: Order thirty-two is a longstanding gap in existence tables. Known algebraic constructions skip it, and complete unrestricted enumeration reaches only order twenty-nine (Drakonis 2011, [Open problems in Costas arrays](https://arxiv.org/abs/1102.5727); Gulec and Abolghasemi 2026, [Universal Costas Matrices: Towards a General Framework for Costas Array Construction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.03407)).
solved_when: Either a permutation of \(\{0,\ldots,31\}\) with all displacement vectors distinct is produced, or a proof/certificate establishes that no such permutation exists.
why: It would fill the first missing entry in the existence tables of ideal discrete time-frequency ambiguity patterns, which underlie optimal radar waveform design under finite-alphabet and bandwidth constraints.
key_works: Konstantinos Drakakis (2011), [*Open problems in Costas arrays*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1102.5727); Gulec and Abolghasemi (2026), [*Universal Costas Matrices: Towards a General Framework for Costas Array Construction*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.03407).

bib.title: A Costas array of order thirty-two

title: Exact dynamic exponent of critical two-dimensional Ising
open: For critical nearest-neighbor Ising heat-bath dynamics on the \(L\times L\) torus, with each site updated at rate one, prove that the inverse spectral gap scales as \(L^{z+o(1)}\) for some exponent \(z\), and determine \(z\) exactly.
status: Numerical work suggests \(z\approx 2.17\). Lubetzky–Sly (2012) establish polynomial relaxation at criticality ([Critical Ising on the square lattice mixes in polynomial time](https://arxiv.org/abs/1001.1613)). Masaoka–Soejima–Watanabe's 2025 theorem gives the rigorous lower bound \(z\ge 2\), if the exponent exists, without identifying its exact value ([Rigorous Lower Bound of the Dynamical Critical Exponent of the Ising Model](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10955-025-03456-3)).
solved_when: The exponent \(z\) is proven to exist and its exact value is identified for heat-bath dynamics on the \(L\times L\) torus at criticality, matching or improving on the numerical estimate of approximately \(2.17\) and the rigorous lower bound \(z\ge 2\).
why: It would quantify critical slowing down for the standard local Ising sampler, telling us precisely how relaxation time grows with system size at criticality.
key_works: Eyal Lubetzky and Allan Sly (2012), [*Critical Ising on the square lattice mixes in polynomial time*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1001.1613); Rintaro Masaoka, Tomohiro Soejima and Haruki Watanabe (2025), [*Rigorous Lower Bound of the Dynamical Critical Exponent of the Ising Model*](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10955-025-03456-3).

bib.title: Exact dynamic exponent of critical two-dimensional Ising

title: Existence of forbidden-poset density limits
open: For every fixed finite poset \(P\), does the ratio \(\operatorname{La}(n,P)/\binom n{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\) converge as \(n\to\infty\), where containment means an injective order-preserving map? In particular, can convergence be established without assuming the limit must be an integer?
status: Convergence is known for several classes, including posets whose Hasse diagram is a tree. A 2026 diamond counterexample invalidates stronger predictions about the value of the limit but does not settle general convergence.
solved_when: For every fixed finite poset \(P\), the existence of the limit of \(\operatorname{La}(n,P)/\binom n{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\) is proved.
why: It would assign a stable extremal density invariant to every finite forbidden order pattern, giving forbidden-poset problems the same limiting structure that graph extremal functions enjoy.
key_works: Boris Bukh (2009), [*Set families with a forbidden subposet*](https://arxiv.org/abs/0803.3840); Jerrold R. Griggs and Wei-Tian Li (2017), [*Progress on poset-free families of subsets*](https://people.math.sc.edu/griggs/Survey20171001.pdf).

title: Strong coincidence for irreducible Pisot substitutions
open: For every primitive irreducible unimodular Pisot substitution \( \sigma \), must each pair of letters \(a,b\) be strongly coincident — that is, some iterates satisfy \(\sigma^k(a)=pcu\) and \(\sigma^k(b)=qcv\), where the common letter \(c\) is preceded by prefixes \(p,q\) with identical letter-count vectors?
status: Verified for substantial special classes and large computational families. No general proof or counterexample is known.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) covering all primitive irreducible unimodular Pisot substitutions is given.
why: It would supply a finite combinatorial mechanism behind spectral and tiling properties of substitution systems.
key_works: Marcy Barge and Luca Q. Zamboni (2013), [*Central sets and substitutive dynamical systems*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1301.5745); Scott Balchin (2017), [*A Computational Method for Large Scale Searching of Counterexamples to the Strong Coincidence Conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.05277).

bib.title: Strong coincidence for irreducible Pisot substitutions

title: Polynomial-time colorful Carathéodory search
open: Given \(d+1\) finite rational point sets in \(\mathbb R^d\), each having the origin in its convex hull, find one point of each color whose convex hull contains the origin in time polynomial in the input bit length.
status: The existence theorem dates to Bárány's 1982 work. Meunier–Mulzer–Sarrabezolles–Stein place the search problem in \(\mathrm{PPAD}\cap\mathrm{PLS}\), now known to equal \(\mathrm{CLS}\). General exact polynomial-time search remains unresolved.
solved_when: An algorithm outputs a colorful choice whose convex hull contains the origin, running in time polynomial in the total bit length of the rational input.
why: A polynomial-time search would turn Bárány's fundamental existential convexity theorem into an efficiently usable tool in geometric optimization and related reductions.
key_works: Frédéric Meunier, Wolfgang Mulzer, Pauline Sarrabezolles and Yannik Stein (2017), [*The Rainbow at the End of the Line—A PPAD Formulation of the Colorful Carathéodory Theorem with Applications*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.01921).

title: Deterministic fully polynomial approximation for DNF counting
open: Given a Boolean formula in disjunctive normal form and \(0<\epsilon<1\), deterministically approximate its number of satisfying assignments within relative error \(\epsilon\) in time polynomial in the formula length and \(1/\epsilon\).
status: Karp–Luby’s randomized scheme dates to the 1980s. Deterministic methods handle structural restrictions, but no fully polynomial deterministic scheme handles unrestricted DNF formulas. The 2026 scalable algorithms continue to use randomization.
solved_when: A deterministic algorithm exists that, for any DNF formula and any \(0<\epsilon<1\), outputs an estimate within relative error \(\epsilon\) of the true satisfying-assignment count in time polynomial in the formula length and \(1/\epsilon\).
why: It would remove randomness from a central approximate-counting primitive used in reliability estimation and probabilistic databases.
key_works: Richard Karp and Michael Luby (1983), *Monte-Carlo algorithms for enumeration and reliability problems*; Salil Vadhan (2012), [*Pseudorandomness*](https://people.seas.harvard.edu/~salil/pseudorandomness/pseudorandomness-Apr11.pdf), Open Problems 2.36 and 7.31; Paul Burkhardt, David Harris and Kevin Schmitt (2026), [*Scalable Algorithms for Approximate DNF Model Counting*](https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2026/244).

bib.title: Deterministic fully polynomial approximation for DNF counting

title: Decidability of four-sphere recognition
open: Is there an algorithm that, given a finite triangulation of a closed PL four-manifold, always decides whether it is PL-homeomorphic to the standard four-sphere? A terminating general algorithm or an undecidability theorem would settle the question.
status: Three-sphere recognition is decidable, while sphere recognition in dimensions at least five is undecidable. Dimension four remains exceptional. Discrete-Morse and bistellar-flip searches handle many examples but give no universally terminating procedure.
solved_when: Either a provably terminating algorithm for PL four-sphere recognition on all finite triangulations of closed PL four-manifolds is given, or it is proved that no such algorithm exists.
why: Determines whether complete automated recognition is possible for the most basic four-dimensional manifold.
key_works: Michael Joswig, Davide Lofano, Frank H. Lutz and Mimi Tsuruga (2022), [*Frontiers of sphere recognition in practice*](https://doi.org/10.1007/s41468-022-00092-8), [arXiv:1405.3848](https://arxiv.org/abs/1405.3848).

title: Pair-sum periods for three-move subtraction games
open: Let \(S=\{a,b,c\}\), with \(2\le a<b<c\), \(\gcd(a,b,c)=1\), and \(c\ne a+b\). If the associated Sprague–Grundy sequence is periodic from the start, must its least period belong to \(\{a+b,a+c,b+c\}\)?
status: Explicitly conjectured by Manabe in September 2026. His rotation criterion establishes pure periodicity and exact periods in substantial regions; a necessity result handles period \(a+b\) when \(c\ge2(a+b)\). Key work: H. Manabe (2026), [*Purely Periodic Three-move Subtraction Games*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05358).
solved_when: It is proved (or disproved by explicit counterexample) that every such purely periodic three-move subtraction game with \(2\le a<b<c\), \(\gcd(a,b,c)=1\), \(c\ne a+b\) has least period exactly one of \(a+b\), \(a+c\), or \(b+c\).
why: It would constrain the global behavior of a game sequence using only three elementary numerical combinations of its legal moves.
key_works: H. Manabe (2026), [*Purely Periodic Three-move Subtraction Games*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05358).

bib.title: Pair-sum periods for three-move subtraction games

title: Meissner’s minimum-volume constant-width problem
open: Is the Meissner tetrahedron the least-volume convex body of constant width one in \(\mathbb R^3\)? Either prove that minimum volume among such bodies is attained by a Meissner tetrahedron, or find a smaller body and identify the true minimizers.
status: This is the three-dimensional Blaschke–Lebesgue problem, long standing and open; the planar analogue is solved. Bogosel's 2026 work develops explicit volume formulas for Meissner polyhedra and necessary conditions for minimizing examples, without establishing global optimality.
solved_when: A proof that a Meissner tetrahedron minimizes volume among all convex bodies of constant width one in \(\mathbb R^3\), or an explicit constant-width-one body of strictly smaller volume together with a characterization of the minimizers.
why: It determines how little volume can support the same width in every direction, and supplies a precise target for certified shape optimization.
key_works: Beniamin Bogosel (2026), [*Volume Computation for Meissner Polyhedra and Applications*](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00454-024-00688-0); Bogosel (2026), [*Dangling points in area-minimizing Meissner polyhedra*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19747).

title: Exceptional APN classification
open: Is every polynomial over a characteristic-two finite field that is APN over infinitely many extensions of the base field CCZ-equivalent to a Gold or Kasami–Welch monomial? If not, construct a genuinely new exceptional family.
status: The Aubry–McGuire–Rodier conjecture remains open. Agrinsoni–Janwa–Delgado resolve the Gold-degree case in 2025 and advance the Kasami–Welch-degree case in 2026; the complete classification remains unavailable.
solved_when: A complete classification of exceptional APN polynomials over characteristic-two finite fields is established — either a proof that all such polynomials are CCZ-equivalent to Gold or Kasami–Welch monomials, or an explicit exceptional family inequivalent to these.
why: It would classify the nonlinear difference structures that persist over arbitrarily large field extensions, the core objects in the study of APN functions and their applications to vectorial Boolean functions.
key_works: Agrinsoni, Janwa and Delgado (2025), [*Resolution of the exceptional APN conjecture in the Gold degree case*](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10623-025-01607-x); the same authors (2026), [*Toward resolution of the exceptional APN conjecture in the Kasami–Welch degree case*](https://doi.org/10.1142/S0219498825410269).

s2_matches.title: On the classification of non-exceptional APN functions

title: Dynamic optimality of splay trees
open: Prove that splay trees serve every access sequence within a universal constant factor of the optimal offline binary-search-tree execution, allowing the customary initialization additive term, or exhibit a family with unbounded competitive ratio.
status: Conjectured by Sleator–Tarjan in 1985. A July 2026 preprint by Chmel, Haeupler, Hladík, Koucký, Roeyskoe, Rozhoň, Sladký, and Tarjan proves \(O(\log\log n\,\log^2\log\log n)\) competitiveness — a major improvement, but still superconstant, leaving the conjecture open.
solved_when: Either a proof establishes constant-factor competitiveness of splay trees against the optimal offline BST (with the customary additive initialization term) for all access sequences, or a family of access sequences is exhibited on which splay trees' competitive ratio is unbounded.
why: A positive resolution would show that a simple adaptive data structure exploits every access pattern that any binary-search-tree algorithm can exploit, making splay trees a universal benchmark for BST performance.
key_works: Daniel Sleator and Robert Tarjan (1985), *Self-adjusting binary search trees*; Petr Chmel, Bernhard Haeupler, Richard Hladík, Michal Koucký, Antti Roeyskoe, Václav Rozhoň, Ondřej Sladký and Robert Tarjan (2026), [*Splay trees are almost dynamically optimal*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.18498).

title: Rigorous Coulomb phase of the cubic-lattice dimer model
open: Does the uniform dimer (perfect-matching) model on the cubic lattice in three dimensions, in its zero-flux thermodynamic state, exhibit the predicted Coulomb phase — with connected dimer correlations decaying like \(|x|^{-3}\) and a divergence-free Gaussian-field scaling limit?
status: Huse–Krauth–Moessner–Sondhi's 2003 gauge-field analysis and simulations predict this phase, but no proof exists: planar determinant and height-function methods do not extend to establish the cubic-lattice scaling theory. Three-dimensional dimer behavior remains an active numerical subject, as in Peng–Yan–Yin (2026) on short-time critical dynamics in the classical cubic dimer model.
solved_when: A rigorous proof establishes, for the zero-flux state of the uniform perfect-matching model on the 3D cubic lattice, the dipolar \(|x|^{-3}\) asymptotics of connected dimer correlations and convergence to a divergence-free Gaussian field in the scaling limit.
why: It would derive an emergent gauge field directly from a purely local combinatorial matching constraint, putting the predicted Coulomb phase on rigorous footing.
key_works: David Huse, Werner Krauth, Roderich Moessner and Shivaji Sondhi (2003), [*Coulomb and Liquid Dimer Models in Three Dimensions*](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0305318); Hu-Xiao Peng, Zheng Yan and Shuai Yin (2026), [*Short-time critical dynamics in the classical cubic dimer model*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.15730).

bib.title: Rigorous Coulomb phase of the cubic-lattice dimer model

title: Optimal real sum–product exponent
open: What is the slowest possible growth of both the sumset and the product set of a set of real numbers? Formally, for \(m(n)=\min_{A\subset\mathbb R,\ |A|=n}\max(|A+A|,|AA|)\), determine \(\liminf \log m(n)/\log n\).
status: A 2026 construction of Bloom–Sawin–Schildkraut–Zhelezov, [*The sum-product conjecture is false for real numbers*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.28781), puts the exponent strictly below two; the matching lower and upper exponents remain unknown.
solved_when: The value of \(\liminf \log m(n)/\log n\) is determined, with matching upper and lower bounds.
why: It identifies the correct replacement for the classical real sum-product conjecture, which was refuted by recent counterexamples.
key_works: Bloom–Sawin–Schildkraut–Zhelezov (2026), [*The sum-product conjecture is false for real numbers*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.28781).

title: Polynomial Freiman–Ruzsa over general abelian groups
open: Can every set with small doubling be efficiently covered by structured sets — specifically, if \(|A+A|\le K|A|\) in an arbitrary abelian group, must \(A\) be coverable by \(K^{O(1)}\) translates of a convex coset progression of dimension \(O(\log K)\) and size \(K^{O(1)}|A|\)?
status: The bounded-characteristic cases are solved. Raghavan's 2026 revision gives losses controlled by \((\log K)^{1+\varepsilon}\) [Raghavan (2025/2026), *Improved Bounds for the Freiman–Ruzsa Theorem*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.11217).
solved_when: A proof (or construction) establishes, for every abelian group and every \(A\) with \(|A+A|\le K|A|\), a cover by \(K^{O(1)}\) translates of a convex coset progression of dimension \(O(\log K)\) and size \(K^{O(1)}|A|\).
why: It would give quantitatively efficient structure theorems for approximate additive groups, with polynomial rather than wasteful bounds.
key_works: Raghavan (2025/2026), [*Improved Bounds for the Freiman–Ruzsa Theorem*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.11217).

bib.title: Polynomial Freiman–Ruzsa over general abelian groups

title: Dense infinite Sidon sequences
open: Can one build an infinite Sidon set that is essentially as dense as the trivial upper bound allows — that is, a set \(A\subset\mathbb N\) with all pairwise sums distinct and \(|A\cap[1,N]|=N^{1/2-o(1)}\) for all sufficiently large \(N\)?
status: The problem has been open since the mid-twentieth century. Ruzsa's exponent \(\sqrt2-1\) remains the benchmark as reported in 2026; see Ruzsa (1998), [*An Infinite Sidon Sequence*](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022314X97921922) and Táfula (2026), [*Infinite Sidon-type sets for zero-sum linear forms*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20753).
solved_when: An explicit or probabilistic construction of an infinite Sidon sequence \(A\subset\mathbb N\) is given, with \(|A\cap[1,N]|=N^{1/2-o(1)}\) holding for all sufficiently large \(N\).
why: It would show that the optimal \(N^{1/2}\)-type density achieved by finite Sidon packings can be maintained compatibly along an infinite sequence, closing the gap between finite optimality and infinite construction.
key_works: Ruzsa (1998), [*An Infinite Sidon Sequence*](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022314X97921922); Táfula (2026), [*Infinite Sidon-type sets for zero-sum linear forms*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20753).

title: Distinct subset sums
open: If \(n\) positive integers have all \(2^n\) subset sums distinct, how large must the largest of them be? Prove that the largest element is at least \(c2^n\) for some absolute constant \(c>0\).
status: The problem dates to Erdős in the 1930s. Known lower bounds remain on the \(2^n/\sqrt n\) scale. Dubroff–Fox–Xu (2021), *A note on the Erdős distinct subset sums problem*, and Costa–Della Fiore (2026), [bandwidth refinement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27941), represent recent work on the problem.
solved_when: An absolute constant \(c>0\) is exhibited such that every set of \(n\) positive integers with all subset sums distinct has maximum element at least \(c2^n\).
why: It determines the compression limit for uniquely decodable additive encodings — how small the entries of such a system can be while keeping all subset sums distinct.
key_works: Dubroff–Fox–Xu (2021), *A note on the Erdős distinct subset sums problem*; Costa–Della Fiore (2026), [bandwidth refinement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27941).

title: Chowla’s cosine minimum
open: Prove every \(n\)-element \(A\subset\mathbb N\) has a real \(t\) with \(\sum_{a\in A}\cos(2\pi at)\le-c\sqrt n\).
status: A decades-old target. Shankar’s September 2026 preprint proves a negative excursion of order \(n^{1/5}\).
why: Would sharply control negative excursions of sparse trigonometric polynomials.
key_works: Bedert (2025), [*Polynomial bounds for the Chowla Cosine Problem*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.05260); Shankar (2026), [log-free bound](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05338).

title: Sharp Roth bounds
open: What is the true asymptotic size of the largest subset of \(\{1,\dots,N\}\) containing no three-term arithmetic progression? That is, determine the correct order of \(r_3(N)\) up to constants in the exponent.
status: Roth (1953) initiated the problem. On the upper bound side, Raghavan's 2026 dissertation reports a saving of \(\exp[-(\log N)^{1/6-o(1)}]\); on the lower bound side, constructions achieve square-root logarithmic scale. Key works include Kelley–Meka (2023), *Strong bounds for 3-progressions*, and Raghavan (2026), [*Quantitative Topics in Arithmetic Combinatorics*](https://escholarship.org/uc/item/3f10x5g1).
solved_when: The asymptotic scale of \(r_3(N)\) is pinned down: either the upper and lower bounds are matched, or the gap between the known upper bound saving \(\exp[-(\log N)^{1/6-o(1)}]\) and the square-root-logarithmic scale of the known constructions is closed.
why: \(r_3(N)\) measures how much density is possible in the integers while avoiding the simplest additive pattern, and the gap between upper and lower bounds is a basic quantitative test of our understanding of arithmetic structure.
key_works: Kelley–Meka (2023), *Strong bounds for 3-progressions*; Raghavan (2026), [*Quantitative Topics in Arithmetic Combinatorics*](https://escholarship.org/uc/item/3f10x5g1).

title: Divergent reciprocal sums force long progressions
open: If a set of positive integers has divergent reciprocal sum, must it contain arithmetic progressions of every finite length? Formally, does \(\sum_{a\in A}1/a=\infty\) with \(A\subset\mathbb N\) force \(k\)-term arithmetic progressions in \(A\) for every \(k\)?
status: Posed by Erdős in the 1970s. The three-term case follows from modern bounds; already four terms remains open. See Green (2026), [*Arithmetic progressions at the Journal of the LMS*](https://doi.org/10.1112/jlms.70483).
solved_when: Every set \(A\subset\mathbb N\) with \(\sum_{a\in A}1/a=\infty\) is shown to contain arithmetic progressions of each finite length (with the four-term case being the first open hurdle).
why: It would extend additive-structure phenomena beyond sets of positive density, showing that a purely multiplicative largeness condition already forces long arithmetic progressions.
key_works: Green (2026), [*Arithmetic progressions at the Journal of the LMS*](https://doi.org/10.1112/jlms.70483).

bib.title: Divergent reciprocal sums force long progressions

title: Polynomial saving for square-difference-free sets
open: Must every subset of \([N]\) containing no nonzero square difference have size at most \(N^{1-c}\) for some absolute constant \(c>0\)? In other words, does avoiding square differences force a polynomial power saving over the trivial bound \(N\)?
status: The Furstenberg–Sárközy theorem establishes density decay for such sets; Green–Sawhney (2024/2025) obtain the current best bound \(N\exp(-c\sqrt{\log N})\) in [*New bounds for the Furstenberg–Sárközy theorem*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.17448), which still falls short of a polynomial power saving.
solved_when: An absolute constant \(c>0\) is exhibited such that any \(A\subset[N]\) with no nonzero square difference satisfies \(|A|\le N^{1-c}\) for all sufficiently large \(N\).
why: It would reveal much stronger nonlinear additive expansion than current bounds provide, showing that forbidding square differences is quantitatively far more restrictive than known methods demonstrate.
key_works: Green–Sawhney (2024/2025), [*New bounds for the Furstenberg–Sárközy theorem*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.17448).

title: Sixth Schur number
open: What is the sixth Schur number — the largest \(N\) for which the integers \([N]\) can be colored with six colors so that no monochromatic solution of \(x+y=z\) exists? Equivalently, determine \(S(6)\).
status: \(S(5)=160\) is settled (Heule, 2018, [*Schur Number Five*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.08076)). For six colors, the lower bound \(S(6)\ge536\) stands and remains cited in July 2026 work (Bengone et al., 2026, [*Shifted S-templates and improved lower bounds for Schur numbers*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15034)).
solved_when: The exact value of \(S(6)\) is determined, ideally together with an explicit coloring witnessing \(S(6)\ge N\) and a machine-checkable proof that no such coloring exists beyond it.
why: It is the next concrete frontier for exhaustive arithmetic search, directly testing whether SAT-based proof methods that settled \(S(5)\) can scale to six colors.
key_works: Heule (2018), [*Schur Number Five*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.08076); Bengone et al. (2026), [*Shifted S-templates and improved lower bounds for Schur numbers*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15034).

title: Hales–Jewett number \(HJ(3,3)\)
open: What is the smallest dimension \(n\) such that every three-coloring of the cube \(\{1,2,3\}^n\) contains a monochromatic combinatorial line? Formally, determine the exact value of the Hales–Jewett number \(HJ(3,3)\).
status: The best known lower bound is \(HJ(3,3)\ge22\), established by Mouhib's 2026 work through checkable coloring certificates; see Mouhib (2026), [*Lower Bounds for the Hales–Jewett Numbers via Symmetric and One-Weight Colorings*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22155).
solved_when: The exact value of \(HJ(3,3)\) is determined — that is, an \(n\) is found such that every three-coloring of \(\{1,2,3\}^n\) yields a monochromatic combinatorial line, together with a three-coloring of \(\{1,2,3\}^{n-1}\) avoiding one.
why: It converts the Hales–Jewett theorem, a high-dimensional existence result, into a single exact finite target, sharpening our understanding of how quickly combinatorial lines become unavoidable.
key_works: Mouhib (2026), [*Lower Bounds for the Hales–Jewett Numbers via Symmetric and One-Weight Colorings*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22155).

title: Symmetry of the valley Delta generating function
open: Is the valley Delta generating function symmetric as a polynomial in its label variables? A proof is sought that establishes this symmetry directly, without passing through the full valley Delta operator identity.
status: This is viewed as a distinct intermediate problem. Shin's 2026 preprint proves the symmetry for the area-zero and area-one slices.
solved_when: The symmetry of the valley Delta generating function in the label variables is proved independently of the full operator identity.
why: Symmetry is necessary for any representation-theoretic interpretation of the generating function; without it, such an interpretation cannot get off the ground.
key_works: Shin (2026), [*Exchange identities and symmetric slices of the valley Delta conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14877).

title: Gaussian coefficient \(q\)-Foulkes positivity
open: When do Gaussian binomial coefficients compare coefficientwise? Specifically, for integers \(a\le c\le d\le b\) with \(ab=cd\), is it true that \(\binom{c+d}{c}_q-\binom{a+b}{a}_q\) has all nonnegative coefficients?
status: Generalized Foulkes positivity remains open in general. A corrected July 2026 preprint by Gangl–Gutiérrez–Szwej (2026), *On the generalised Foulkes conjecture for \(\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb C)\) under divisibility conditions* (https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.06220v3), establishes divisibility cases.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof, via an explicit negative coefficient) of the coefficientwise nonnegativity of \(\binom{c+d}{c}_q-\binom{a+b}{a}_q\) for all \(a\le c\le d\le b\) with \(ab=cd\).
why: The statement compares the number of partitions fitting in equal-area rectangles of more balanced shape versus less balanced shape, so a proof would establish a fundamental monotonicity in partition combinatorics.
key_works: Gangl–Gutiérrez–Szwej (2026), [*On the generalised Foulkes conjecture for \(\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb C)\) under divisibility conditions*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.06220v3).

title: Explicit \(q,t\)-Catalan symmetry bijection
open: Is there an explicit, uniform bijection on Dyck paths that simultaneously exchanges the area and bounce statistics (equivalently, area and dinv), explaining the symmetry of the \(q,t\)-Catalan numbers combinatorially?
status: Open since the 1990s. Algebraic symmetry is known, as are bijections for special families; see Lee–Li–Loehr (2018), [*A Combinatorial Approach to the Symmetry of \(q,t\)-Catalan Numbers*](https://doi.org/10.1137/16M1059916), and Qu–Zhang's [refined variants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08196).
solved_when: A single direct bijection on Dyck paths, defined uniformly for all \(n\), is constructed and proved to exchange area with bounce (or area with dinv), thereby giving a bijective proof of the \(q,t\)-Catalan symmetry.
why: It would reveal the mechanism behind a fundamental two-statistic symmetry, replacing algebraic symmetry arguments with a concrete combinatorial explanation.
key_works: Lee–Li–Loehr (2018), [*A Combinatorial Approach to the Symmetry of \(q,t\)-Catalan Numbers*](https://doi.org/10.1137/16M1059916); Qu–Zhang, [refined variants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08196).

title: Trivariate diagonal-harmonic dimension
open: Is the dimension of the trivariate diagonal-harmonic module $DH_n^{(3)}$ equal to $2^n(n+1)^{n-2}$, as Haiman predicted — and if so, what symmetric-group character realizes it?
status: A longstanding Haiman prediction. The corresponding Tamari enumeration is proved, but its identification with the trivariate module is not.
solved_when: A proof that $\dim DH_n^{(3)} = 2^n(n+1)^{n-2}$, ideally together with an identification of the predicted symmetric-group character.
why: It would extend the diagonal-harmonics correspondence to three sets of variables, anchoring the module's combinatorial structure.
key_works: Bergeron–Préville-Ratelle (2012), [*Higher Trivariate Diagonal Harmonics via generalized Tamari Posets*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1105.3738).

title: Combinatorial invariance of Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials
open: Do isomorphic Bruhat intervals always carry the same Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials, even when the intervals come from different Coxeter groups? In other words, is \(M_{x,w}(q)\) determined by the isomorphism type of the interval \([u,w]\) as a poset?
status: The conjecture is attributed to Lusztig and Dyer, around 1983. A 2026 result of Barkley–Gaetz–Lam proves invariance of the coefficient of \(q\), which settles the conjecture for intervals of length at most six. See Barkley–Gaetz–Lam (2026), [*Combinatorial invariance for the coefficient of \(q\) in Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.07793).
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the conjecture for all Bruhat intervals in all Coxeter groups; in particular, a proof that poset-isomorphic intervals \([u,w]\cong[u',w']\) satisfy \(M_{x,w}(q)=M_{x',w'}(q)\) for all corresponding elements.
why: It would show that local intersection cohomology of Schubert varieties can be read off from abstract order data of the Bruhat poset, with no reference to the ambient group.
key_works: Barkley–Gaetz–Lam (2026), [*Combinatorial invariance for the coefficient of \(q\) in Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.07793).

title: Vanishing density of character-table zeros
open: For independently uniform partitions \(\lambda,\mu\vdash n\), prove or refute \(\Pr[\chi^\lambda(\mu)=0]\to0\).
status: Large-scale experiments support the conjecture. Related zero-pattern theorems do not establish overall density.
why: Determines the global sparsity of symmetric-group character tables.
key_works: Miller–Scheinerman (2025), [*Large-scale Monte Carlo simulations for zeros in character tables of symmetric groups*](https://doi.org/10.1090/mcom/3964); Peluse–Soundararajan (2026), [*Zeros in the character table of the symmetric group*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.28510).

title: Subpolynomially many zero-free character columns
open: Can the number of conjugacy classes of \(S_n\) on which every irreducible character takes a nonzero value be subpolynomial in \(n\)? Formally, if \(D(n)\) counts such zero-free columns of the \(S_n\) character table, prove \(D(n)=O_\varepsilon(n^\varepsilon)\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\).
status: The problem was conjectured in August 2026. The best proved general bound is \(D(n)\ll n^{3/4}\); see Defant–Hariharan–Lau–Ono (2026), [*Zero-free columns in character tables of symmetric groups*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27718).
solved_when: A proof establishes \(D(n)=O_\varepsilon(n^\varepsilon)\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\).
why: It quantifies how rare the exceptional conjugacy classes are — those seen nontrivially by every irreducible character of \(S_n\).
key_works: Defant–Hariharan–Lau–Ono (2026), [*Zero-free columns in character tables of symmetric groups*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27718).

title: Natural ASM–TSSCPP bijection
open: Is there a natural, direct bijection between \(n\times n\) alternating-sign matrices and totally symmetric self-complementary plane partitions in the corresponding \(2n\)-box? Equivalently, a structural map explaining their equal counts without passing through indirect enumeration machinery.
status: Equal enumeration has been known since the 1990s, but a natural general bijection remains missing. Related progress appears in Holmlund–Striker on [magog matrices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.03564) and Bansal–Striker (2026), [*The Many Faces of Magog Matrices*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.00079).
solved_when: An explicit bijection is given between \(n\times n\) alternating-sign matrices and totally symmetric self-complementary plane partitions in the \(2n\)-box, for all \(n\), in a form regarded as natural (structural rather than a composition of artificial steps).
why: It would explain a striking correspondence between integrable combinatorial models, turning a mysterious equinumerosity into structural insight.
key_works: Holmlund–Striker, [magog matrices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.03564); Bansal–Striker (2026), [*The Many Faces of Magog Matrices*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.00079).

title: Explicit binary codes meeting Gilbert–Varshamov
open: Can we deterministically construct, in time polynomial in the blocklength, a binary linear code whose relative distance is \(\delta\) and whose rate is at least \(1 - H_2(\delta) - \varepsilon\)?
status: Random codes achieve the existential target. Recent trace-code approaches require stronger character-sum estimates; see Cohen–Doron–Goldgraber–Manket (2026), [*Tracing AG Codes: Toward Meeting the Gilbert–Varshamov Bound*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.08788).
solved_when: A deterministic algorithm outputs, in time polynomial in the blocklength, a binary linear code with relative distance \(\delta\) and rate at least \(1 - H_2(\delta) - \varepsilon\), for any given \(\delta\) and \(\varepsilon\).
why: It would make the probabilistic Gilbert–Varshamov benchmark reproducibly constructible rather than merely existential.
key_works: Cohen–Doron–Goldgraber–Manket (2026), [*Tracing AG Codes: Toward Meeting the Gilbert–Varshamov Bound*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.08788).

title: Asymptotically good binary cyclic codes
open: Can binary cyclic linear codes achieve both positive rate and positive relative distance in the limit of unbounded code lengths?
status: Open since the 1960s; good quasi-cyclic constructions are known but do not settle the cyclic case. Related work includes Aliabadi–Kalaycı–Zadehdabbagh (2026), [*Asymptotic performance of double circulant and four circulant codes with small hull dimension*](https://doi.org/10.1007/s12095-025-00861-z); connections run to Artin's primitive-root conjecture and finite-field uncertainty principles.
solved_when: An explicit infinite family of binary cyclic linear codes is exhibited whose rates and relative distances are each bounded below by positive absolute constants as the length grows without bound.
why: It tests whether maximal shift symmetry is compatible with efficient error correction.
key_works: Aliabadi–Kalaycı–Zadehdabbagh (2026), [*Asymptotic performance of double circulant and four circulant codes with small hull dimension*](https://doi.org/10.1007/s12095-025-00861-z).
