title: Remaining finite cases of Brualdi–Stein
open: Does every Latin square of order \(n\) contain a partial transversal of size \(n-1\), for every order \(n\)?
status: The sufficiently-large-\(n\) case is proved; eliminating all remaining finite exceptions is unresolved. Key works: Stein (1975), *Transversals of Latin squares and their generalizations*; Montgomery (2024), [*Transversals in Latin Squares*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.19873).
solved_when: Every Latin square of every finite order \(n\) — with no exceptions — is shown to have a partial transversal of size \(n-1\); all remaining finite cases beyond the proved sufficiently-large-\(n\) range are eliminated.
why: It would convert the existing asymptotic guarantee into an exact all-order theorem, closing the Brualdi–Stein conjecture completely.
key_works: Stein (1975), *Transversals of Latin squares and their generalizations*; Montgomery (2024), [*Transversals in Latin Squares*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.19873).

title: Existence of \(S(3,6,46)\)
open: Does a Steiner system \(S(3,6,46)\) exist — 759 six-element blocks on 46 points covering every triple exactly once?
status: The necessary arithmetic conditions are satisfied, but the 2025–2026 construction table (Kiermaier–Krčadinac–Wassermann, *Steiner 3-designs as extensions*, [arXiv:2509.23483](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.23483); [construction table](https://web.math.pmf.unizg.hr/~krcko/results/steiner3.html)) leaves existence unresolved.
solved_when: An explicit \(S(3,6,46)\) is constructed, or a proof of nonexistence is given.
why: It probes the gap between arithmetic admissibility and actual realizability of a design.
key_works: Kiermaier–Krčadinac–Wassermann, [*Steiner 3-designs as extensions*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.23483); [construction table](https://web.math.pmf.unizg.hr/~krcko/results/steiner3.html).

title: Tusnády’s box-discrepancy problem
open: How large must the discrepancy of axis-parallel boxes be for \(n\) points in fixed dimension \(d\)? Formally, determine the worst-case box discrepancy up to constant factors depending only on \(d\).
status: The 2026 monograph records a lower bound of \(\Omega(\log^{d-1}n)\) and an upper bound of \(O(\log^{d-1/2}n)\), leaving a half-logarithmic gap. See Nikolov (2017), [*Tighter Bounds for the Discrepancy of Boxes and Polytopes*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.05532); Bansal–Nikolov (2026), [*Discrepancy Theory*](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.00140v1).
solved_when: Matching upper and lower bounds are proved for the worst-case discrepancy of axis-parallel boxes on \(n\) points in fixed dimension \(d\), closing the gap between \(\Omega(\log^{d-1}n)\) and \(O(\log^{d-1/2}n)\).
why: The answer directly controls the error of geometric sampling and range counting, since box discrepancy governs how uniformly a point set estimates axis-parallel range counts.
key_works: Nikolov (2017), [*Tighter Bounds for the Discrepancy of Boxes and Polytopes*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.05532); Bansal–Nikolov (2026), [*Discrepancy Theory*](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.00140v1).

title: Optimal star-discrepancy exponent
open: What is the correct logarithmic exponent in the minimum star discrepancy of \(n\) points in \([0,1]^d\), for each fixed \(d\ge3\)? That is, determine the power of \(\log n\) governing the best achievable star discrepancy in fixed dimension.
status: Classical lower and upper powers of \(\log n\) remain separated, so the optimal exponent is unknown in dimensions \(d\ge3\); dimension two behaves differently. Related work includes Clément–Doerr–Klamroth–Paquete (2025), [*Searching permutations for constructing uniformly distributed point sets*](https://doi.org/10.1090/bproc/254), and the problem is connected to the Brownian-sheet small-ball inequality.
solved_when: For each fixed \(d\ge3\), the exponent of \(\log n\) in the minimum star discrepancy of \(n\) points in \([0,1]^d\) is determined, closing the gap between the classical lower and upper powers.
why: A solution would identify the optimal deterministic integration accuracy achievable by uniformly distributed point sets.
key_works: Clément–Doerr–Klamroth–Paquete (2025), [*Searching permutations for constructing uniformly distributed point sets*](https://doi.org/10.1090/bproc/254).

title: Fractional complex illumination
open: Is every complex norm ball in \(\mathbb C^d\) fractionally illuminable with weight at most \(2^d\)? Formally, does the fractional illumination number of every complex norm ball in \(\mathbb C^d\) not exceed \(2^d\)?
status: Proposed in 2024; known results cover complex zonoids only, leaving arbitrary norm balls unresolved (Rotem–Schejter–Slomka (2026), *The complex Illumination problem*, Conjecture 1.2).
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given for the bound \(2^d\) on the fractional illumination number of every complex norm ball in \(\mathbb C^d\).
why: It would establish the sharp weighted relaxation of complex illumination, settling the natural fractional analogue of the complex illumination problem for arbitrary norm balls.
key_works: Rotem–Schejter–Slomka (2026), [*The complex Illumination problem*](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00493-025-00195-7), Conjecture 1.2.

title: Borsuk’s problem in four dimensions
open: What is the smallest number of pieces of smaller diameter into which every bounded subset of four-dimensional Euclidean space can be partitioned? Equivalently, determine the exact value of the Borsuk number \(b(4)\).
status: The remaining interval is \(5\le b(4)\le 8\), following a 2026 upper-bound preprint by Tolmachev–Voronov (2026), [*Reducing the upper bound for the Borsuk number in \(\mathbb R^4\) to 8*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.19068).
solved_when: The exact value of \(b(4)\) is determined; the currently open interval is \(5\le b(4)\le 8\).
why: It settles the last low-dimensional frontier of Borsuk's problem, since counterexamples are known in high dimensions while the four-dimensional case remains unresolved.
key_works: Tolmachev–Voronov (2026), [*Reducing the upper bound for the Borsuk number in \(\mathbb R^4\) to 8*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.19068).

title: Five-dimensional kissing number
open: How many unit spheres in five dimensions can all touch a central unit sphere at once? Formally, determine the exact value of the kissing number in \(\mathbb R^5\).
status: The verified interval remains 40–44. Recent constructions, including those of Cohn–Rajagopal (2026), [*Variations on Five-Dimensional Sphere Packings*](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00454-026-00841-x), produce inequivalent 40-point configurations without closing the gap.
solved_when: The kissing number of \(\mathbb R^5\) is determined exactly, pinning it down from the currently known interval of 40 to 44.
why: It resolves the next low-dimensional exact sphere-contact problem, continuing the program of determining kissing numbers dimension by dimension.
key_works: Cohn–Rajagopal (2026), [*Variations on Five-Dimensional Sphere Packings*](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00454-026-00841-x).

title: Convex Moser worm problem
open: What is the smallest possible area of a convex planar set that can contain a copy of every unit-length planar arc, allowing rigid motions? Formally, determine the infimum of the areas of convex sets that are universal covers for all curves of length 1.
status: Open since the 1960s. A September 2026 preprint by Keller reports bounds of approximately 0.239–0.24633.
solved_when: The exact minimum area of a convex universal cover for unit-length arcs is determined, or matching upper and lower bounds are proven for it.
why: It identifies the optimal universal container for flexible one-dimensional objects, resolving the convex variant of a classical covering question in geometry.

title: Extremal exponent of \(K_{4,4}\)
open: What is the true order of growth of the maximum number of edges in an \(n\)-vertex graph with no copy of \(K_{4,4}\)? In particular, is the general upper bound \(O(n^{7/4})\) tight, i.e., is the extremal exponent \(7/4\) attainable?
status: This is a classical Zarankiewicz gap: known constructions give \(\Omega(n^{5/3})\) while the Kővári–Sós–Turán theorem gives \(O(n^{7/4})\). A relevant recent work is Bayer–Mészáros–Rónyai–Szabó (2026), [*Subgraphs of the projective norm graph*](https://doi.org/10.1017/fms.2026.10245).
solved_when: The exponent of \(\operatorname{ex}(n,K_{4,4})\) is determined — either by a construction matching the Kővári–Sós–Turán upper bound \(O(n^{7/4})\), or by an improved upper bound matching the known lower bound \(\Omega(n^{5/3})\).
why: This is among the smallest forbidden bipartite graphs whose extremal exponent is still unknown, so resolving it would close a classical Zarankiewicz gap and set the template for the remaining open bipartite exponents.
key_works: Bayer–Mészáros–Rónyai–Szabó (2026), [*Subgraphs of the projective norm graph*](https://doi.org/10.1017/fms.2026.10245).

title: Binary \(q\)-Fano plane
open: Does there exist a collection of 381 three-dimensional subspaces of \(\mathbb F_2^7\) such that every two-dimensional subspace is contained in exactly one of them? Equivalently, does a binary \(q\)-analogue of the Fano plane — a \(q\)-Steiner system \(S_2(2,3,7)\) — exist?
status: Decades of structural restrictions and partial constructions, including work on putative \(q\)-Fano planes by Honold–Kiermaier (2015) and on alpha-points by Kiermaier (2021), have not settled existence.
solved_when: An explicit set of 381 three-dimensional subspaces of \(\mathbb F_2^7\) is produced in which each two-dimensional subspace lies in exactly one member, or a proof of impossibility is given.
why: It would resolve the first and smallest open case of the vector-space analogue of the Fano plane, and bears directly on optimal constant-dimension network codes.
key_works: Honold–Kiermaier (2015), [putative \(q\)-Fano planes](https://arxiv.org/abs/1504.06688); Kiermaier (2021), [alpha-points](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.00365).

title: Classification of hyperovals
open: Which hyperovals — the \((q+2)\)-point sets of \(\mathrm{PG}(2,q)\) with no three collinear, \(q\) even — actually exist, up to projective semilinear equivalence?
status: Many infinite and exceptional families are known, and low-degree polynomial classifications (e.g., Caullery–Schmidt 2015, [*On the classification of hyperovals*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.aim.2015.07.016)) cover part of the landscape, but they do not extend to arbitrary hyperovals.
solved_when: A complete list of equivalence classes of \((q+2)\)-arcs in \(\mathrm{PG}(2,q)\) for even \(q\) is obtained, with a proof that no further classes exist.
why: Hyperovals are the extremal arcs of finite projective planes, and their classification determines the associated optimal codes and extremal combinatorial structures built from them.

title: Classification of even-characteristic ovoids
open: Can every ovoid of \(\mathrm{PG}(3,q)\) — that is, every \((q^2+1)\)-point cap — be described explicitly when \(q\) is even? A complete classification would determine whether the elliptic quadrics and Tits ovoids exhaust all such objects.
status: Elliptic quadrics and Tits ovoids are known; the general even-characteristic classification remains open. Key works include Tits (1962), *Ovoides et groupes de Suzuki*, and Hirschfeld–Thas (2025), [*Arcs, Caps and Generalisations in a Finite Projective Space*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.06243).
solved_when: Every \((q^2+1)\)-point cap in \(\mathrm{PG}(3,q)\) for even \(q\) is shown to be either an elliptic quadric or a Tits ovoid, or an additional family is exhibited.
why: Ovoids govern extremal finite incidence structures and projective codes, so a classification pins down the sharp examples in both settings.
key_works: Tits (1962), *Ovoides et groupes de Suzuki*; Hirschfeld–Thas (2025), [*Arcs, Caps and Generalisations in a Finite Projective Space*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.06243).

title: Regularity of pseudo-ovals
open: Must every pseudo-oval of \(q^n+1\) mutually disjoint \((n-1)\)-spaces in \(\mathrm{PG}(3n-1,q)\), any three spanning, arise by field reduction? Equivalently, is every such configuration the field-reduction image of a classical oval?
status: All known examples are regular; positive theorems require additional spread hypotheses. Key reference: Hirschfeld–Thas (2025), [*Arcs, Caps and Generalisations in a Finite Projective Space*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.06243), Open Problem 3.
solved_when: A proof that every such pseudo-oval arises by field reduction, or an explicit counterexample that does not.
why: It asks whether a larger geometric category contains fundamentally new objects beyond the classical ones obtainable by field reduction.
key_works: Hirschfeld–Thas (2025), [*Arcs, Caps and Generalisations in a Finite Projective Space*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.06243), Open Problem 3.

title: Alon–Tarsi shortest cycle-cover bound
subfield: Flows, perfect matchings, and cycle covers
open: Can every bridgeless cubic graph have its \(m\) edges covered by cycles whose total length is at most \(7m/5\)? In other words, is the Alon–Tarsi shortest cycle-cover conjecture true in its original form, with no additional connectivity hypotheses?
status: Proposed in the 1980s. The \(7m/5\) target has been proved under substantial additional connectivity assumptions, but for general bridgeless cubic graphs the known bounds remain larger; see Luo–Hao–Luo–Zhang (2026), [*A Note on Alon–Tarsi Shortest Cycle Cover Conjecture*](https://doi.org/10.1002/jgt.70026).
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given for whether every bridgeless cubic graph with \(m\) edges admits a cycle cover of total length at most \(7m/5\); the bound must hold without any extra connectivity assumptions.
why: It settles the optimal redundancy of covering a graph's edges by closed routes — the exact constant for shortest cycle covers in the cubic bridgeless case.
key_works: Luo–Hao–Luo–Zhang (2026), [*A Note on Alon–Tarsi Shortest Cycle Cover Conjecture*](https://doi.org/10.1002/jgt.70026).

title: Smallest Petersen-coloring obstruction
subfield: Flows, perfect matchings, and cycle covers
open: What is the smallest bridgeless cubic graph that admits no Petersen coloring — that is, no edge map onto the Petersen graph preserving the triple of incident edges at every vertex?
status: The universal conjecture was disproved in 2026 by Goedgebeur–Jooken–Máčajová–Mattiolo–Mazzuoccolo–Ulyanov ([*Disproving the Petersen Coloring Conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10028v4)); their September revision narrows the minimum order of a non-Petersen-colorable bridgeless cubic graph to between 40 and 52.
solved_when: The exact minimum order of such an obstruction graph is determined; it is currently known only to lie between 40 and 52.
why: Pinpointing the minimal obstruction reveals the essential structure behind the refutation of the Petersen coloring conjecture.
key_works: Goedgebeur–Jooken–Máčajová–Mattiolo–Mazzuoccolo–Ulyanov (2026), [*Disproving the Petersen Coloring Conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10028v4).

title: Exponential growth of diagonal Ramsey numbers
open: What is the true exponential growth rate of the diagonal Ramsey number \(R(k,k)\) — in particular, does the limit \(\lim_{k\to\infty} R(k,k)^{1/k}\) exist, and what is it?
status: Random constructions give a base of at least \(\sqrt2\); the classical upper base of four has been improved by Campos–Griffiths–Morris–Sahasrabudhe (2026), [*An exponential improvement for diagonal Ramsey*](https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2026.203.3.4), but a large exponential gap remains.
solved_when: The base \(\lim_{k\to\infty} R(k,k)^{1/k}\) is determined, or at least the exponential gap between the lower base \(\sqrt2\) and the improved upper base is closed.
why: It measures the maximum persistence of binary relations without large homogeneous sets, the central quantitative question of diagonal Ramsey theory.
key_works: Campos–Griffiths–Morris–Sahasrabudhe (2026), [*An exponential improvement for diagonal Ramsey*](https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2026.203.3.4).

title: Logarithmic factors in fixed-clique off-diagonal Ramsey numbers
open: For each fixed clique size \(s\ge4\), what are the correct logarithmic factors in the growth of the off-diagonal Ramsey number \(R(s,t)\) — is the truth closer to the known lower or upper logarithmic exponent?
status: Bradač's 2026 preprint [*Off-diagonal Ramsey numbers*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.28793) establishes the lower bound \(\Omega_s(t^{s-1}/\log^{2s-4}t)\), while the best upper bound is \(O_s(t^{s-1}/\log^{s-2}t)\), leaving a gap of a factor \(\log^{s-2}t\).
solved_when: For each fixed \(s\ge4\), matching lower and upper bounds for \(R(s,t)\) are established, pinning the power of \(\log t\) between the current \(\Omega_s(t^{s-1}/\log^{2s-4}t)\) and \(O_s(t^{s-1}/\log^{s-2}t)\).
why: The polynomial exponents in \(t\) are already matched, so the logarithmic factors are the last remaining gap in the asymptotic scale of \(R(s,t)\); resolving them completes the order of magnitude of these fundamental Ramsey numbers.
key_works: Bradač (2026), [*Off-diagonal Ramsey numbers*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.28793).

title: Exact value of \(R(5,5)\)
open: What is the smallest number of vertices \(N\) such that every red–blue coloring of the edges of the complete graph \(K_N\) contains a monochromatic \(K_5\)? That is, determine the exact value of the diagonal Ramsey number \(R(5,5)\).
status: The verified interval is \(43\le R(5,5)\le46\), with four candidate values still possible. The upper bound \(R(5,5)\le46\) is due to Angeltveit–McKay (2026), [*\(R(5,5)\le46\)*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.15709).
solved_when: \(R(5,5)\) is determined exactly — equivalently, the value is pinned down within the verified interval \(43\le R(5,5)\le46\), leaving no candidate value unresolved.
why: \(R(5,5)\) is the next unresolved diagonal graph Ramsey number, so settling it would advance the frontier of exact Ramsey knowledge and likely require progress on scalable certified SAT solving.
key_works: Angeltveit–McKay (2026), [*\(R(5,5)\le46\)*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.15709).

title: Sharp growth of multicolor triangle Ramsey numbers
open: How fast do multicolor triangle Ramsey numbers actually grow as the number of colors increases — what is the asymptotic behavior of \(\log R_q(K_3)/(q\log q)\)?
status: The exponential-versus-superexponential question was resolved in 2026. Current bounds leave the relevant coefficient between \(1/3\) and one. See Steiner (2026), [*Locally bipartite subgraphs via multicolor Ramsey numbers*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02522v2).
solved_when: The limit behavior of \(\log R_q(K_3)/(q\log q)\) is determined, in particular whether the expression converges and, if so, to which constant.
why: It establishes the true cost of increasing the number of colors in Ramsey-theoretic guarantees for triangles, the most basic forbidden graph.
key_works: Steiner (2026), [*Locally bipartite subgraphs via multicolor Ramsey numbers*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02522v2).

title: Worst-case ordered matching Ramsey numbers
open: How large can the multicolor Ramsey number of an ordered matching be forced by the ordering alone? Formally, determine the maximum, over all orderings of the vertices of an \(n\)-vertex matching, of its ordered \(q\)-color Ramsey number, for fixed \(q\ge2\).
status: A September 2026 lower bound is \(\exp(c_q(\log n)^q/(\log\log n)^{q-1})\), while the best upper bound is \(\exp(O_q((\log n)^q))\), so the truth lies somewhere within a factor of \((\log\log n)^{q-1}\) inside the exponent. Key work: Li (2026), [*Multicolor Ramsey numbers of ordered matchings*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.08157).
solved_when: The worst-case ordered \(q\)-color Ramsey number of \(n\)-vertex matchings is determined up to constant factors in the exponent — that is, the gap between the known lower bound \(\exp(c_q(\log n)^q/(\log\log n)^{q-1})\) and the upper bound \(\exp(O_q((\log n)^q))\) is closed.
why: It quantifies how a vertex order amplifies unavoidable-pattern complexity: without resolving it, we cannot say whether the ordering alone can force the Ramsey number to grow exponentially faster in \((\log n)^q\) than the polylogarithmic regime of unordered matchings.
key_works: Li (2026), [*Multicolor Ramsey numbers of ordered matchings*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.08157).

title: Shannon capacity of the seven-cycle
subfield: Graph homomorphisms, invariants, and zero-error information
open: What is the Shannon capacity of the seven-cycle, that is, the zero-error capacity of the smallest odd-cycle channel still unresolved? Formally, determine \(\Theta(C_7)=\sup_m\alpha(C_7^{\boxtimes m})^{1/m}\).
status: The best known lower bound, from 2026, is \(3.258805369885\ldots\); Lovász's upper bound remains approximately \(3.317668\). Key works: Shannon (1956), *The zero error capacity of a noisy channel*; Buys–Polak–Zuiddam (2026), *Lean-verified lower bounds for the Shannon capacity of odd cycles* (https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29681).
solved_when: The exact value of \(\Theta(C_7)\) is determined.
why: It yields the exact zero-error rate of the smallest unresolved odd-cycle channel, a basic test case for whether Shannon capacity can be computed beyond the few known cases.
key_works: Shannon (1956), *The zero error capacity of a noisy channel*; Buys–Polak–Zuiddam (2026), [*Lean-verified lower bounds for the Shannon capacity of odd cycles*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29681).

title: Degree-57 Moore graph
subfield: Graph parameters and topological graph theory
open: Does a strongly regular graph with parameters (3250, 57, 0, 1) — the "missing Moore graph" of degree 57 — actually exist? Either construct such a graph or prove that none exists.
status: Open since 1960. A June 2026 preprint by Ishida, *No involutions in the missing Moore graph* (https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.29183), rules out involutions in the automorphism group of such a graph.
solved_when: An explicit construction of a strongly regular graph with parameters (3250, 57, 0, 1) is given, or its nonexistence is proved.
why: This is the last unresolved case of the diameter-two Moore graph classification; resolving it would complete a classification whose other cases have long been settled.
key_works: Ishida (2026), [*No involutions in the missing Moore graph*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.29183).
aliases: Missing Moore graph; Hoffman–Singleton degree-57 problem.

title: Lovász’s vertex-transitive Hamiltonian-path problem
open: Does every finite connected vertex-transitive graph have a Hamiltonian path?
status: The problem was posed in 1969. The best current progress is Li–Methuku's September 2026 preprint, which proves a nearly linear \(n^{1-o(1)}\) cycle-length bound for the Lovász conjecture.
solved_when: A proof that every finite connected vertex-transitive graph contains a Hamiltonian path, or a counterexample — a finite connected vertex-transitive graph with no Hamiltonian path.
why: It asks whether global symmetry eliminates all spanning-path obstructions: a positive answer would make vertex-transitivity an automatic certificate of traceability.
key_works: Li–Methuku (2026), [*A nearly linear bound for the Lovász conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38135).

title: Square-lattice connective constant
subfield: Lattice paths, growth models, and statistical mechanics
open: What is the exact value of the connective constant for self-avoiding walks on the square lattice? Formally, determine the limit \(\mu=\lim_n c_n^{1/n}\), where \(c_n\) is the number of \(n\)-step self-avoiding walks from the origin.
status: Numerical estimates place \(\mu\) near 2.63815853, while the best rigorous upper bound is 2.662343, due to Couronné (2022), [*New upper bound for the connective constant for square-lattice self-avoiding walks*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.16146).
solved_when: The constant \(\mu\) is determined exactly (as a closed-form value or otherwise rigorously identified), rather than merely approximated or bounded.
why: The connective constant gives the exact exponential entropy of planar self-avoiding walks, the foundational quantity underlying the model's combinatorics and statistical mechanics.
key_works: Couronné (2022), [*New upper bound for the connective constant for square-lattice self-avoiding walks*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.16146).

title: Fractal dimension of planar DLA
subfield: Lattice paths, growth models, and statistical mechanics
open: What is the fractal dimension of planar diffusion-limited aggregation? Formally, prove that the cluster mass grows as a power of its radius and determine that asymptotic mass–radius exponent.
status: Simulations suggest a dimension near 1.71, while existing rigorous growth and arm bounds do not establish the exponent. Key works: Losev–Smirnov (2023), [*How long are the arms in DBM?*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.14931).
solved_when: A rigorous proof establishes the existence of an asymptotic mass–radius exponent for planar DLA and identifies its value.
why: It would explain the scaling of a canonical nonequilibrium fractal-growth process, whose geometry currently rests on simulation alone.
key_works: Losev–Smirnov (2023), [*How long are the arms in DBM?*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.14931).

title: Algebraicity of hard-square entropy
subfield: Lattice paths, growth models, and statistical mechanics
open: Is the hard-square entropy constant, approximately 1.503048…, algebraic or transcendental?
status: The arithmetic nature of the constant remains unknown. A 2026 preprint by Svoray, [*The Algebraicity Problem for Hard-Core Entropy Constants on the Discrete Hypertori*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28332), develops criteria but does not resolve the constant.
solved_when: The arithmetic nature of the hard-square entropy constant is determined: either it is shown to be algebraic, or it is proved transcendental.
why: It would tie the entropy of a fundamental lattice hard-core model to a definite arithmetic classification, extending transcendence questions from combinatorial constants to statistical mechanics.
key_works: Svoray (2026), [*The Algebraicity Problem for Hard-Core Entropy Constants on the Discrete Hypertori*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28332).

title: Cyclic orders preserving prescribed basis blocks
open: Given a matroid whose ground set is partitioned into bases, does there always exist a cyclic ordering of the ground set in which each basis of the partition appears as a contiguous block, and in which every window of rank-many consecutive elements is again a basis?
status: The problem was explicitly proposed as Conjecture 3 in recent split-matroid work by Bérczi–Jánosik–Mátravölgyi (2026), [*Cyclic Ordering of Split Matroids*](https://doi.org/10.37236/13537); it has been proved for split matroids and remains open for general matroids.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) that for every matroid with a partition of its ground set into bases, such a cyclic ordering exists — each prescribed basis contiguous and every rank-sized window forming a basis.
why: Such an ordering makes feasible batches continuously interchangeable while preserving their grouping, enabling flexible scheduling or reordering of interchangeable resources without destroying the partition structure.
key_works: Bérczi–Jánosik–Mátravölgyi (2026), [*Cyclic Ordering of Split Matroids*](https://doi.org/10.37236/13537), Conjecture 3.

title: List coloring the intersection of two matroids
open: Is every intersection of two matroids list-colorable with exactly its ordinary chromatic number, where each color class must be independent in both matroids? Formally, does \(\chi_\ell(M_1\cap M_2)=\chi(M_1\cap M_2)\) always hold?
status: A longstanding extension of matroid list coloring. A factor-two upper bound on the list-chromatic number is known, as are special cases for partition matroids, notably in Aharoni–Berger–Guo–Kotlar (2024), [*Coloring, list coloring, and fractional coloring in intersections of matroids*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.08789).
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) establishing equality of the list-chromatic number and the chromatic number for arbitrary pairs of matroids \(M_1, M_2\) on a common ground set.
why: It would eliminate the extra cost imposed by item-specific eligibility constraints, showing that restricting each element's available colors never forces more colors in matroid intersection problems.
key_works: Aharoni–Berger–Guo–Kotlar (2024), [*Coloring, list coloring, and fractional coloring in intersections of matroids*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.08789).

title: Weak White quadratic generation
open: Is every toric ideal of a matroid — the ideal attached to its basis-exchange relations — generated by binomials of degree two? A positive answer would establish quadratic generation in the weakest natural sense, with no restriction to symmetric exchanges.
status: The generation question originates with White (1980), [*A unique exchange property for bases*](https://doi.org/10.1016/0024-3795(80)90209-8). Symmetric-exchange generation was refuted in July 2026 by Larson, [*Counterexamples to two conjectures about matroids*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02208); arbitrary quadratic generation explicitly remains open. The problem is related to Bøgvad's smooth toric Koszulness conjecture.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that every matroid basis toric ideal admits a generating set consisting entirely of quadratic binomials, of unrestricted exchange type.
why: Since the stronger symmetric-exchange generation rule has failed, quadratic generation by arbitrary binomials is the remaining route to bounding the complexity of the relations among matroid bases; without it, no degree bound on the ideal's generators is known.
key_works: White (1980), [*A unique exchange property for bases*](https://doi.org/10.1016/0024-3795(80)90209-8); Larson (2026), [*Counterexamples to two conjectures about matroids*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02208).

title: Koszulness of every matroid base ring
open: Is every matroid base ring Koszul, i.e., does its residue field always admit a linear minimal free resolution?
status: Asked by Herzog–Hibi in 2002. Quadratic Gröbner bases need not exist, but Koszulness remains open, including for the Fano base ring; see Backman–Cheung–Lasoń–Liu–Michałek (2026), [*The Gröbner Version of White’s Conjecture is False*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.13960).
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) that the base ring of every matroid is Koszul, in particular settling the case of the Fano base ring.
why: It constrains all higher syzygies of matroid toric varieties.
key_works: Backman–Cheung–Lasoń–Liu–Michałek (2026), [*The Gröbner Version of White’s Conjecture is False*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.13960).

title: Quadratic Gröbner basis for \(T_8\)
open: Does the rank-four matroid \(T_8\) on eight elements admit a quadratic Gröbner basis for its basis toric ideal? Equivalently, does the basis toric ideal of \(T_8\) possess a Gröbner basis consisting entirely of degree-two polynomials?
status: The problem was isolated in June 2026 after a computational classification settled the other eight-element Fano/dual-Fano-minor-free cases, leaving \(T_8\) as the remaining open case; see Backman et al. (2026), *The Gröbner Version of White's Conjecture is False*, Problem 6.3.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that the basis toric ideal of \(T_8\) has a quadratic Gröbner basis; disproof may be by exhibiting a term order with no quadratic Gröbner basis or an algebraic obstruction.
why: It tests the boundary of the first known algebraic obstructions to the Gröbner version of White's conjecture.
key_works: Backman et al. (2026), [*The Gröbner Version of White’s Conjecture is False*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.13960), Problem 6.3.

title: Real-rootedness of matroid \(Z\)-polynomials
open: Is the \(Z\)-polynomial \(Z_M(t)=\sum_F t^{r(F)} P_{M/F}(t)\) real-rooted for every matroid \(M\)? That is, does this invariant, built from the Kazhdan–Lusztig-type polynomials \(P_{M/F}\), always have only real zeros?
status: The problem originates with Proudfoot–Xu–Young in the 2010s. Sparse paving matroids were settled in a September 2026 preprint by Xie–Zhang, [*Real-rootedness of the \(Z\)-polynomials of sparse paving matroids and strict interlacing for uniform matroids*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.07636); the general case remains open.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that \(Z_M(t)\) has only real roots for every matroid \(M\); the statement must cover the general case, not just restricted classes such as sparse paving matroids.
why: It would upgrade cohomological positivity of the \(Z\)-polynomial to global control over its roots, a far stronger structural property than nonnegativity of coefficients alone.
key_works: Xie–Zhang (2026), [*Real-rootedness of the \(Z\)-polynomials of sparse paving matroids and strict interlacing for uniform matroids*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.07636).

title: \(9/16\) derangement limit for \(123\)-avoiders
open: Does the proportion of fixed-point-free (derangement) permutations avoiding the pattern 123 tend to 9/16 as the permutation length grows? Formally, the conjectured limit of derangements among 123-avoiders is 9/16.
status: This is Pantone's conjecture, recorded in 2026 as Conjecture 4.1 in Vatter (2026), [*An assortment of problems in permutation patterns*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16355). It is supported by analysis of 200 terms of the sequence, but the available multiple sums have not yielded the limit.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that the fraction of 123-avoiding permutations of length n with no fixed points converges to 9/16 as n → ∞.
why: It would establish an exact fixed-point law for permutations under a pattern constraint, analogous to the classical derangement limit but sharpened to a restricted class.
key_works: Vatter (2026), [*An assortment of problems in permutation patterns*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16355), Conjecture 4.1.

title: Vanishing derangement density for \(231\)-avoiders
open: Does the proportion of fixed-point-free (derangement) permutations among 231-avoiding permutations tend to zero as the length grows? Equivalently, does the derangement density of the class Av(231) vanish asymptotically?
status: Explicitly posed as open in Vatter's 2026 list (Question 4.2 of *An assortment of problems in permutation patterns*, arXiv:2602.16355); continued fractions and finite computations do not establish the limit.
solved_when: A proof that the fraction of 231-avoiding permutations of length n with no fixed points tends to 0 as n → ∞, or a disproof with a nonzero limiting density.
why: It separates the fixed-point behavior of Catalan-equinumerous permutation classes that enumeration alone cannot distinguish.
key_works: Vatter (2026), [*An assortment of problems in permutation patterns*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16355), Question 4.2.

title: Oda’s mixed Minkowski-sum question
open: If \(Q\) is a smooth lattice polytope whose normal fan refines that of a lattice polytope \(P\), must every lattice point in the Minkowski sum \(P+Q\) decompose as the sum of a lattice point of \(P\) and a lattice point of \(Q\)?
status: A longstanding mixed strengthening of the classical decomposition questions; known special cases do not settle the problem for arbitrary smooth \(Q\). Related work appears in Crespo–Pelayo–Santos (2026), [*Ewald’s Conjecture and integer points in algebraic and symplectic toric geometry*](https://doi.org/10.1112/plms.70144).
solved_when: The statement is proved for arbitrary lattice polytopes \(P\) and all smooth \(Q\) whose normal fan refines that of \(P\), or a counterexample is exhibited.
why: The property governs how sections of ample and nef toric divisors multiply, so a proof or refutation directly constrains the multiplier ideals and section rings arising in toric geometry.
key_works: Crespo–Pelayo–Santos (2026), [*Ewald’s Conjecture and integer points in algebraic and symplectic toric geometry*](https://doi.org/10.1112/plms.70144).

title: Symmetric chains in rectangular partition lattices
open: Can the lattice \(L(m,n)\) of partitions fitting inside an \(m\times n\) rectangle always be decomposed into saturated chains whose endpoint ranks sum to \(mn\) — that is, does it admit a symmetric chain decomposition? A constructive answer would give the chains explicitly for all \(m\) and \(n\).
status: This is a longstanding conjecture of Stanley. Symmetric chain decompositions are known for several small widths, and a 2026 preprint of Wen supplies the decomposition for \(L(6,n)\) (arXiv:2604.23042). Key works: Stanley (1980), *Weyl groups, the hard Lefschetz theorem, and the Sperner property*; Wen (2026), *\(L(6,n)\) decomposition*.
solved_when: An explicit symmetric chain decomposition of \(L(m,n)\) is given for all \(m, n\), with every chain saturated and its endpoint ranks summing to \(mn\).
why: A symmetric chain decomposition would explain the unimodality (indeed Gaussian) profile of the rank numbers through explicit chains rather than abstract positivity arguments.
key_works: Stanley (1980), *Weyl groups, the hard Lefschetz theorem, and the Sperner property*; Wen (2026), [*\(L(6,n)\) decomposition*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.23042).

title: Approximate counting of bipartite independent sets
open: Does there exist a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme for \(\#\mathrm{BIS}\), the problem of approximately counting independent sets in an arbitrary bipartite graph? Equivalently, can unrestricted bipartite independent sets be counted to within any constant relative error in time polynomial in the graph size?
status: A central unresolved approximate-counting problem. Known results cover bounded-degree graphs and the uniqueness region — see Chen–Liu–Yin (2023), [*Uniqueness and Rapid Mixing in the Bipartite Hardcore Model*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.00186) — but these do not settle the case of arbitrary bipartite graphs.
solved_when: An FPRAS for \(\#\mathrm{BIS}\) on arbitrary bipartite graphs is given, or the existence of such a scheme is ruled out.
why: \(\#\mathrm{BIS}\) sits between tractable and intractable counting problems; resolving it would classify this major intermediate family of approximate-counting problems.
key_works: Chen–Liu–Yin (2023), [*Uniqueness and Rapid Mixing in the Bipartite Hardcore Model*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.00186).

title: Deterministic FPTAS for the nonnegative permanent
open: Is there a deterministic fully polynomial-time approximation scheme for the permanent of a nonnegative matrix? That is, can every nonnegative matrix permanent be approximated within relative error \(\varepsilon\) deterministically in time polynomial in the input size and \(1/\varepsilon\)?
status: A randomized approximation scheme is known. Recent work of Kudria–Luo–Majid (2026), [*Subexponential Approximation of the Permanent in Deterministic Polynomial Time*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.10516), improves deterministic approximation factors but does not yield an FPTAS.
solved_when: A deterministic algorithm approximates the permanent of any nonnegative matrix within relative error \(\varepsilon\) in time polynomial in the input size and \(1/\varepsilon\).
why: It would derandomize a landmark randomized approximate-counting algorithm, and bears directly on the P versus BPP question.
key_works: Kudria–Luo–Majid (2026), [*Subexponential Approximation of the Permanent in Deterministic Polynomial Time*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.10516).

title: Exact independence density of random regular graphs
open: What fraction of vertices can a largest independent set occupy in a random \(d\)-regular graph, in the limit as the number of vertices grows? For fixed degrees such as \(d=3\), determine this limiting maximum-independent-set density exactly.
status: The existence of the limiting density and increasingly sharp bounds are known, following replica-symmetry-breaking bounds of Harangi (2023) ([J. Stat. Phys.](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10955-022-03062-7)) and a [2025 refinement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.09458), but exact fixed-degree values and the general replica predictions remain unproved.
solved_when: A rigorous closed-form value (or provably exact characterization) of the limiting independence density of random \(d\)-regular graphs is established for fixed \(d\), at least for \(d=3\), and in general the replica-symmetry-breaking predictions are rigorously proved.
why: An exact value would validate replica-symmetry-breaking predictions for sparse disordered optimization, turning heuristic physics formulas into theorems for a canonical random-optimization model.
key_works: Harangi (2023), [replica-symmetry-breaking bounds](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10955-022-03062-7); [2025 refinement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.09458).

title: Exact random 3-SAT threshold
open: Determine the exact limiting satisfiability threshold \(\alpha_3\) for random 3-SAT — in particular, whether the statistical-physics prediction of approximately 4.267 is correct.
status: Classical bounds leave the threshold within approximately 3.52–4.490. Hajiaghayi–Sorkin (2003) gave a threshold upper bound. An October 5, 2026 preprint by Carenini, [*A polynomial scaling window for random k-SAT and a proof of the satisfiability conjecture*](https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2026/229/), claims threshold existence, but not its exact value.
solved_when: The threshold \(\alpha_3\) is pinned down exactly, or at least the current gap of approximately 3.52–4.490 is closed; a satisfying answer also confirms or refutes the predicted value ≈ 4.267.
why: It would rigorously identify a fundamental random-constraint phase transition, anchoring the theory of random constraint satisfaction.

title: Sharp oriented chromatic number of planar graphs
open: What is the smallest number of colors needed to properly color every orientation of a planar graph so that no two arcs join the same pair of colors in opposite directions? Formally, determine the exact oriented chromatic number of the class of planar graphs.

solved_when: The exact value of \(C\) is determined; currently it is only known that \(18\le C\le80\), so success means either constructing a planar orientation requiring more than any proposed bound or proving a matching upper and lower bound.
why: It determines how much directional information planar adjacency forces a finite target digraph to retain, pinning down the cost of encoding orientation in a coloring.

title: Optimal polynomial relation between linear coloring and treedepth
open: What is the tightest possible asymptotic upper bound on the treedepth of a graph in terms of its linear chromatic number \(k\), where a \(k\)-linear coloring requires every simple path to contain a color appearing exactly once on it?
status: Hodor–Micek's August 2026 preprint disproves a linear relationship, obtaining a separation of \(\Omega(k^2/\log k)\). The best known upper bound is \(k^{10}(\log k)^{O(1)}\). Key works: Hilaire–Krnc–Milanič–Raymond (2026), *Linear colorings of graphs*; Hodor–Micek (2026), [*Superlinear separation between linear and centered colorings*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.18620).
solved_when: Matching upper and lower bounds for treedepth as a function of the linear chromatic number \(k\) are established, closing the gap between the lower bound \(\Omega(k^2/\log k)\) and the upper bound \(k^{10}(\log k)^{O(1)}\).
why: It quantifies how a uniqueness condition imposed on individual paths controls the global recursive structure of a graph, determining whether linear colorings can serve as compact stand-ins for treedepth.
key_works: Hilaire–Krnc–Milanič–Raymond (2026), *Linear colorings of graphs*; Hodor–Micek (2026), [*Superlinear separation between linear and centered colorings*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.18620).

title: Orientable cycle double covers
open: Does every bridgeless graph admit an orientable cycle double cover — a family of consistently oriented simple cycles such that each edge is traversed exactly once in each direction, with no cycle permitted to traverse an edge forward and immediately backward?
status: This is a classical strengthening of the cycle double cover conjecture. The 2026 ordinary existence theorem does not supply compatible orientations, though many special classes are known. Key works include Bagheri Gh.–Omoomi (2016), *Small oriented cycle double cover of graphs*, and Hušek–Šámal (2020), *Homomorphisms of Cayley graphs and Cycle Double Covers*.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) that every bridgeless graph has such a consistently oriented family of simple cycles covering each edge exactly once in each direction.
why: A solution would tie circuit decompositions of graphs to orientable embeddings and algebraic flows, extending the ordinary cycle double cover statement to the oriented setting.
key_works: Bagheri Gh.–Omoomi (2016), *Small oriented cycle double cover of graphs*; Hušek–Šámal (2020), [*Homomorphisms of Cayley graphs and Cycle Double Covers*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.03112).

title: Exponentially many circuit double covers
open: Does every 2-edge-connected cubic graph on \(n\) vertices admit exponentially many circuit double covers — specifically, at least \(2^{n/2-1}\) distinct collections of connected 2-regular subgraphs?
status: Hušek–Šámal exhibit an infinite sharp family showing the constant cannot be improved. Their July 2026 preprint proves the target bound for 3-edge-colorable graphs and a weaker exponential bound for graphs with higher connectivity and girth at least sixteen.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof via counterexample) of the claim that every 2-edge-connected cubic graph on \(n\) vertices has at least \(2^{n/2-1}\) distinct circuit double covers, counted as collections of connected 2-regular subgraphs.
why: It upgrades the mere existence of circuit double covers to quantitative abundance, showing how scarce such covers can be in the worst case.
key_works: Hušek–Šámal (2025), *Counting circuit double covers*; the same authors (2026), [*Exponentially Many Circuit Double Covers*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24724).

title: Mader’s sharp connectivity-preserving tree bound
open: Does every \(k\)-connected graph of minimum degree at least \(\lfloor3k/2\rfloor+m-1\) contain every \(m\)-vertex tree as a subgraph whose deletion leaves the graph \(k\)-connected? In other words, is Mader's degree bound exactly the threshold at which any prescribed tree can be carved out without destroying \(k\)-connectivity?
status: Mader (2012), *Connectivity keeping trees in \(k\)-connected graphs*, settled paths and several tree families. Ma–Liu–Zhang–Hong's September 2026 preprint, [*Connectivity keeping pendant extensions of paths in \(k\)-connected graphs and triangle-free graphs*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23634), proves all pendant extensions of paths. The general case remains open.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given for arbitrary \(m\)-vertex trees in \(k\)-connected graphs of minimum degree at least \(\lfloor3k/2\rfloor+m-1\).
why: It quantifies precisely how much degree surplus is needed to delete a prescribed structure from a network without reducing its fault tolerance, turning a folklore robustness intuition into a sharp threshold.
key_works: Mader (2012), *Connectivity keeping trees in \(k\)-connected graphs*; Ma et al. (2026), [*Connectivity keeping pendant extensions of paths in \(k\)-connected graphs and triangle-free graphs*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23634).

title: Every longest cycle has a chord in 3-connected graphs
open: Must every longest cycle in every finite simple 3-connected graph have a chord? Equivalently, is no longest cycle chordless in any 3-connected graph?
status: Thomassen raised the question in 1976. His 2026 paper, [*Chords in longest cycles in 3-connected graphs*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jctb.2026.03.001), proves that at least one longest cycle has a chord; the statement for every longest cycle remains open.
solved_when: A proof, or a counterexample, is given for the statement that every longest cycle of every finite simple 3-connected graph contains a chord.
why: It tests whether 3-connectivity forces internal structure not just on some extremal cycle but on an arbitrarily chosen one, sharpening our understanding of how connectivity shapes longest cycles.
key_works: Thomassen (2026), [*Chords in longest cycles in 3-connected graphs*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jctb.2026.03.001).

title: Bounded longest-path transversals
open: Is there an absolute constant \(C\) such that every connected graph contains a set of at most \(C\) vertices intersecting every longest path? Equivalently, do all connected graphs admit longest-path transversals of uniformly bounded size?
status: The problem is motivated by Gallai's 1966 question of whether a single vertex can meet every longest path; one vertex need not suffice. The best known bound is due to Norin–Steiner–Thomassé–Wollan's 2026 paper [*Small hitting sets for longest paths and cycles*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.08634), which shows that \(\sqrt{8n}\) vertices always suffice.
solved_when: A finite constant \(C\) is exhibited, together with a proof that every connected graph has a set of at most \(C\) vertices meeting all of its longest paths; alternatively, a proof that for every \(C\) such a transversal fails for some connected graph.
why: A bounded transversal would give a constant-size certificate that controls all maximum-length routes in any connected graph, reducing questions about longest paths to checking a fixed-size set of vertices.
key_works: Norin–Steiner–Thomassé–Wollan (2026), [*Small hitting sets for longest paths and cycles*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.08634).

title: Degree two in minimally 1-tough graphs
open: Must every minimally 1-tough graph — a graph of toughness exactly one in which deleting any edge lowers the toughness below one — contain a vertex of degree two?

The general prediction of degree \(\lceil 2t\rceil\) in minimally \(t\)-tough graphs is false, but the original \(t=1\) case survives the 2026 constructions of Cheng–Li–Liu (2026), [*Constructions of minimally \(t\)-tough regular graphs*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.disc.2026.114993).
solved_when: A proof that every minimally 1-tough graph has a degree-two vertex, or an explicit construction of one that does not.
why: It tests whether a critical global condition such as toughness forces a simple local structural feature, and it is the sole surviving case of the broader conjecture that minimally \(t\)-tough graphs have a vertex of degree \(\lceil 2t\rceil\).

title: Linear induced Ramsey numbers for bounded-degree graphs
open: For graphs of fixed maximum degree \(\Delta\), is there a host graph of size linear in \(n\) that realizes every induced Ramsey instance? Formally: for fixed \(\Delta\) and number of colors \(r\), does every \(n\)-vertex graph \(H\) of maximum degree \(\Delta\) have induced Ramsey number \(O_{\Delta,r}(n)\)?
status: Polynomial bounds have been known since Łuczak–Rödl. Carenini's July 2026 preprint ("Embedding Induced Bounded Degree Graphs") gives the bound \(Cn^{\Delta+2}(\log n)^A\); general linearity remains open.
solved_when: For every fixed \(\Delta\) and \(r\), there is a constant \(C = C(\Delta, r)\) such that every \(n\)-vertex graph \(H\) with maximum degree \(\Delta\) has induced Ramsey number at most \(Cn\).
why: It determines whether preserving all nonedges — the defining constraint of induced Ramsey theory — forces an unavoidable superlinear cost, separating induced from ordinary Ramsey numbers for bounded-degree graphs.
key_works: Łuczak–Rödl (1996), *On induced Ramsey numbers for graphs with bounded maximum degree*; Carenini (2026), [*Embedding Induced Bounded Degree Graphs*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.04532).

title: Linear top exponent for \(r_4(5,n)\)
open: Does the 4-uniform Ramsey number \(r_4(5,n)\) grow at least like a double exponential with a linear exponent — that is, is \(r_4(5,n)\ge 2^{2^{cn}}\) for some absolute constant \(c>0\)? Formally, the question is whether the top exponent in the known double-exponential tower can be pushed up to order \(n\).
status: The double-exponential tower height for \(r_4(5,n)\) was established in 2026 by Du–Hu–Liu–Wang, [*A double-exponential lower bound for \(r_4(5,n)\)*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.23986). Fan–Li–Lin–Ning then improved the lower bound to \(2^{2^{cn^{1/5}}}\) in [*An improved double-exponential lower bound for \(r_4(5,n)\)*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04105v2). The linear top exponent remains open even after the analogous target for \(r_4(6,n)\) was proved.
solved_when: A proof that \(r_4(5,n)\ge 2^{2^{cn}}\) for an absolute constant \(c>0\).
why: It isolates the last quantitative obstruction in the off-diagonal 4-uniform Ramsey problem at the smallest nontrivial clique size \(s=5\), where the tower height is already settled but its top exponent is not.
key_works: Du–Hu–Liu–Wang (2026), [*A double-exponential lower bound for \(r_4(5,n)\)*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.23986); Fan–Li–Lin–Ning (2026), [*An improved double-exponential lower bound for \(r_4(5,n)\)*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04105v2).

title: Multicolor ordered path powers with exponent independent of bandwidth
open: Does the ordered Ramsey number of the \(t\)-th power of a path have an exponent, in the number of colors \(r\), that does not grow with \(t\)? Formally: for fixed \(r\) and \(t\), prove \(R_<^r(P_n^t)\le C_{r,t}n^{Cr}\) with an absolute constant \(C\) independent of the path power \(t\).
status: Girão–Janzer–Janzer's 2026 paper proves the two-color bound \(n^{4+o(1)}\) and formulates the multicolor target as Conjecture 4.4. Related work: Gishboliner–Jin–Sudakov (2024), *Ramsey Problems for Monotone Paths in Graphs and Hypergraphs*.
solved_when: A bound \(R_<^r(P_n^t)\le C_{r,t}n^{Cr}\) is established for all fixed \(r,t\), where \(C\) is an absolute constant independent of \(t\).
why: It asks whether the bandwidth of the graph affects only the prefactor rather than the exponent of its ordered Ramsey number.
key_works: Gishboliner–Jin–Sudakov (2024), *Ramsey Problems for Monotone Paths in Graphs and Hypergraphs*; Girão–Janzer–Janzer (2026), [*Ordered Ramsey Numbers of Powers of Paths*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.02360).

title: Sharp tree supersaturation at the Erdős–Sós threshold
open: Must every \(n\)-vertex graph of average degree \(d\ge t-1\) contain at least \(n\,d(d-1)\cdots(d-t+1)\) injective labeled copies of every \(t\)-edge tree? In other words, does the Erdős–Sós threshold for existence extend to a sharp supersaturation bound on the number of embeddings?

title: Shareshian–Wachs coefficientwise \(q\)-\(e\)-positivity
open: For every natural unit interval order \(P\), is the chromatic quasisymmetric function \(X_{\operatorname{inc}(P)}(\mathbf x;q)\) positive when expanded in the elementary basis, coefficientwise in \(q\), where \(q\) records the number of ascending edges of a proper coloring?

Sagan–Tom (2026), [*Chromatic symmetric functions and change of basis*](https://doi.org/10.5802/alco.468), gives further 2026 results on three-column coefficients. Foundational reference: Shareshian–Wachs (2016), [*Chromatic quasisymmetric functions*](https://www.math.miami.edu/~wachs/papers/chrom.advances.pdf).
solved_when: A proof that, for every natural unit interval order \(P\), all elementary-basis coefficients of \(X_{\operatorname{inc}(P)}(\mathbf x;q)\) lie in \(\mathbb N[q]\).
why: It is a coefficientwise refinement of the Stanley–Stembridge positivity statement, and a proof would sharpen the representation-theoretic information carried by the cohomology of Hessenberg varieties.

title: Elementary-basis unimodality of chromatic quasisymmetric functions
open: Is every elementary-basis coefficient of the chromatic quasisymmetric function \(X_G(\mathbf{x};q)\) unimodal — with the symmetry centered at \(|E(G)|/2\) — whenever \(G\) is a natural unit interval graph? Formally, each \(e_\lambda\)-coefficient is conjectured to be a symmetric unimodal polynomial in \(q\).
status: This is a conjecture of Shareshian–Wachs. Symmetry and various special cases are known, including work of Cho–Huh (2017) on \(e\)-positivity and \(e\)-unimodality. A stronger coefficientwise log-concavity proposal was refuted by a reported 13-vertex counterexample in 2026. Key works: Shareshian–Wachs (2016), *Chromatic quasisymmetric functions*; Cho–Huh (2017), [*On \(e\)-positivity and \(e\)-unimodality of chromatic quasisymmetric functions*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.07152).
solved_when: A proof that for every natural unit interval graph \(G\), each elementary-basis coefficient of \(X_G(\mathbf{x};q)\) is unimodal and symmetric about \(q = |E(G)|/2\).
why: It would establish a hard-Lefschetz-like distributional shape in the coordinates relevant to permutation representations, giving the elementary basis the kind of structural regularity the Schur basis is known to enjoy.
key_works: Shareshian–Wachs (2016), *Chromatic quasisymmetric functions*; Cho–Huh (2017), [*On \(e\)-positivity and \(e\)-unimodality of chromatic quasisymmetric functions*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.07152).

title: Positive combinatorial formula for Stanley–Stembridge coefficients
open: Is there a uniform, cancellation-free combinatorial rule that counts the coefficients \([e_\lambda]X_G\) for every unit interval graph \(G\)? That is, can the expansion of the chromatic symmetric function in the elementary basis be described by an explicit positive counting rule valid for all such graphs at once?
status: Nonnegativity is proved, but a general combinatorial interpretation remains open. Siegl's 2025–2026 work supplies tableau-based lower bounds and special coefficient formulas; see Siegl (2025, revised 2026), [*Toward Lower Bounds for Chromatic Symmetric Functions in the Elementary Basis*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.02841), and Sagan–Tom (2026), *Chromatic symmetric functions and change of basis*.
solved_when: A single combinatorial interpretation is given that, for all unit interval graphs \(G\) and all partitions \(\lambda\), computes \([e_\lambda]X_G\) as the count of a manifestly nonnegative set of objects.
why: It would make the positivity theorem computationally transparent and could expose its \(q\)-refinement.
key_works: Siegl (2025, revised 2026), [*Toward Lower Bounds for Chromatic Symmetric Functions in the Elementary Basis*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.02841); Sagan–Tom (2026), *Chromatic symmetric functions and change of basis*.

title: Positivity of shifted Jack structure constants
open:
Do the shifted Jack functions multiply with a positivity that mirrors the classical Littlewood–Richardson rule? That is, for the expansion \(P_\mu^\# P_
u^\# = \sum_\lambda d_{\mu
u}^\lambda P_\lambda^\#\), is it true that \(H_\mu H_
u H'_\lambda d_{\mu
u}^\lambda\) lies in \(\mathbb{N}[\alpha, \alpha^{-1}]\), where \(H_\mu, H_
u, H'_\lambda\) are the standard Jack hook products?
status: Alexandersson–Féray (2019) established Laurent polynomiality of these coefficients and proved positivity in special cases; Mickler's 2026 congruences add structural relations but do not resolve positivity.
solved_when:
A proof (or disproof with counterexample) that \(H_\mu H_
u H'_\lambda d_{\mu
u}^\lambda \in \mathbb{N}[\alpha, \alpha^{-1}]\) for all partitions \(\mu, 
u, \lambda\).
why: Shifted recurrences may reveal the mechanism behind otherwise difficult Jack multiplication coefficients, where direct positivity arguments have stalled.

title: Positive restriction rule from \(GL_n\) to \(S_n\)
open: Is there a positive combinatorial formula for the multiplicities of Specht modules when an irreducible polynomial \(GL_n\)-module is restricted along the embedding of \(S_n\) as permutation matrices? That is, describe the branching coefficients from polynomial representations of \(GL_n\) to symmetric-group representations by an explicit rule rather than by character computation.
status: A longstanding branching problem. Hooks and several small-shape families are known; Lee's 2026 theorem handles indexing partitions with at most three columns.
solved_when: A positive combinatorial formula is given that works for every irreducible polynomial \(GL_n\)-module (equivalently, every pair of indexing partitions), yielding the Specht multiplicities in the restriction.
why: It would make the basic transition between continuous symmetry (\(GL_n\)) and finite symmetry (\(S_n\)) computationally explicit, turning a longstanding branching computation into a usable rule.
key_works: Zabrocki (2019), [*The restriction problem*](https://realopacblog.wordpress.com/2019/11/17/the-restriction-problem/); Narayanan (2024), [*Hook restriction coefficients*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.03443); Lee (2026), [*Restriction coefficients for partitions with at most three columns*](https://doi.org/10.5802/alco.476).

title: Monomial-immanant positivity for \(r\)-nonnegative matrices
open: If all minors of a matrix of order at most \(r\) are nonnegative, must every monomial immanant indexed by a partition of length at most \(r\) also be nonnegative?
status: The conjecture originates with Stembridge (1992), *Some conjectures for immanants*. Dong–Wu–Gao's September 2026 preprint proves the case of all hook partitions ([arXiv:2609.36665](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36665)).
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given for all matrices whose minors of order at most \(r\) are nonnegative and all partitions \(\lambda\) with \(\ell(\lambda)\le r\).
why: It would extend determinant positivity to a broader family of matrix functions on \(r\)-nonnegative matrices.
key_works: Stembridge (1992), *Some conjectures for immanants*; Dong–Wu–Gao (2026), [*On the nonnegativity of monomial immanants for hook partitions*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36665).

title: Schur positivity of Giambelli immanants
open: Is every irreducible-character immanant of a Giambelli matrix of hook Schur functions a nonnegative integer combination of Schur functions? Equivalently, does Schur positivity hold for all such immanants?
status: Monomial positivity is known. Zhang (2026), [*Newton polytopes of immanants of some combinatorial matrices*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.06615), establishes saturated Newton polytopes for these immanants, but Schur positivity remains unresolved; the problem also connects to Haiman (1993), *Hecke algebra characters and immanant conjectures*.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof with explicit counterexample) that every irreducible-character immanant of every Giambelli matrix of hook Schur functions is Schur-positive.
why: It tests whether the positive path structures underlying determinantal identities persist beyond the determinant, for every irreducible immanant — a key indicator of whether deeper combinatorial structure governs these symmetric functions.
key_works: Zhang (2026), [*Newton polytopes of immanants of some combinatorial matrices*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.06615); Haiman (1993), *Hecke algebra characters and immanant conjectures*.

title: Saturated Newton support of Jacobi–Trudi immanants
open: Does the Newton polytope of an irreducible-character Jacobi–Trudi immanant have saturated support — that is, does every lattice point in the polytope occur as the exponent of a nonzero monomial? A positive answer would show the monomial exponents realize exactly the integer points of the polytope.
status: Zhang’s 2026 paper proves special Jacobi–Trudi cases and all Giambelli cases; arbitrary Jacobi–Trudi shapes remain open.
solved_when: Saturation is proved for irreducible-character Jacobi–Trudi immanants of arbitrary shapes: every lattice point in the Newton polytope occurs as a nonzero monomial exponent.
why: It would translate questions about monomial support into convex feasibility questions, replacing coefficient-level analysis with polytope-level arguments.
key_works: Zhang (2026), [*Newton polytopes of immanants of some combinatorial matrices*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.06615).

title: Extreme rays of the two-row Schur-product cone
open: Which products of at-most-two-row Schur functions generate the extreme rays of the cone they span in degree \(N\)? Concretely, are the extreme rays precisely the products whose indexing partitions are pairwise nested under White's interlacing convention?
status: White (2009) showed that nonnested products are nonextreme and that nested products with distinct parts are extreme; the case of nested products with repeated parts remains open.
solved_when: Every product with pairwise nested indexing partitions (in White's interlacing convention) is shown to be an extreme ray of the degree-\(N\) two-row Schur-product cone, and every non-nested product is shown to be nonextreme — in particular, the case of nested partitions with repeated parts is settled.
why: It would give a complete classification of the primitive two-row Schur inequalities.
key_works: White (2009), [*The Schur Cone and the Cone of Log Concavity*](https://arxiv.org/abs/0903.2831); White (2019), [OPAC-009](https://realopacblog.wordpress.com/2019/09/22/the-schur-cone-and-the-cone-of-log-concavity/).

title: Additivity of descents under inversion-set partitions
open: When the left inversion set of an element \(w\) is partitioned into a disjoint union of left inversion sets \(N_L(u)\), \(u\in\mathcal P\), do the right descents add up — that is, \(d_R(w)=\sum_{u\in\mathcal P}d_R(u)\)? The question is whether this additivity holds for arbitrary Coxeter systems.
status: Hohlweg–Pons prove the statement for Coxeter systems of types \(A\) and \(B\) in their 2026 paper [*A conjecture on descents, inversions and the weak order on Coxeter groups*](https://doi.org/10.5802/alco.501); the conjecture remains open for general Coxeter systems.
solved_when: A proof that \(d_R(w)=\sum_{u\in\mathcal P}d_R(u)\) holds for every Coxeter system whenever \(N_L(w)\) is the disjoint union of the left inversion sets \(N_L(u)\) for \(u\in\mathcal P\).
why: These partitions describe multiplicity-one phenomena in Belkale–Kumar products and Littlewood–Richardson cones, so a general proof would extend those structural descriptions beyond the known cases.
key_works: Hohlweg–Pons (2026), [*A conjecture on descents, inversions and the weak order on Coxeter groups*](https://doi.org/10.5802/alco.501).

title: Electrical canonical bases in every degree
open: Is there a canonical basis for the grove algebra of an electrical network in every degree, mirroring what is known in degree two? Concretely, construct bases of each graded component indexed by nested Dyck-path fans, with nonnegative evaluation, positive grove-monomial expansions, and cyclic-rotation/promotion equivariance.
status: Gao–Lam–Xu construct the degree-two bush basis [Gao–Lam–Xu (2024), *Electrical networks and the grove algebra*](https://doi.org/10.4153/S0008414X24000105). The all-degree conjecture remains open; establishing it would imply arbitrary-height staircase cyclic sieving, a direction also connected to Hopkins–Kim–Pfannerer (2026), [*Cyclic Sieving for Staircase Plane Partitions via Crystals and Electrical Networks*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14028).
solved_when: A basis of every graded grove-algebra component indexed by nested Dyck-path fans is constructed, satisfying nonnegative evaluation, positive grove-monomial expansions, and equivariance under cyclic rotation and promotion.
why: It would provide an electrical-network counterpart of a dual canonical basis, and would imply cyclic sieving for staircase plane partitions at arbitrary height.
key_works: Gao–Lam–Xu (2024), [*Electrical networks and the grove algebra*](https://doi.org/10.4153/S0008414X24000105); Hopkins–Kim–Pfannerer (2026), [*Cyclic Sieving for Staircase Plane Partitions via Crystals and Electrical Networks*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14028).

title: Real-rooted matroid Chow polynomials
open: Is the Hilbert–Poincaré polynomial of the ordinary Chow ring of every loopless matroid — taken with the maximal building set — always real-rooted? Equivalently, does this Chow-theoretic analogue of the characteristic polynomial have only real zeros?
status: The conjecture, due to Huh–Stevens, strengthens symmetry, unimodality, and gamma-positivity statements. Real-rootedness is settled for uniform matroids (Brändén–Vecchi, 2026, [Chow polynomials of uniform matroids are real-rooted](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.07364)); counterexamples known for other building sets do not refute the maximal-building-set statement. See also Stevens (2021), [Real-rootedness conjectures in matroid theory](https://mcs0042.github.io/bachelor.pdf).
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that for every loopless matroid, the Hilbert–Poincaré polynomial of its Chow ring with the maximal building set has all real roots.
why: Real-rootedness would impose strictly stronger inequalities — via the resulting symmetry, unimodality, and gamma-positivity consequences — on the intersection-theoretic dimensions of matroids than are currently available.
key_works: Stevens (2021), [*Real-rootedness conjectures in matroid theory*](https://mcs0042.github.io/bachelor.pdf); Brändén–Vecchi (2026), [*Chow polynomials of uniform matroids are real-rooted*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.07364).

title: Real-rooted augmented matroid Chow polynomials
open: Is the Hilbert–Poincaré polynomial of the augmented Chow ring of every loopless matroid real-rooted? Equivalently, does this polynomial — which is distinct from the ordinary matroid Chow polynomial — have only real zeros for arbitrary loopless matroids?
status: Uniform cases have real-rootedness results and explicit interpretations; arbitrary matroids remain unresolved. Key works: Hoster (2026), [*The Chow and Augmented Chow Polynomials of Uniform Matroids*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.22329); Brändén–Vecchi (2026), *Chow polynomials of uniform matroids are real-rooted*.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of real-rootedness of the Hilbert–Poincaré polynomial of the augmented Chow ring for every loopless matroid; current evidence is limited to uniform matroids.
why: It would extend the strong coefficient regularity known for Chow polynomials to the augmented ring, the ring used in matroid Hodge theory.

title: A universal degree bound for matroid Gröbner bases
open: Is there an absolute constant \(D\), independent of both the rank and the ground-set size, such that every matroid toric ideal admits some Gröbner basis in which every element has degree at most \(D\)?
status: A factorial bound depending on rank is known (Lasoń 2021, *On the toric ideals of matroids of a fixed rank*). Two independent 2026 results disprove \(D=2\), using the Fano matroid and its dual (Backman–Cheung–Lasoń–Liu–Michałek 2026, [The Gröbner Version of White's Conjecture is False](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.13960)). Any universal constant remains open.
solved_when: Such a universal constant \(D\) is exhibited with a proof that every matroid toric ideal has a Gröbner basis of degree at most \(D\), or a proof that no such constant exists.
why: It would give uniform control over the algebraic complexity of matroid toric ideals, restoring a degree bound in the regime where the quadratic formulation has failed.
key_works: Lasoń (2021), *On the toric ideals of matroids of a fixed rank*; Backman–Cheung–Lasoń–Liu–Michałek (2026), [*The Gröbner Version of White’s Conjecture is False*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.13960).

title: Quadratic Gröbner bases for all dyadic matroids
open: Does every dyadic matroid have a toric ideal with a quadratic Gröbner basis? Equivalently, is the toric ideal of every matroid representable over a field of characteristic two generated in degree two by a Gröbner basis under some term order?
status: The unrestricted statement was refuted via the Fano matroid counterexample, and the dyadic case was explicitly conjectured in 2026 in Backman et al. (2026), [*The Gröbner Version of White’s Conjecture is False*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.13960), Conjecture 6.5; see also De Loera–Ferroni–Morales–Rambau (2026), [*There are matroid toric ideals without quadratic Gröbner bases*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.11014). Computations support the conjecture for surviving representability-based subclasses.
solved_when: A proof that every dyadic matroid’s toric ideal admits a quadratic Gröbner basis (or a counterexample of a dyadic matroid whose toric ideal has none).
why: It would identify a broad, representability-defined class of matroids where efficient quadratic commutative algebra survives, salvaging the Gröbner-strengthened form of White’s conjecture after the unrestricted statement failed.
key_works: Backman et al. (2026), [*The Gröbner Version of White’s Conjecture is False*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.13960), Conjecture 6.5; De Loera–Ferroni–Morales–Rambau (2026), [*There are matroid toric ideals without quadratic Gröbner bases*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.11014).

title: Counting permutations three entries above a fixed pattern
open: Is there a uniform formula, in terms of explicit structural statistics of a permutation pattern \(\beta\in S_m\), for the number of permutations in \(S_{m+3}\) that contain \(\beta\) as a pattern? Formally, give such a formula for \(|\{\pi\in S_{m+3}:\beta\le\pi\}|\).
status: Posed in 2007. With one extra entry the count is \(m^2+1\); for two extra entries the Ray–West formula is known. No comparable formula for three extra entries is known. See Ray–West (2003), *Posets of matrices and permutations with forbidden subsequences*, and Vatter (2026), [*An Assortment of Problems in Permutation Patterns*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16355), Problem 3.8.
solved_when: An explicit uniform formula in structural statistics of \(\beta\in S_m\) is given for \(|\{\pi\in S_{m+3}:\beta\le\pi\}|\), comparable in spirit to the \(m^2+1\) count for one extra entry and the Ray–West formula for two.
why: It would reveal which structural features of a pattern are the first to distinguish containment counts of permutations just three entries larger, sharpening our understanding of how pattern structure governs nearby containment counts.
key_works: Ray–West (2003), *Posets of matrices and permutations with forbidden subsequences*; Vatter (2026), [*An Assortment of Problems in Permutation Patterns*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16355), Problem 3.8.

title: The shortest permutation unsortable by three stacks in series
open: What is the shortest permutation that cannot be sorted by passing it through three unrestricted stacks in series? Equivalently, determine the minimum length of a permutation that is not sortable by three stacks connected sequentially.
status: The bounds reported in 2026 are \(14\le n\le38\): all permutation lengths through thirteen are sortable, while Atkinson gives a length-38 obstruction.
solved_when: The exact minimum length \(n\) is determined; the answer is currently confined to \(14\le n\le38\).
why: It locates the first point of failure in a basic multistage storage model, sharpening our understanding of what three stacks in series can and cannot sort.
key_works: Atkinson (1992), [*Sorting permutations with networks of stacks*, TR-210](https://carleton.ca/scs/?p=15050); Vatter (2026), [*An Assortment of Problems in Permutation Patterns*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16355), Problem 5.4.
