title: Forbidden patterns for general \((r,s)\)-stacks
open: Which permutations are minimally excluded by a stack that permits insertion into its top \(r\) positions and removal from its top \(s\) positions — and is the resulting forbidden basis finite for every fixed \(r,s\ge2\)?
status: Atkinson's 1998 work determines the eight-element \((2,2)\) basis; a general theorem remains open. Key works: Atkinson (1998), [*Generalized stack permutations*](https://doi.org/10.1017/S096354839800354X); Vatter (2026), *An Assortment of Problems in Permutation Patterns*, Problem 5.10.
solved_when: An explicit characterization of the minimal forbidden permutations for the \((r,s)\)-stack is given, including a determination of whether the basis is finite for every fixed \(r,s\ge2\).
why: It would convert an operational sorting rule into explicit structural obstructions, making the class checkable directly through its forbidden patterns.
key_works: Atkinson (1998), [*Generalized stack permutations*](https://doi.org/10.1017/S096354839800354X); Vatter (2026), *An Assortment of Problems in Permutation Patterns*, Problem 5.10.

title: Algebraicity of generalized-stack generating functions
open: Is the generating function for permutations sortable by an \((r,s)\)-stack algebraic for every fixed \(r,s\ge1\)? In other words, does bounded stack access always force an algebraic enumerative structure?
status: One-sided families are known. The \((2,2)\) case now satisfies a proved cubic equation; arbitrary pairs remain unresolved. Key works: Atkinson (1998), [*Generalized stack permutations*](https://doi.org/10.1017/S096354839800354X); Vatter (2026), [*An Assortment of Problems in Permutation Patterns*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16355), Question 5.12.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) of algebraicity of the generating function for \((r,s)\)-stack-sortable permutations for every fixed \(r,s\ge1\).
why: It tests whether bounded stack access always imposes algebraic enumerative structure on the corresponding permutation classes.
key_works: Atkinson (1998), [*Generalized stack permutations*](https://doi.org/10.1017/S096354839800354X); Vatter (2026), [*An Assortment of Problems in Permutation Patterns*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16355), Question 5.12.

title: Exact enumeration of \(\operatorname{Av}(4123,4231)\)
open: What is the generating function for permutations that avoid both of the patterns \(4123\) and \(4231\)? In other words, determine an exact enumeration of the class \(\operatorname{Av}(4123,4231)\).
status: One thousand terms of the sequence have been computed. The counts for lengths four through eight are \(22, 89, 380, 1677, 7566\), and the numerical growth estimate \(4.97689\) remains unproved. Key works: Albert et al. (2018), *Generating permutations with restricted containers*, §5.2; Vatter and contributors, [OEIS A165542](https://oeis.org/A165542).
solved_when: A generating function for \(\operatorname{Av}(4123,4231)\) is determined; the computed data includes one thousand terms, with counts for lengths four through eight equal to \(22, 89, 380, 1677, 7566\), and the numerical growth estimate \(4.97689\) would then be rigorously established (or refuted).
why: A solution would test whether efficient coefficient generation can be converted into an exact structural enumeration, a key question for pattern-avoidance classes where data is plentiful but proofs are not.
key_works: Albert et al. (2018), *Generating permutations with restricted containers*, §5.2; Vatter and contributors, [OEIS A165542](https://oeis.org/A165542).

title: Exact enumeration of \(\operatorname{Av}(4123,4312)\)
open: What is the generating function for permutations that avoid both of the patterns 4123 and 4312? A precise formula — rational, algebraic, or D-finite — would settle the conjectural growth behavior of this class.
status: One thousand terms of the sequence have been computed, with initial relevant counts 22, 89, 382, 1711, 7922; the apparent growth constant \(3+2\sqrt2\) remains unproven. Related work includes Albert et al. (2018), *Generating permutations with restricted containers*, §5.2, and Vatter and contributors' OEIS A165545, which represents an equivalent symmetry class.
solved_when: An explicit generating function for Av(4123,4312) is determined and proved, matching the computed data (whose first relevant counts are 22, 89, 382, 1711, 7922 among one thousand computed terms) and settling whether the growth constant is \(3+2\sqrt2\).
why: It provides a concrete, conjecturally algebraic enumeration target, connecting the class to the well-studied machinery of permutation class enumeration and OEIS A165545.
key_works: Albert et al. (2018), *Generating permutations with restricted containers*, §5.2; Vatter and contributors, [OEIS A165545](https://oeis.org/A165545), representing an equivalent symmetry class.

title: Exact enumeration of \(\operatorname{Av}(4231,4321)\)
open: What is the exact enumeration of permutations that avoid both patterns 4231 and 4321? More precisely, determine the generating function for the class \(\operatorname{Av}(4231,4321)\).
status: Six hundred terms of the sequence have been computed, with counts for lengths four through eight equal to 22, 90, 396, 1837, and 8864, and numerical growth approximately 5.89249. Albert et al. (2018), *Generating permutations with restricted containers*, §5.2 treats related machinery, and Apagodu and contributors' [OEIS A053617](https://oeis.org/A053617) represents the complementary class.
solved_when: A closed form or otherwise exact expression for the generating function of \(\operatorname{Av}(4231,4321)\) is obtained, reproducing the known counts 22, 90, 396, 1837, 8864 for lengths four through eight among the six hundred computed terms (with approximate growth rate 5.89249).
why: It would settle another distinct two-pattern length-four enumeration, advancing the project of classifying all such pairs.
key_works: Albert et al. (2018), *Generating permutations with restricted containers*, §5.2; Apagodu and contributors, [OEIS A053617](https://oeis.org/A053617), representing the complementary class.

title: Plabic promotion maps are quasi-cluster homomorphisms
open: Is every promotion map arising from the plabic-tangle construction a quasi-cluster homomorphism between the corresponding products of Grassmannian cluster algebras?
status: This is the central conjecture of the 2026 paper of Even-Zohar–Parisi–Sherman-Bennett–Tessler–Williams, [*Plabic tangles and cluster promotion maps*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.02891). Several promotion classes have been established, but the full construction remains conjectural.
solved_when: Every promotion map from the plabic-tangle construction is proved to be a quasi-cluster homomorphism between the corresponding products of Grassmannian cluster algebras.
why: A proof would explain the preservation of cluster coordinates and positivity in recursive amplituhedron constructions, which underlie positive-geometry descriptions of all-loop planar scattering amplitudes.
key_works: Even-Zohar–Parisi–Sherman-Bennett–Tessler–Williams (2026), [*Plabic tangles and cluster promotion maps*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.02891).

title: Davenport’s constant for rank-three abelian groups
open: Is Davenport's constant for every rank-three abelian group \(G=C_a\oplus C_b\oplus C_c\) with \(1<a\mid b\mid c\) equal to \(a+b+c-2\), where \(D(G)\) denotes the least length of a sequence over \(G\) that forces a nonempty zero-sum subsequence?
status: The problem has been central since the 1960s. Equality is known to hold for \(p\)-groups and for many rank-three families (Girard–Schmid 2019, [Direct zero-sum problems for certain groups of rank three](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.07636); Geroldinger–Yang 2026, [On a classical zero-sum invariant](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19090)), but no general proof and no rank-three counterexample is known.
solved_when: A proof that \(D(G)=a+b+c-2\) for all rank-three abelian groups \(G=C_a\oplus C_b\oplus C_c\) with \(1<a\mid b\mid c\), or an explicit rank-three counterexample.
why: The constant governs which zero-sum relations are irreducible and thereby controls factorization lengths in the corresponding block monoid, so settling it pins down the arithmetic of invariants for a large class of groups.
key_works: Girard–Schmid (2019), [*Direct zero-sum problems for certain groups of rank three*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.07636); Geroldinger–Yang (2026), [*On a classical zero-sum invariant*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19090).

title: Gao’s Property D for rank two
open: If a length-\(4n-4\) sequence over \(C_n^2\) has no zero-sum subsequence of length \(n\), must it be of the form \(T^{[n-1]}\) for some length-four sequence \(T\)?
status: The extremal length \(4n-4\) follows from Kemnitz's theorem, but the general extremal structure remains open despite multiplicative reductions and many solved moduli (see Gao–Geroldinger (2006), *Zero-sum problems in finite abelian groups: a survey*; Girard–Schmid (2019), *Direct zero-sum problems for certain groups of rank three*).
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) determines the full extremal structure: every zero-sum-free-of-length-\(n\) sequence of length \(4n-4\) in \(C_n^2\) is shown to equal \(T^{[n-1]}\) for some length-four \(T\), or an exception is exhibited.
why: It would classify the extremizers needed to pin down exact zero-sum constants in larger groups.
key_works: Gao–Geroldinger (2006), *Zero-sum problems in finite abelian groups: a survey*; Girard–Schmid (2019), [*Direct zero-sum problems for certain groups of rank three*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.07636).

title: Nonabelian short-product-one versus exact-length constants
open: Does every finite nonabelian group \(G\) satisfy \(s(G)=\eta(G)+\exp(G)-1\)? In other words, can the classical relation between the Erdős–Ginzburg–Ziv constant and the short product-one constant be established using reorderable product-one subsequences of exact or bounded exponent length?
status: The unrestricted extension remains open. Qu–Wang–Li's August 2026 preprint proves the equality when a cyclic subgroup has index equal to the smallest prime divisor of \(|G|\) ([Qu–Wang–Li (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15568)).
solved_when: The identity \(s(G)=\eta(G)+\exp(G)-1\) is proved for all finite nonabelian groups \(G\) (or a counterexample is found).
why: A proof would separate the effects of noncommutativity from the difficulty of pinning down exact subsequence length in product-one problems over nonabelian groups.
key_works: Qu–Wang–Li (2026), [*The equality between the Erdős–Ginzburg–Ziv constant and the short product-one constant for finite nonabelian groups*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15568).

title: Sun’s zero sums divisible by exactly one power of the modulus
open: For \(n>2\), must every \(2n+1\) integers, none divisible by \(n\), contain \(n\) of them whose sum is divisible by \(n\) but not by \(n^2\)? In other words, does the exponent-\(1\) Erdős–Ginzburg–Ziv constant satisfy \(s_1(n)=2n+1\)?
status: Conjectured by Sun in June 2026. It is known that for \(n\ge4\) the threshold satisfies \(2n+1\le s_1(n)\le n^2-2n+2\).
solved_when: A proof (or disproof, with counterexample) is given that for every \(n>2\), any \(2n+1\) integers with none divisible by \(n\) contain \(n\) terms whose sum is divisible by \(n\) but not \(n^2\); equivalently, that the lower bound \(2n+1\) matches \(s_1(n)\).
why: Classical zero-sum selection guarantees a subsum divisible by \(n\); this problem asks for control of the divisibility depth, refining zero-sum theory with a valuation constraint.
key_works: Sun (2026), [*On zero-sum problems of two new types*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18234).

bib.title: Sun’s zero sums divisible by exactly one power of the modulus

title: Sharp valuation-sensitive zero sums among units
open: Among integers coprime to \(n>2\), how many terms must a sequence have before it necessarily contains an \(n\)-term subsequence whose sum is divisible by \(n\) but not by \(n^2\)? Is the sharp threshold exactly \(2n-(-1)^n\), as conjectured?
status: Known bounds are \(2n-(-1)^n\le t_1(n)\le(n-1)\varphi(n)+1\); for odd primes, a 2026 result improves the upper bound to \(3p-2\). Key works: Gao–Jiang–Lei–Lin–Yang (2026), [*A new problem from zero-sum theory*](https://doi.org/10.4064/aa251115-21-1); Sun (2026), [*On zero-sum problems of two new types*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18234).
solved_when: The threshold \(t_1(n)\) is determined exactly, specifically by proving \(t_1(n)=2n-(-1)^n\) for all \(n>2\) (or otherwise identifying the exact value and closing the gap with the known bounds \(2n-(-1)^n\le t_1(n)\le(n-1)\varphi(n)+1\)).
why: It determines how restricting to units changes exact divisibility thresholds in zero-sum theory, sharpening the classical Erdős–Ginzburg–Ziv-type picture to a valuation-sensitive regime.
key_works: Gao–Jiang–Lei–Lin–Yang (2026), [*A new problem from zero-sum theory*](https://doi.org/10.4064/aa251115-21-1); Sun (2026), [*On zero-sum problems of two new types*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18234).

title: Expected 3-subsquare count in a random Latin square
open: Does a uniformly random order-\(n\) Latin square contain, on average, about a bounded number of order-three subsquares as \(n\) grows? Specifically, prove that the expected number of \(3\times 3\) subsquares tends to \(1/18\) as \(n\to\infty\).
status: McKay–Wanless (1999) is the baseline reference (*Most Latin Squares Have Many Subsquares*). Divoux–Kelly–Kennedy–Sidhu (2026, [*Subsquares in Random Latin Squares and Rectangles*](https://doi.org/10.1002/jcd.70004)) establish the corresponding asymptotic for rectangles with fewer than \((1/2-\alpha)n\) rows, but the square case remains open.
solved_when: A proof that the expected number of order-three subsquares in a uniformly random order-\(n\) Latin square converges to \(1/18\) as \(n\) tends to infinity.
why: It is a sharp test case for whether local independence heuristics survive under the global design constraints defining a Latin square.
key_works: McKay–Wanless (1999), *Most Latin Squares Have Many Subsquares*; Divoux–Kelly–Kennedy–Sidhu (2026), [*Subsquares in Random Latin Squares and Rectangles*](https://doi.org/10.1002/jcd.70004).

title: Absence of large proper subsquares in random Latin squares
open: Does a uniformly random order-\(n\) Latin square almost surely contain no proper Latin subsquare of order at least four — that is, does the probability of having no such subsquare tend to one?
status: McKay–Wanless (1999), *Most Latin Squares Have Many Subsquares*. The 2026 bound of Divoux–Kelly–Kenneth–Sidhu — careful, exact names: Divoux–Kelly–Kennedy–Sidhu (2026), *Subsquares in Random Latin Squares and Rectangles* — excludes proper subsquares larger than \(C\sqrt{n\log n}\); rectangle analogues reach the desired cutoff.
solved_when: It is proved that a uniformly random order-\(n\) Latin square has no proper Latin subsquare of order at least four with probability tending to one as \(n \to \infty\).
why: A proof would determine the typical square's complete local subsquare profile.
key_works: McKay–Wanless (1999), *Most Latin Squares Have Many Subsquares*; Divoux–Kelly–Kennedy–Sidhu (2026), [*Subsquares in Random Latin Squares and Rectangles*](https://doi.org/10.1002/jcd.70004).

title: Polynomial worst-case canonization of Latin squares
open: Is there a polynomial-time algorithm that assigns to every Latin square a canonical representative under the full symmetry group of row, column, and symbol permutations — that is, worst-case polynomial-time canonization of Latin squares?
status: The best known worst-case bound is \(n^{O(\log n)}\); Gill–Mammoliti–Wanless (2025) established polynomial average running time in [*Canonical Labeling of Latin Squares in Average-Case Polynomial Time*](https://doi.org/10.1002/rsa.70015), leaving the worst case open.
solved_when: A deterministic procedure outputs, for any \(n \times n\) Latin square, a canonical form invariant under row, column, and symbol permutations, with worst-case running time polynomial in \(n\).
why: It would make reliable equivalence rejection fast in quasigroup and design searches, where currently no polynomial worst-case guarantee exists.
key_works: Gill–Mammoliti–Wanless (2025), [*Canonical Labeling of Latin Squares in Average-Case Polynomial Time*](https://doi.org/10.1002/rsa.70015).

title: Uniform optimal covering arrays
open: For every strength-two parameter pair \((k,v)\), does there exist an optimal covering array in which the symbol frequencies within each column differ by at most one?
status: This is the Stevens–Meagher uniformity conjecture (2005). All known optimal unconstrained examples support it, and nonuniform constrained examples do not refute the conjecture; see Stevens (2019), [*Non-uniform covering array with symmetric forbidden edge constraints*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.02479).
solved_when: A proof that such a balanced optimal covering array exists for every pair \((k,v)\), or a counterexample pair for which no optimal array with nearly-uniform column frequencies exists.
why: It would justify enforcing balanced columns as a constraint in exact searches for optimal covering arrays, with no loss of optimality.
key_works: Stevens (2019), [*Non-uniform covering array with symmetric forbidden edge constraints*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.02479).

title: Sharp chromatic coefficient for excluded odd minors
open: For graphs with no odd \(K_t\) minor, what is the true leading constant in the chromatic number — is the maximum \(\chi(G)\) asymptotic to \((3/2)t\), or does the coefficient lie strictly between 1 and 3/2? Formally, determine the sharp asymptotic coefficient \(g(t)/t\) where \(g(t)=\max\{\chi(G):G\text{ has no odd }K_t\text{ minor}\}\).
status: The coefficient-one conjecture was refuted in a December 2025 preprint by Kühn–Sauermann–Steiner–Wigderson ([*Disproof of the Odd Hadwiger Conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.20392)), whose examples require \((3/2-o(1))t\) colors. A linear upper bound follows from known reductions and the 2026 linear Hadwiger theorem.
solved_when: The limit \(g(t)/t\) is determined (or pinned to explicit constants \(c_1,c_2\) with matching asymptotics if the exact constant resists).
why: With the coefficient-one conjecture refuted, odd Hadwiger's conjecture no longer gives the right quantitative bound; this problem supplies its correct quantitative replacement.
key_works: Kühn–Sauermann–Steiner–Wigderson (2025), [*Disproof of the Odd Hadwiger Conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.20392).

bib.title: Sharp chromatic coefficient for excluded odd minors

title: Sharp triangle-free extraction threshold
open: How triangle-free must a highly chromatic graph be — what is the slowest-growing function \(f(k)\) such that every graph with \(\chi(G)\ge f(k)\) contains a triangle-free subgraph of chromatic number at least \(k\)?
status: Rödl proved the existence of such an \(f(k)\) in 1977. Steiner's 2026 preprint, [*Locally bipartite subgraphs via multicolor Ramsey numbers*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02522v2), improves the previously known tower-type bound to a single exponential; the correct scale remains unknown.
solved_when: The optimal growth rate of \(f(k)\) is determined (up to the current bounds, whether \(f(k)\) is polynomial, or otherwise below the single-exponential regime).
why: It quantifies how much chromatic complexity survives after removing all triangles, calibrating the interplay between local constraints and global chromatic structure.
key_works: Steiner (2026), [*Locally bipartite subgraphs via multicolor Ramsey numbers*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02522v2).

title: Domatic growth excluding an induced double star
open: For each fixed diameter-three tree \(T\), must the domatic number of induced-\(T\)-free graphs tend to infinity with the minimum degree? In other words, is every such \(T\) a "domatic-growth" tree, in the sense that graphs of large minimum degree avoiding \(T\) as an induced subgraph admit arbitrarily many pairwise disjoint dominating sets?
status: An unresolved case of a 2026 classification conjecture. Strong positive results are known for stars and for \(P_4\). Key work: Chuet–Djelloul–La–Pirot–Zaredehabadi (2026), [*A Domatic Analogue of χ-Bounded Graph Classes and the Gyárfás–Sumner Conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.02030).
solved_when: For every fixed diameter-three tree \(T\), it is proved that the domatic number of induced-\(T\)-free graphs tends to infinity with the minimum degree — i.e., for each \(k\), all induced-\(T\)-free graphs of sufficiently large minimum degree have domatic number at least \(k\).
why: A positive answer guarantees many disjoint dominating "service layers" purely from local density, giving a domatic analogue of \(\chi\)-boundedness for these hereditary classes.
key_works: Chuet–Djelloul–La–Pirot–Zaredehabadi (2026), [*A Domatic Analogue of χ-Bounded Graph Classes and the Gyárfás–Sumner Conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.02030).

title: Optimal induced-forest density in planar graphs
open: How large an induced forest must every planar graph contain? Formally, determine the largest \(c\) such that every planar \(n\)-vertex graph contains an induced forest on at least \(cn-O(1)\) vertices.
status: The historical conjecture that \(c=1/2\) was refuted in 2026 preprints. Current guarantees and constructions leave \(2/5\le c\le25/52\). Key work: Cames van Batenburg–Goedgebeur–Jooken (2026), [*Counterexamples to the Albertson–Berman conjecture: minimum order, connectivity and an improved ratio bound*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23260).
solved_when: The constant \(c\) is pinned down exactly: matching upper and lower bounds are established for the leading coefficient of the induced-forest size in planar \(n\)-vertex graphs, closing the gap currently given by \(2/5\le c\le25/52\).
why: It determines the intrinsic vertex-deletion cost of eliminating all cycles from a planar graph.
key_works: Cames van Batenburg–Goedgebeur–Jooken (2026), [*Counterexamples to the Albertson–Berman conjecture: minimum order, connectivity and an improved ratio bound*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23260).

title: Exact cyclic abelian repetition thresholds
open: What is the least integer \(A(d)\) such that every length \(n\) admits a \(d\)-letter word whose periodic repetition avoids abelian \(A(d)\)-powers with block length below \(n\)? In other words, determine the exact cyclic abelian repetition threshold for each alphabet size \(d\).
status: For \(d=2,3,4\), bounds are respectively \(5\)–\(8\), \(3\)–\(4\), and \(2\)–\(3\) (Peltomäki–Whiteland 2020, [Avoiding abelian powers cyclically](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.06307)).
solved_when: The exact value of \(A(d)\) is determined for each \(d\), replacing the current bounds: \(A(2)\in\{5,\dots,8\}\), \(A(3)\in\{3,\dots,4\}\), and \(A(4)\in\{2,\dots,3\}\).
why: A solution distinguishes circular from ordinary infinite-word avoidance, clarifying how cyclicity changes abelian power avoidance.
key_works: Peltomäki–Whiteland (2020), [*Avoiding abelian powers cyclically*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.06307).

title: Hadwiger’s exact coloring conjecture
open: Is it true that every graph needing at least \(t\) colors contains the complete graph \(K_t\) as a minor? That is, does \(\chi(G) \ge t\) force a \(K_t\)-minor for every \(t\)?
status: Proposed in 1943, the conjecture is proved through \(t=6\). A 2026 preprint of Norin–Steiner, [*A Proof of the Linear Hadwiger Conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05291), establishes a linear bound, leaving only the exact coefficient unresolved.
solved_when: The statement holds for every integer \(t\), recovering the exact form of the conjecture rather than an asymptotic or linear-bound approximation.
why: A proof would tie chromatic complexity directly to complete-minor structure, giving a precise structural characterization of what forces high chromatic number.
key_works: Norin–Steiner (2026), [*A Proof of the Linear Hadwiger Conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05291).

title: Erdős–Hajnal conjecture
open: For every fixed graph \(H\), is there an exponent \(\varepsilon(H)>0\) such that every \(n\)-vertex graph with no induced copy of \(H\) contains a clique or independent set of size \(n^{\varepsilon(H)}\)?
status: Open since 1977. The conjecture is settled for all five-vertex forbidden graphs, and 2026 work by Huang–Ju–Zhou ([*Erdős–Hajnal beyond the five-vertex path*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06258)) extends it to additional six-vertex examples.
solved_when: A proof (for every fixed \(H\)) of a clique or independent set of size \(n^{\varepsilon(H)}\) in every induced-\(H\)-free \(n\)-vertex graph, for some \(\varepsilon(H)>0\) depending only on \(H\).
why: It would show that excluding a fixed induced subgraph forces polynomially large homogeneous sets, sharply distinguishing hereditary structure from the polylogarithmic behavior of unrestricted Ramsey graphs.
key_works: Huang–Ju–Zhou (2026), [*Erdős–Hajnal beyond the five-vertex path*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06258).

title: Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture
open: For every fixed tree \(T\), prove that graphs with no induced copy of \(T\) have chromatic number bounded by a function of their clique number — equivalently, that every induced-\(T\)-free graph class is \(\chi\)-bounded with a bound depending only on \(T\) and the clique number.
status: The conjecture originates in the 1970s, and many trees have been settled. The 2026 theorem of Davies–Yuditsky, [*Polynomial Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture for graphs of bounded boxicity*](https://igt.centre-mersenne.org/articles/10.5802/igt.17/), proves the polynomial version for graphs of bounded boxicity but does not resolve the conjecture for arbitrary graphs.
solved_when: For every fixed tree \(T\), there exists a function \(f\) such that every induced-\(T\)-free graph \(G\) satisfies \(\chi(G) \le f(\omega(G))\).
why: A solution would complete the classification of single forbidden induced subgraphs whose exclusion forces bounded coloring behavior in terms of clique number.
key_works: Davies–Yuditsky (2026), [*Polynomial Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture for graphs of bounded boxicity*](https://igt.centre-mersenne.org/articles/10.5802/igt.17/).

title: Graph reconstruction conjecture
open: Is every finite simple graph on at least three vertices determined, up to isomorphism, by the multiset of its vertex-deleted subgraphs (its "deck")?
status: Open since the 1940s; trees, regular graphs, and numerous other classes are known to be reconstructible. Recent work includes Dufresne–Jeronimo–Kenkel–Lindo–Villamizar (2026), [*Shuffling the Deck: Invariant Theory and the Graph Reconstruction Conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.16567).
solved_when: A proof that all finite simple graphs with at least three vertices are reconstructible from their decks, or a counterexample exhibiting a non-reconstructible graph.
why: It asks whether complete overlapping partial observations determine a network — a fundamental question about how much global structure is encoded in local deletions.
key_works: Dufresne–Jeronimo–Kenkel–Lindo–Villamizar (2026), [*Shuffling the Deck: Invariant Theory and the Graph Reconstruction Conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.16567).

title: Edge reconstruction conjecture
open: Can every finite simple graph with at least four edges be recovered from its collection of edge-deleted subgraphs, with isolated vertices retained? Formally, is every such graph determined by its edge-deleted deck?
status: Open since the 1960s; many dense and structured graph classes are settled. A recent perspective is Calle–Gould (2025), [*A combinatorial K-theory perspective on the Edge Reconstruction Conjecture in graph theory*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14986).
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) shows whether every finite simple graph with at least four edges is uniquely determined by its edge-deleted deck.
why: It asks whether observing the graph after every possible single-edge deletion suffices to identify the original — a fundamental test of how much local deletion information determines global structure.
key_works: Calle–Gould (2025), [*A combinatorial K-theory perspective on the Edge Reconstruction Conjecture in graph theory*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14986).

title: Borodin–Kostochka conjecture
open: Is every graph of maximum degree at least 9 that contains no clique on Δ vertices colorable with only Δ−1 colors? Formally, does the exclusion of a single \(K_\Delta\) suffice to lower the chromatic number one step below Δ throughout the range \(\Delta\ge9\)?
status: Proposed in 1977; the conjecture is known to hold for sufficiently large maximum degree, but the full range beginning at Δ=9 remains open.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given covering all graphs with \(\Delta\ge9\) and no \(K_\Delta\); in particular, the remaining small values of Δ above the known sufficiently-large range must be settled.
why: It would pinpoint the exact threshold at which Brooks' theorem's Δ-coloring guarantee improves by a full color, resolving a basic extremal question in graph coloring.
key_works: Dvořák–Kang–Mikšaník (2026), [*On Borodin–Kostochka conjecture for correspondence coloring*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.14427).

title: List edge-coloring conjecture
open: Does every loopless multigraph have the same list chromatic index as its ordinary chromatic index, i.e., is \(\chi'_\ell(G)=\chi'(G)\) always true?
status: Open since the 1970s. Galvin settled the bipartite multigraph case in 1995; asymptotic results and further special-family results are known, including Jafari (2026), [*The List Edge-Coloring Conjecture for New Infinite Families*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.22895).
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) establishing \(\chi'_\ell(G)=\chi'(G)\) for every loopless multigraph \(G\).
why: It would show that allowing each edge its own list of eligible colors never forces additional colors beyond the classical edge-chromatic number.
key_works: Jafari (2026), [*The List Edge-Coloring Conjecture for New Infinite Families*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.22895).

title: Erdős–Nešetřil strong edge-coloring conjecture
open: Is every graph of maximum degree \(\Delta\) strongly edge-colorable with at most \(5\Delta^2/4\) colors when \(\Delta\) is even, and at most \((5\Delta^2-2\Delta+1)/4\) when \(\Delta\) is odd?
status: The conjecture was proposed in 1985; five-cycle blow-ups attain these bounds, so they would be optimal. The best known general upper bound is \(1.73\Delta^2\) for sufficiently large \(\Delta\), due to Davey–Hurley–de Joannis de Verclos–Kang–Volec (2026), [Strong edge-colouring via local flag algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17421).
solved_when: The conjectured bounds are proved in general: strong chromatic index \(\le 5\Delta^2/4\) for even \(\Delta\) and \(\le (5\Delta^2-2\Delta+1)/4\) for odd \(\Delta\), matching the five-cycle blow-up constructions.
why: It pins down the exact number of channels needed for scheduling under distance-two interference, where edges within distance two of each other cannot share a color.
key_works: Davey–Hurley–de Joannis de Verclos–Kang–Volec (2026), [*Strong edge-colouring via local flag algebras*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17421).

title: Linear arboricity conjecture
open: Can every graph of maximum degree \(\Delta\) have its edges partitioned into at most \(\lceil(\Delta+1)/2\rceil\) linear forests — spanning subgraphs of maximum degree 2? The conjecture asserts this tight bound holds for all \(\Delta\).
status: Proposed in 1981. The best known bounds include \(\Delta/2+O(\sqrt\Delta\log^4\Delta)\); exact rounding remains unresolved. Key works: Lang–Postle (2023), [*An Improved Bound for the Linear Arboricity Conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.04251); Christoph et al. (2025), [*New bounds for linear arboricity and related problems*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.20500).
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) settles the partition into \(\lceil(\Delta+1)/2\rceil\) linear forests for every maximum-degree-\(\Delta\) graph, eliminating the current \(\Delta/2+O(\sqrt\Delta\log^4\Delta)\) error term and resolving the rounding question.
why: The answer determines the minimum number of nonbranching routing layers needed, i.e., how few paths-and-cycles layers suffice to decompose any bounded-degree network.
key_works: Lang–Postle (2023), [*An Improved Bound for the Linear Arboricity Conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.04251); Christoph et al. (2025), [*New bounds for linear arboricity and related problems*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.20500).

title: Tutte’s 5-flow conjecture
subfield: Flows, perfect matchings, and cycle covers
open: Does every bridgeless graph admit a nowhere-zero 5-flow? Equivalently, can every bridgeless graph be given a nowhere-zero integer flow with all flow values of absolute value at most four?
status: Proposed by Tutte in 1954. Seymour's 1981 theorem (*Nowhere-zero 6-flows*) guarantees a nowhere-zero 6-flow for every bridgeless graph, and the one-unit improvement to 5 remains open. Related work includes Cranston–Li–Su–Wang–Xu (2026), [*Reconfiguration of Nowhere-zero Flows*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.24685).
solved_when: A proof, for every bridgeless graph, of the existence of a nowhere-zero integer flow with absolute values at most four (equivalently, a nowhere-zero 5-flow); or a counterexample.
why: It would establish the sharp universal integrality bound for conservative flows, completing the program initiated by Tutte's flow conjectures.
key_works: Seymour (1981), *Nowhere-zero 6-flows*; Cranston–Li–Su–Wang–Xu (2026), [*Reconfiguration of Nowhere-zero Flows*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.24685).

title: Tutte’s 3-flow conjecture
subfield: Flows, perfect matchings, and cycle covers
open: Does every 4-edge-connected graph admit a nowhere-zero integer 3-flow?
status: Proposed in 1972. Six-edge-connectivity suffices; connectivity four remains unresolved. Key works include Lovász–Thomassen–Wu–Zhang (2013), *Nowhere-zero 3-flows and modulo k-orientations*, and Li–Li (2026), [*Nowhere-zero 3-flows in graphs with forbidden edge-cuts*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.08377).
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) resolves the statement for all 4-edge-connected graphs; currently the best confirmed sufficiency is 6-edge-connectivity.
why: It connects network redundancy to exceptionally economical circulation, showing how strong edge-connectivity forces the existence of flows with the smallest possible nonzero flow values.
key_works: Lovász–Thomassen–Wu–Zhang (2013), *Nowhere-zero 3-flows and modulo k-orientations*; Li–Li (2026), [*Nowhere-zero 3-flows in graphs with forbidden edge-cuts*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.08377).

title: Berge–Fulkerson conjecture
subfield: Flows, perfect matchings, and cycle covers
open: Can every bridgeless cubic graph have its edges covered by exactly six perfect matchings, with each edge used exactly twice (repetitions allowed)?
status: Open since 1971. Many classes of graphs are settled, and a 2026 paper by Magalhães Júnior–Silva, *On some perfect matching conjectures in infinite, cubic, bridgeless graphs* (https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29511), relates the finite and locally finite infinite versions.
solved_when: A proof, for every bridgeless cubic graph, of the existence of six perfect matchings whose multiset union contains each edge exactly twice; a counterexample would also resolve the conjecture.
why: It would let fractional matching decompositions of cubic graphs be replaced by six exact, integral perfect matchings.
key_works: Magalhães Júnior–Silva (2026), [*On some perfect matching conjectures in infinite, cubic, bridgeless graphs*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29511).

title: Erdős–Gyárfás power-of-two cycle conjecture
open: Must every graph of minimum degree at least three contain a cycle whose length is a power of two? In other words, is there some graph with all degrees three or more in which no cycle has length 2^k for any k?
status: The conjecture was posed in 1995. A 2026 search by Ducoffe–Dumitru ([*Towards a More Structured Search for Erdős–Gyárfás Counter-Examples*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28594)) excludes counterexamples through 40 vertices in general, through 48 vertices for cubic graphs, and through 66 vertices for bipartite graphs.
solved_when: Either a proof that every graph of minimum degree at least 3 contains a cycle of length a power of two, or an explicit counterexample graph of minimum degree at least 3 with no such cycle.
why: It asks an extremely weak local condition — minimum degree three — to force an exact arithmetic pattern on cycle lengths, so a solution would reveal a deep structural link between degree and the arithmetic of cycles.
key_works: Ducoffe–Dumitru (2026), [*Towards a More Structured Search for Erdős–Gyárfás Counter-Examples*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28594).

title: Hajós’ cycle decomposition conjecture
open: Can every simple Eulerian graph on \(n\) vertices have its edges partitioned into at most \(\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor\) simple cycles? In other words, is the bound of \(\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor\) cycles a universal budget for cycle-decomposing every even-degree network?
status: The conjecture originates in the 1960s; numerous classes have been verified, and Heinrich–Natale–Streicher (2017), [*Hajós' cycle conjecture for small graphs*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.08724), confirmed it for all Eulerian graphs through 12 vertices.
solved_when: A proof that every simple Eulerian \(n\)-vertex graph admits an edge partition into at most \(\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor\) simple cycles, or a counterexample graph exceeding this budget.
why: It determines the sharp universal cost of decomposing even-degree networks into cycles, a basic parameter for how economically cycle structure covers all of Eulerian graph theory.
key_works: Heinrich–Natale–Streicher (2017), [*Hajós’ cycle conjecture for small graphs*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.08724).

title: Tuza’s triangle packing–covering conjecture
open: Is the minimum number of edges needed to hit all triangles of a graph always at most twice the maximum number of pairwise edge-disjoint triangles? Formally, does \(\tau_\triangle(G)\le 2\nu_\triangle(G)\) hold for every graph \(G\)?
status: The conjecture was proposed in 1981. A 2026 preprint by Gupta, [*Tuza’s conjecture for graphs of maximum degree at most seven*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06538), settles the case of maximum degree at most seven; the general factor two remains open.
solved_when: The inequality \(\tau_\triangle(G)\le 2\nu_\triangle(G)\) is proven for all graphs (or a counterexample is produced).
why: It would sharply tie the cost of eliminating all triangles to the count of disjoint local obstructions, giving a tight structural link between covering and packing of triangles.
key_works: Gupta (2026), [*Tuza’s conjecture for graphs of maximum degree at most seven*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06538).

title: Ryser’s hypergraph covering conjecture
open: Is the covering number of every \(r\)-partite \(r\)-uniform hypergraph at most \((r-1)\) times its matching number? In symbols, does \(\tau(H)\le(r-1)\nu(H)\) always hold?
status: Open since the 1960s; the full statement is known for \(r\le3\). A September 2026 preprint settles the case \(r=4,\nu=2\) [White (2026), *Tuza's Ryser-conjecture claim for four-partite hypergraphs with matching number two*, https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14281].
solved_when: The inequality \(\tau(H)\le(r-1)\nu(H)\) is proved for all \(r\)-partite \(r\)-uniform hypergraphs \(H\), for every \(r\).
why: It would extend the exact matching–cover duality of bipartite graphs (\(\tau=\nu\)) to the multipartite hypergraph setting, giving the right general form of König's theorem beyond graphs.
key_works: White (2026), [*Tuza’s Ryser-conjecture claim for four-partite hypergraphs with matching number two*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14281).

title: Turán’s tetrahedron problem
open: What is the maximum number of triples on an \(n\)-element set that contains no tetrahedron, i.e. four triples on four points? Is the conjectured density \(5/9\) correct, in the sense that \(\operatorname{ex}(n,K_4^{(3)})=(5/9+o(1))\binom n3\), or does some other density govern?
status: Open since 1941 (Turán's \((3,4)\)-problem). A construction gives lower bound \(5/9\). An October 2026 revision by Jeong–Park–Im–Lee–Yang, [*A New Upper Bound for the Turán Density of the Tetrahedron*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27495v2), gives a Lean-checked upper bound below \(0.557789\). A historical Erdős prize of US$500 is attached.
solved_when: A proof that \(\operatorname{ex}(n,K_4^{(3)})=(5/9+o(1))\binom n3\), or alternatively a determination of the correct Turán density together with matching constructions and upper bounds.
why: This is the central first example of genuinely hypergraphic extremal behavior: unlike the graph case, the natural hypergraph analogue of Turán's theorem has resisted exact resolution, so settling it shapes our understanding of extremal combinatorics beyond graphs.
key_works: Jeong–Park–Im–Lee–Yang (2026), [*A New Upper Bound for the Turán Density of the Tetrahedron*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27495v2).

title: Vizing’s domination product conjecture
subfield: Graph parameters and topological graph theory
open: Does the domination number of a Cartesian product graph always dominate the product of the domination numbers of its factors — that is, is \(\gamma(G\square H)\ge\gamma(G)\gamma(H)\) for all graphs \(G\) and \(H\)?
status: Open since the 1960s. A factor-one-half bound and refinements are known: Clark–Suen (2000), [An Inequality Related to Vizing’s Conjecture](https://doi.org/10.37236/1542), and Suen–Tarr (2012), [An Improved Inequality Related to Vizing’s Conjecture](https://doi.org/10.37236/15). A 2026 claim of a stronger factor was withdrawn.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of \(\gamma(G\square H)\ge\gamma(G)\gamma(H)\) for all pairs of graphs \(G,H\).
why: It would establish that domination requirements genuinely multiply across product coordinates, giving exact worst-case behavior for networks built as products.
key_works: Clark–Suen (2000), [*An Inequality Related to Vizing’s Conjecture*](https://doi.org/10.37236/1542); Suen–Tarr (2012), [*An Improved Inequality Related to Vizing’s Conjecture*](https://doi.org/10.37236/15).

title: Zarankiewicz’s crossing-number conjecture
subfield: Graph parameters and topological graph theory
open: Is the crossing number of the complete bipartite graph \(K_{m,n}\) exactly \(\lfloor m/2\rfloor\lfloor(m-1)/2\rfloor\lfloor n/2\rfloor\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor\), as conjectured by Zarankiewicz?

Christian–Richter–Salazar (2013), [*Zarankiewicz’s Conjecture is finite for each fixed m*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jctb.2012.11.001); Brosch–Polak (2024), [semidefinite lower bounds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.02755).
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the identity \(\operatorname{cr}(K_{m,n})=\lfloor m/2\rfloor\lfloor(m-1)/2\rfloor\lfloor n/2\rfloor\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor\) for all \(m,n\).
why: It would give the exact crossing cost of complete bipartite interconnections, the basic building block for crossing-number lower bounds in topological graph theory.
key_works: Christian–Richter–Salazar (2013), [*Zarankiewicz’s Conjecture is finite for each fixed m*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jctb.2012.11.001); Brosch–Polak (2024), [semidefinite lower bounds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.02755).

title: Tower height of diagonal 3-uniform Ramsey numbers
open: Can the diagonal 3-uniform Ramsey number \(r_3(t,t)\) be shown to grow at least doubly exponentially in \(t\), or can its current doubly exponential upper bound be substantially reduced?
status: The fundamental gap remains \(2^{\Omega(t^2)}\) versus \(2^{2^{O(t)}}\); see Mubayi–Suk (2020), [*A survey of hypergraph Ramsey problems*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.04229).
solved_when: The gap between the lower bound \(2^{\Omega(t^2)}\) and the upper bound \(2^{2^{O(t)}}\) is meaningfully closed — either by proving a doubly exponential lower bound for \(r_3(t,t)\) or by materially lowering the \(2^{2^{O(t)}}\) upper bound.
why: It controls the central tower-height distinction between graph and hypergraph Ramsey numbers, determining where the jump from single to double exponential growth occurs.
key_works: Mubayi–Suk (2020), [*A survey of hypergraph Ramsey problems*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.04229).

title: Seymour’s second-neighborhood conjecture
open: Does every finite oriented graph contain a vertex whose second neighborhood — the set of vertices at directed distance exactly two from it — is at least as large as its out-neighborhood?
status: Proposed in 1990; the conjecture is known for tournaments and several other classes of oriented graphs. A 2026 preprint, the Sadhukhan–Sandeep–Sen [minimum-outdegree-seven theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30588), settles minimum outdegree seven.
solved_when: A proof that every finite oriented graph has a vertex with at least as many vertices at directed distance exactly two as at distance one, or a counterexample.
why: It asserts that directed expansion is unavoidable even with no degree assumptions whatsoever, making it a fundamental test of how orientation alone forces local growth.
key_works: Sadhukhan–Sandeep–Sen (2026), [minimum-outdegree-seven theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30588).

title: Bermond–Thomassen disjoint-cycle conjecture
open: Does every digraph of minimum outdegree at least \(2k-1\) contain \(k\) vertex-disjoint directed cycles? In other words, is this outdegree threshold the sharp local condition forcing many disjoint cycles?
status: Proposed in 1981, the conjecture is known for \(k\le3\). A 2026 relaxation by Bessy–Muis–Sereni–Steiner–Wiederrecht ([*A relaxation of the Bermond–Thomassen conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12948)) permits reversing one arc in each selected cycle.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) for general \(k\) of the statement that minimum outdegree at least \(2k-1\) guarantees \(k\) vertex-disjoint directed cycles.
why: It would give the sharp local threshold for independent feedback loops in directed graphs.
key_works: Bessy–Muis–Sereni–Steiner–Wiederrecht (2026), [*A relaxation of the Bermond–Thomassen conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12948).

title: Woodall’s disjoint-dijoin conjecture
open: If every directed cut in a digraph contains at least \(k\) edges, must the edge set contain \(k\) pairwise disjoint dijoins — subsets of edges each meeting every directed cut?
status: Proposed in 1976. Fractional duality and several structural cases are known; the integral packing question remains open. Gutiérrez (2024), [*Towards a Dual Version of Woodall’s Conjecture for Partial 3-Trees*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.05703).
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) that minimum directed-cut size \(k\) guarantees \(k\) disjoint dijoins.
why: A proof would convert cut redundancy into disjoint global connectivity certificates, a directed analogue of Lucchesi–Younger-type packing.
key_works: Gutiérrez (2024), [*Towards a Dual Version of Woodall’s Conjecture for Partial 3-Trees*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.05703).

title: Erdős–Neumann-Lara orientation conjecture
open: For every integer \(k\), does every graph of sufficiently large chromatic number admit an orientation whose dichromatic number is at least \(k\)? Equivalently, is the class of graphs with dichromatic number less than \(k\), over all orientations, of bounded undirected chromatic number?
status: The conjecture originates in the 1970s and remains open. A 2026 preprint by Harutyunyan–Picasarri-Arrieta–Puig i Surroca, *On the list version of a conjecture of Erdős and Neumann-Lara* (arXiv:2603.01020), proves the corresponding list version, but the ordinary version is still unresolved.
solved_when: For each fixed \(k\), a bound \(f(k)\) is established such that every undirected graph with chromatic number at least \(f(k)\) has some orientation with dichromatic number at least \(k\).
why: It asks whether undirected incompatibility — high chromatic number — can always be converted, by a suitable orientation, into directed feedback complexity; a proof would give a genuine directed analogue of chromatic-number forcing.
key_works: Harutyunyan–Picasarri-Arrieta–Puig i Surroca (2026), [*On the list version of a conjecture of Erdős and Neumann-Lara*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.01020).

title: Sidorenko’s conjecture
subfield: Graph homomorphisms, invariants, and zero-error information
open: Is every bipartite graph a weakest host for its own patterns — that is, does every graph contain at least as many copies of any fixed bipartite pattern, relative to its size, as a random graph of the same edge density? Formally, is \(t_H(G)\ge t_{K_2}(G)^{e(H)}\) for every bipartite \(H\) and every graph \(G\), where \(t_H(G)=\operatorname{hom}(H,G)/|V(G)|^{|V(H)|}\)?
status: The conjecture was proposed around 1991–1993. Many families of bipartite graphs are settled, but no general proof is known; a May 2026 spectral equivalence (Li–Lin–Liu–Zhang, 2026, [*Spectral Sidorenko inequalities and edge-spectral supersaturation*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26614)) is a reformulation rather than a general proof.
solved_when: The inequality \(t_H(G)\ge t_{K_2}(G)^{e(H)}\) is proved for all bipartite graphs \(H\) and all graphs \(G\), or disproved by an explicit counterexample.
why: A proof would make random-like graphs universal minimizers of bipartite pattern densities, giving a complete common generalization of the many known graph-homomorphism inequalities.
key_works: Li–Lin–Liu–Zhang (2026), [*Spectral Sidorenko inequalities and edge-spectral supersaturation*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26614).

title: Stanley’s tree-distinguishing conjecture
subfield: Graph homomorphisms, invariants, and zero-error information
open: Does the chromatic symmetric function \(X_T=\sum_\kappa\prod_v x_{\kappa(v)}\), summed over proper colorings, take a different value on every pair of nonisomorphic trees? In other words, is Stanley's chromatic symmetric function a complete invariant for trees?
status: The conjecture was posed in 1995. It has been verified for many classes of trees and for all trees on up to 29 vertices. Stronger invariants are known to distinguish trees — notably the Kneser chromatic function (Nishimura 2026, [*The Kneser chromatic function distinguishes trees*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.disc.2026.115009)) and derivative reconstruction (Awan 2026, [arXiv:2609.13464](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13464)) — but these do not settle the question for the chromatic symmetric function itself.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) showing that \(X_T\) distinguishes all nonisomorphic trees — equivalently, that \(X_T = X_{T'}\) forces \(T \cong T'\) for all trees \(T, T'\).
why: It would make a natural algebraic invariant a complete description of a tree, turning the study of tree isomorphism into the study of a single symmetric function.
key_works: Nishimura (2026), [*The Kneser chromatic function distinguishes trees*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.disc.2026.115009); Awan (2026), [derivative reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13464).

title: Integer sum–product conjecture
open: Can a finite set of integers be simultaneously highly structured under both addition and multiplication? Formally, prove that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a constant \(c_\varepsilon>0\) such that \(\max(|A+A|,|AA|)\ge c_\varepsilon|A|^{2-\varepsilon}\) for every finite \(A\subset\mathbb Z\).
status: The conjecture originates with Erdős–Szemerédi (1983), *On sums and products of integers*. Exponents above \(4/3\) are known for the integer problem; a 2026 counterexample for real numbers, due to Bloom–Sawin–Schildkraut–Zhelezov (2026), does not settle the integer case.
solved_when: For every \(\varepsilon>0\), the bound \(\max(|A+A|,|AA|)\ge c_\varepsilon|A|^{2-\varepsilon}\) is established for all finite \(A\subset\mathbb Z\).
why: The conjecture gives a precise measure of how badly additive and multiplicative structure conflict within a single set of integers, a foundational tension throughout additive combinatorics.
key_works: Erdős–Szemerédi (1983), *On sums and products of integers*; Bloom–Sawin–Schildkraut–Zhelezov (2026), [real counterexample](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.28781).

title: Cap-set exponential growth constant
open: What is the true exponential growth rate of the largest cap set in \(\mathbb F_3^n\)? That is, determine \(\lim_n c_n^{1/n}\), where \(c_n\) is the largest progression-free subset of \(\mathbb F_3^n\).
status: Ellenberg–Gijswijt (2016), [large progression-free subsets](https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.09223), give an upper bound on the base of approximately 2.756, while known constructions exceed 2.2203. A 2026 preprint by Hametner–Tyrrell, [*Beating Product Constructions for Linear Equations Over Finite Fields*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.12194), shows that products of any fixed cap set are asymptotically suboptimal.
solved_when: The limit \(\lim_n c_n^{1/n}\) is determined exactly, or the gap is closed between the upper bound base of approximately 2.756 and the best constructive base exceeding 2.2203.
why: The problem directly tests the sharpness of slice-rank methods as an upper-bound technique and of current constructions, making it a benchmark for the limits of both.
key_works: Ellenberg–Gijswijt (2016), [large progression-free subsets](https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.09223); Hametner–Tyrrell (2026), [*Beating Product Constructions for Linear Equations Over Finite Fields*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.12194).

title: Quantitative axis-parallel squares
open: How large can a subset of \([N]^2\) be if it contains no four corners of any nondegenerate axis-parallel square? Formally, determine the maximum size of a square-corner-free subset of \([N]^2\).
status: Multidimensional density theorems imply an \(o(N^2)\) upper bound, but satisfactory quantitative bounds remain missing; see Green (2026), [*Arithmetic progressions at the Journal of the LMS*](https://doi.org/10.1112/jlms.70483).
solved_when: The correct order of magnitude of this maximum is determined up to constant (or logarithmic) factors — in particular, explicit bounds complementing the known \(o(N^2)\) density result.
why: It tests whether density recurrence methods extend beyond three-point configurations to genuinely four-point patterns, sharpening the quantitative content of multidimensional Szemerédi-type theorems.
key_works: Green (2026), [*Arithmetic progressions at the Journal of the LMS*](https://doi.org/10.1112/jlms.70483).

title: Lonely runner conjecture
open: If \(k\) runners set off together on a circular track at constant integer speeds, must there be a time when every runner is at distance at least \(1/(k+1)\) from the start? Formally, for nonzero integers \(v_1,\ldots,v_k\), does there exist \(t\) with \(\|tv_i\|\ge 1/(k+1)\) for all \(i\)?
status: The conjecture originates with Wills in the 1960s. A 2026 computer-assisted preprint reports the cases through \(k=12\) (Sungkawichai–Trakulthongchai, *Eleven, twelve, and thirteen lonely runners*; Beck–Everett, *Lonely Runner Relations*).
solved_when: For every \(k\) and every choice of nonzero integer speeds \(v_1,\ldots,v_k\), a real \(t\) is shown to exist with \(\|tv_i\|\ge 1/(k+1)\) for every \(i\).
why: It ties simultaneous Diophantine avoidance to lattice coverings and to scheduling problems, where such a guarantee describes when all participants can be simultaneously "lonely."
key_works: Sungkawichai–Trakulthongchai (2026), [*Eleven, twelve, and thirteen lonely runners*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.23906); Beck–Everett (2026), [*Lonely Runner Relations*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.06259).

title: Sunflower conjecture
open: For a fixed number of petals \(r\ge3\), how large must a family of distinct \(k\)-element sets be before it necessarily contains a sunflower — \(r\) sets whose pairwise intersections are all identical? Formally, is there a constant \(C_r\) depending only on \(r\) such that any family of more than \(C_r^k\) distinct \(k\)-sets contains such a configuration?
status: The conjecture dates to Erdős–Rado, 1960. The best general bounds have the form \((Cr\log k)^k\); removing the logarithmic factor remains open. Key works include Alweiss–Lovett–Wu–Zhang (2021), *Improved sunflower bounds*, and Rao (2026), [*The story of sunflowers*](https://doi.org/10.1112/jlms.70380).
solved_when: For every fixed \(r\ge3\), a bound of the form \(C_r^k\) (with \(C_r\) depending only on \(r\)) is established for the maximum size of a family of distinct \(k\)-sets containing no sunflower with \(r\) petals.
why: A positive answer would strengthen a pervasive combinatorial compression principle, with consequences such as monotone circuit lower bounds for CLIQUE.
key_works: Alweiss–Lovett–Wu–Zhang (2021), *Improved sunflower bounds*; Rao (2026), [*The story of sunflowers*](https://doi.org/10.1112/jlms.70380).

title: Union-closed sets conjecture
open: Must every finite union-closed family of sets that contains a nonempty set have some element appearing in at least half of the family's members?
status: The conjecture is due to Frankl (1979). Gilmer (2022) established a constant lower bound for the proportion of sets containing a frequent element. A 2026 preprint of Costa–Sadhu, *Beyond Liu's 0.382709 threshold*, reports a universal proportion of 0.3828852549667978 (October 2026).
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given for the claim that every finite union-closed family containing a nonempty set has an element contained in at least half of its sets.
why: It asks whether the closure operation alone forces some coordinate to be frequent, a fundamental structural property of set systems.
key_works: Gilmer (2022), *A constant lower bound for the union-closed sets conjecture*; Costa–Sadhu (2026), [*Beyond Liu’s 0.382709 threshold*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02295).

title: Borg’s uniform hereditary-family conjecture
open: If every maximal member of a hereditary family has size at least \(2k\), must a largest intersecting subfamily of its \(k\)-sets be a star?
status: Known results require maximal-set size larger than \(2k\); Kupavskii (2023), [*Intersection theorems for uniform subfamilies of hereditary families*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.02246), reduces the sufficient threshold to order \(k\log k\).
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given for the threshold \(2k\): either every hereditary family whose maximal members have size at least \(2k\) has a star as a largest intersecting family of \(k\)-sets, or a counterexample is exhibited.
why: It would establish the sharp local-dimension condition guaranteeing that intersection extremality is achieved by stars in hereditary families.
key_works: Kupavskii (2023), [*Intersection theorems for uniform subfamilies of hereditary families*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.02246).

title: Erdős matching conjecture
open: What is the largest family of \(k\)-element subsets of an \(n\)-element set in which no \(s+1\) of the sets are pairwise disjoint? For \(n\ge k(s+1)\), is the answer exactly \(\max\{\binom nk-\binom{n-s}k,\binom{k(s+1)-1}k\}\), as Erdős's matching conjecture predicts?
status: Proposed in 1965; the case \(k=3\) is settled. A September 2026 revision proves \(k=4\) when \(s\ge6004\), in Hou–Hu–Liu (2026), [*The Erdős Matching Conjecture for 4-uniform hypergraphs*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26060).
solved_when: For all \(n\ge k(s+1)\), it is proved that every \(k\)-uniform family with matching number at most \(s\) has at most \(\max\{\binom nk-\binom{n-s}k,\binom{k(s+1)-1}k\}\) edges.
why: It would identify the extremal obstructions to making many disjoint choices from a family of sets, the basic structural question behind Erdős–Ko–Rado–type theorems.
key_works: Hou–Hu–Liu (2026), [*The Erdős Matching Conjecture for 4-uniform hypergraphs*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26060).

title: Černý’s reset-word conjecture
open: Does every complete synchronizing deterministic automaton with \(n\) states admit a reset word of length at most \((n-1)^2\)? In other words, is the quadratic Černý bound tight as a universal worst case?
status: Posed in 1964; the bound is attained by Černý automata. General upper bounds remain cubic, with improvements including Shitov (2019), *An improvement to a recent upper bound for synchronizing words of finite automata*, and Zhu (2026), a one-cluster preprint (arXiv:2607.19675).
solved_when: A proof shows every complete synchronizing deterministic \(n\)-state automaton has a reset word of length at most \((n-1)^2\), matching the length attained by the Černý automata.
why: It pins down the exact worst-case cost of blindly synchronizing a system whose current state is unknown, a benchmark for synchronization algorithms and automata theory.
key_works: Shitov (2019), *An improvement to a recent upper bound for synchronizing words of finite automata*; Zhu (2026), [one-cluster preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.19675).

title: Foulkes’ plethysm conjecture
open: Is the plethysm \(h_n[h_m]\) always at least as large as \(h_m[h_n]\) in the dominance order on symmetric functions — that is, is their difference Schur-positive whenever \(1 \le m \le n\)?
status: Proposed by Foulkes in 1950. Many bounded-parameter and special-representation cases are established, but the general comparison remains open; see Foulkes (1950), *Concomitants of the quintic and sextic up to degree four in the coefficients of the ground form*, and Gangl–Gutiérrez–Szwej (2026) on generalized divisibility cases. Related to defining equations of Chow varieties.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that \(h_n[h_m]-h_m[h_n]\) expands with nonnegative coefficients in the Schur basis for all \(1 \le m \le n\).
why: It would impose a fundamental ordering on composed symmetric powers, governing which symmetric-group representations embed into which.
key_works: Foulkes (1950), *Concomitants of the quintic and sextic up to degree four in the coefficients of the ground form*; Gangl–Gutiérrez–Szwej (2026), [generalized divisibility cases](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.06220v3).

title: Garsia–Bergeron science-fiction conjecture
open: Is there a Macdonald-type interpolation formula, as predicted by the Garsia–Bergeron "science-fiction" conjecture, for the Frobenius characteristic of the intersection of Garsia–Haiman modules attached to corner deletions? That is, for the corner deletions \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_k\) of a partition \(\mu \vdash n+1\), prove the predicted formula for the Frobenius characteristic of \(\bigcap_i V_{\lambda_i}\), including the predicted dimension \(n!/k\).
status: The conjecture originates in the 1990s. Recent shuffle identities — Kim–Lee–Oh (2025), [*Shuffle formula in science fiction for Macdonald polynomials*](https://doi.org/10.1112/S0010437X25007122) — do not establish the full module-intersection interpretation.
solved_when: The Frobenius characteristic of the module intersection \(\bigcap_i V_{\lambda_i}\) is shown to be given by the predicted Macdonald interpolation formula for all \(\mu \vdash n+1\) and their corner deletions, with the dimension \(n!/k\) established.
why: It would explain the compatibility among Garsia–Haiman modules, clarifying how these modules and their intersections fit together.
key_works: Kim–Lee–Oh (2025), [*Shuffle formula in science fiction for Macdonald polynomials*](https://doi.org/10.1112/S0010437X25007122).

title: Valley Delta conjecture
open: Does the valley version of the Delta conjecture hold — that is, does the symmetric function \(\Delta'_{e_{n-k-1}} e_n\) admit an explicit combinatorial formula as a weighted sum over labelled Dyck paths with exactly \(k\) decorated contractible valleys?
status: Proposed in 2015 by Haglund–Remmel–Wilson (*The Delta conjecture*, 2015/2018). The rise version of the conjecture is proved; the valley version remains open. Recent progress includes Shin (2026), [*Exchange identities and symmetric slices of the valley Delta conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14877).
solved_when: An identity is established (with proof) expressing \(\Delta'_{e_{n-k-1}} e_n\) as the prescribed weighted sum over labelled Dyck paths with \(k\) decorated contractible valleys, for all \(n\) and \(k\).
why: The identity would connect the Macdonald eigenoperator \(\Delta'\) directly to decorated parking functions, extending the combinatorial understanding of Delta operators beyond the rise-decorated setting.
key_works: Haglund–Remmel–Wilson (2015/2018), *The Delta conjecture*; Shin (2026), [*Exchange identities and symmetric slices of the valley Delta conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14877).

title: \(1/3\)–\(2/3\) balanced-pair conjecture
open: Does every finite poset that is not a total order contain an incomparable pair \(x,y\) such that a uniformly random linear extension orders \(x<y\) with probability between \(1/3\) and \(2/3\)?
status: Open since the 1960s. The best known universal constant is approximately 0.2764; a September 2026 preprint by Aires–Chan–Pak–Panova, [*Breaking the Infinite Barrier in the \(1/3\)–\(2/3\) Conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30888), announces a strict improvement.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given for the statement that every finite non-total poset has an incomparable pair \(x,y\) with \(\Pr[x<y]\in[1/3,2/3]\) under a uniform random linear extension.
why: A positive answer guarantees that sorting with partial information always admits a balanced comparison, roughly halving the remaining possibilities at each step.
key_works: Aires–Chan–Pak–Panova (2026), [*Breaking the Infinite Barrier in the \(1/3\)–\(2/3\) Conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30888).

title: Rota’s basis conjecture
open: Can the \(n\) vectors of each of \(n\) labelled bases of a rank-\(n\) matroid be rearranged into \(n\) new bases, so that every new basis contains exactly one vector from each original basis? Equivalently, does every such collection admit a partition into \(n\) transversal bases?
status: Proposed in 1989. Asymptotically optimal packing and covering are known (Montgomery–Sauermann, 2025, [arXiv:2508.05601](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.05601)), and approximation algorithms are available (Arndt et al., 2026, [arXiv:2604.03735](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.03735)), but the exact \(n\)-by-\(n\) rearrangement remains open.
solved_when: For every rank-\(n\) matroid and every choice of \(n\) labelled bases, an exact \(n\)-by-\(n\) rearrangement into \(n\) disjoint transversal bases is proved (or a counterexample given).
why: A solution would unify rainbow decomposition and simultaneous independence into a single exact structural statement for all matroids.
key_works: Montgomery–Sauermann (2025), [asymptotically tight packing and covering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.05601); Arndt et al. (2026), [approximation algorithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.03735).

title: Stanley’s pure-\(O\)-sequence conjecture
open: Is every matroid independence-complex \(h\)-vector the degree sequence of a finite pure monomial order ideal? Equivalently, does Stanley's 1977 pure-\(O\)-sequence conjecture hold for all matroids?
status: The conjecture was proposed in 1977. Numerous classes of matroids are settled, and Oh (2026), *Relaxed coparking functions and Stanley's conjecture for matroid \(h\)-vectors* (https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.17446), gives relaxed-coparking constructions that still depend on an unresolved fibre-existence condition, leaving the general conjecture open.
solved_when: A construction (or proof of existence) is given that realizes the \(h\)-vector of every matroid independence complex as the degree sequence of a finite pure monomial order ideal, with no unresolved auxiliary conditions such as the fibre-existence condition in current relaxed-coparking approaches.
why: A positive answer would give an exact discrete model for matroid Hilbert functions, connecting matroid invariants directly to the combinatorics of monomial ideals.
key_works: Oh (2026), [*Relaxed coparking functions and Stanley’s conjecture for matroid \(h\)-vectors*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.17446).

title: Linear MDS conjecture over nonprime fields
open: Is every linear \([N,k]\) MDS code over \(\mathbb F_q\) with \(2 \le k \le q-1\) of length at most \(q+1\), apart from the known exceptional codes over even \(q\) that achieve \(q+2\)? In other words, does the linear MDS conjecture, long settled over prime fields, extend to arbitrary finite fields?
status: The conjecture is settled over prime fields. A 2026 preprint by Fan extends the known range in odd characteristic, but the case of unrestricted extension fields remains open. Key works: Ball–Lavrauw (2020), *Arcs in finite projective spaces* (https://doi.org/10.4171/EMSS/33); Fan (2026), linear-in-\(q\) range (https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03740).
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) of the bound \(N \le q+1\) for all linear \([N,k]\) MDS codes over any \(\mathbb F_q\) with \(2 \le k \le q-1\), with the only exceptions being the known even-\(q\) codes of length \(q+2\).
why: It determines the maximum length of optimally redundant linear erasure codes, the regime relevant to storage and transmission systems that rely on MDS codes.
key_works: Ball–Lavrauw (2020), [*Arcs in finite projective spaces*](https://doi.org/10.4171/EMSS/33); Fan (2026), [linear-in-\(q\) range](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03740).

title: Optimal unit-distance growth
open: What is the true asymptotic growth of the maximum number of unit-distance pairs determined by \(n\) points in the plane? That is, determine the correct exponent \(c\) such that this maximum grows as \(n^{c+o(1)}\).
status: The old conjecture of \(n^{1+o(1)}\) was refuted in 2026. Sawin (2026), [*An explicit lower bound for the unit distance problem*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20579), gives constructions with \(n^{1.014}\) unit distances; the general upper bound remains at scale \(n^{4/3}\). See also Guth (2026), [survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.10791).
solved_when: The maximum number of unit-distance pairs among \(n\) planar points is pinned down to matching asymptotic scale — equivalently, the lower and upper bounds agree up to \(n^{o(1)}\) factors, closing the gap between the known \(n^{1.014}\) constructions and the \(n^{4/3}\) upper bound.
why: It identifies the correct planar incidence exponent, resolving the basic quantitative question of how many unit distances \(n\) points can force.
key_works: Sawin (2026), [*An explicit lower bound for the unit distance problem*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20579); Guth (2026), [survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.10791).

title: Heilbronn’s triangle-area asymptotics
open: How small can the largest unavoidable triangle be — that is, what is the supremal value of the minimum area among all triangles determined by \(n\) points in the unit square? A sharper formulation asks for the true asymptotic order of this extremal minimum area as \(n\) grows.
status: Open since the 1940s. The best known lower scale is \((\log n)/n^2\); recent upper bounds reach \(n^{-7/6+o(1)}\), via Cohen–Pohoata–Zakharov (2024), [Lower bounds for incidences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.07658), building on [earlier triangle-area work](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18253).
solved_when: The maximum, over all configurations of \(n\) points in the unit square, of the minimum triangle area is determined up to constant (or asymptotic) factors — in particular, closing the gap between the known lower scale of \((\log n)/n^2\) and the recent upper bound of \(n^{-7/6+o(1)}\).
why: It quantifies how much near-collinearity among points is genuinely unavoidable, a fundamental limit on how "uniformly spread" a finite point set in the square can be.
key_works: Cohen–Pohoata–Zakharov (2024), [*Lower bounds for incidences*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.07658); [earlier triangle-area work](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18253).

title: Levi–Hadwiger illumination conjecture
open: Can every convex body in \(\mathbb R^d\) be illuminated by at most \(2^d\) directions? Equivalently, is the illumination number of every convex body in dimension \(d\) bounded by \(2^d\)?
status: Proposed in the mid-twentieth century, the conjecture remains open even in dimension three; recent progress includes Arman–Kaire–Prymak (2026), [*Illumination number of 3-dimensional cap bodies*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.disc.2026.115025).
solved_when: A proof establishes the bound \(2^d\) for every convex body in \(\mathbb R^d\) (at minimum, settling the case \(d = 3\)).
why: The bound would pin down the universal covering and illumination complexity of convex bodies, quantities tied to covering estimates and other classical problems on the geometry of convex sets.
key_works: Arman–Kaire–Prymak (2026), [*Illumination number of 3-dimensional cap bodies*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.disc.2026.115025).

title: Dürer’s edge-unfolding conjecture
open: Can every convex polyhedron be cut along a spanning tree of its edges so that the faces unfold into a single nonoverlapping planar polygon? In other words, does an edge-unfolding without overlap always exist?
status: The underlying question is centuries old. General unfoldings and affine-transformation results do not settle edge-only unfolding. See O'Rourke (2019), [edge-unfolding discussion](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.07152); [The Open Problems Project, problem 9](https://topp.openproblem.net/p9).
solved_when: A proof that every convex polyhedron admits an edge-unfolding into a nonoverlapping planar polygon, or a counterexample convex polyhedron for which every spanning tree of edges produces an overlapping unfolding.
why: A positive answer would guarantee, for any convex polyhedron, a fabrication pattern made purely of existing edges that cuts and flattens without self-intersection.
key_works: O’Rourke (2019), [edge-unfolding discussion](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.07152); [The Open Problems Project, problem 9](https://topp.openproblem.net/p9).

title: Ewald’s symmetric lattice-basis conjecture
open: Does every smooth reflexive lattice polytope \(P\) have enough lattice symmetry that its centrally symmetrized body \(P\cap(-P)\) contains a full lattice basis? A proof would show that toric smoothness forces this strong form of lattice symmetry in every dimension.
status: Proposed in 1988, the conjecture has been verified through dimension seven and for further infinite families, while arbitrary dimensions remain open; see Crespo–Pelayo–Santos (2026), [*Ewald's Conjecture and integer points in algebraic and symplectic toric geometry*](https://doi.org/10.1112/plms.70144).
solved_when: It is shown, for every dimension \(n\), that whenever \(P\) is a smooth reflexive lattice polytope, the intersection \(P\cap(-P)\) contains a basis of the ambient lattice.
why: A solution would establish that smoothness of a reflexive polytope rigidly constrains its lattice geometry — a structural fact with consequences for integer points in algebraic and symplectic toric geometry, including connections to nondisplaceable Lagrangian torus fibers.
key_works: Crespo–Pelayo–Santos (2026), [*Ewald’s Conjecture and integer points in algebraic and symplectic toric geometry*](https://doi.org/10.1112/plms.70144).

title: Bárány–Larman colored Tverberg conjecture
open: Can \(d+1\) color classes, each consisting of \(r\) points in \(\mathbb R^d\), always be partitioned into \(r\) rainbow tuples — one point of each color per tuple — whose convex hulls have a point in common?
status: The conjecture was proposed by Bárány–Larman in 1992. A September 2026 preprint by Soberón proves the topological case for prime \(r\); the general affine cases for composite \(r\) remain open. Key works: Bárány–Larman (1992), [colored Tverberg theorem](https://doi.org/10.1112/jlms/s2-45.2.314); Soberón (2026), [prime-number theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37876).
solved_when: A proof (or construction refuting it) is given for all \(r\) and \(d\); currently the prime-\(r\) topological case is settled, so the criterion is a proof covering general affine composite \(r\).
why: It would give the optimal balanced colorful intersection theorem, the colored analogue of Tverberg's theorem with the tight number of points.
key_works: Bárány–Larman (1992), [colored Tverberg theorem](https://doi.org/10.1112/jlms/s2-45.2.314); Soberón (2026), [prime-number theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37876).

title: Sierksma’s Tverberg-partition count
open: Is Sierksma's conjectured lower bound on the number of Tverberg partitions tight? That is, does every configuration of \((r-1)(d+1)+1\) points in \(\mathbb R^d\) admit at least \(((r-1)!)^d\) distinct Tverberg partitions?
status: The conjecture is a longstanding strengthening of Tverberg's existence theorem, and special parameter cases are known; Soberón (2026) gives an elementary proof for seven points in the plane ([arXiv:2604.18485](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.18485)).
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given for the bound \(((r-1)!)^d\) on the number of Tverberg partitions of every \((r-1)(d+1)+1\)-point set in \(\mathbb R^d\).
why: The conjecture quantifies how abundant intersecting partitions must be, turning Tverberg's theorem from a pure existence statement into a sharp counting one; it also pins down which configurations are extremal.
key_works: Soberón (2026), [*An elementary proof of Sierksma’s conjecture for seven points in the plane*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.18485).

title: Zeeman’s collapsibility conjecture
open: Does every finite contractible two-dimensional complex \(K\) admit a triangulation of \(K\times I\) that collapses to a single vertex? In Zeeman's formulation: if \(K\) is a finite contractible 2-complex, is \(K\times I\) collapsible?
status: Proposed in 1963. Known results either use more interval factors or reduce the question to special polyhedra, and none settle the case of a single interval factor. See Adiprasito–Benedetti, [products and collapsibility](https://arxiv.org/abs/1202.6606), and Dynnikov (2026), [*On Zeeman's collapsibility conjecture for non-standard polyhedra*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23331).
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) that for every finite contractible two-dimensional complex \(K\), the product \(K\times I\) with a single interval factor is collapsible.
why: A positive answer would tie contractibility — a purely homotopy-theoretic property — to explicit combinatorial simplification by collapses, and connects to the Andrews–Curtis conjecture.
key_works: Adiprasito–Benedetti, [products and collapsibility](https://arxiv.org/abs/1202.6606); Dynnikov (2026), [*On Zeeman’s collapsibility conjecture for non-standard polyhedra*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23331).
