title: Komlós vector-balancing conjecture
open: Given vectors \(v_i\in\mathbb R^n\) with \(\|v_i\|_2\le1\), can one always choose signs \(\varepsilon_i\) so that the signed sum has uniformly bounded coordinates? Formally, is there an absolute constant \(C\) with \(\|\sum_i \varepsilon_i v_i\|_\infty\le C\)?
status: Open since the 1960s. The best known bounds reach \(O((\log n)^{1/4}(\log\log n)^{7/4})\), via work such as Bansal–Jiang, [*Decoupling via Affine Spectral-Independence*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.03961); see also the [2026 exposition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28452).
solved_when: An absolute constant \(C\), independent of both the number of vectors and the dimension \(n\), is proved to suffice, together with an argument producing such signs.
why: It would establish dimension-independent discrepancy rounding, removing all dependence on \(n\) from vector-balancing guarantees.
key_works: Bansal–Jiang, [*Decoupling via Affine Spectral-Independence*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.03961); [2026 exposition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28452).

title: Scalable certificates for optimal discrepancy point sets
open: Can we build star-discrepancy optimization with end-to-end global certificates that scales to roughly an order of magnitude more points than today's exact certificates allow, under fixed precision and resource budgets? Formally, the goal is certified-optimal point sets at about ten times the currently certified point counts without increasing the computational budget.
status: This is a proposed engineering target; the state of the art in published exact certificates reaches 21 points in dimension two and eight in dimension three (Clément–Doerr–Klamroth–Paquete (2025), [Searching permutations for constructing uniformly distributed point sets](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12002279/)).
solved_when: A globally certified construction or optimization pipeline produces provably optimal star-discrepancy point sets at roughly ten times the currently certified point counts (i.e., beyond 21 points in dimension two and beyond 8 points in dimension three) under fixed precision and resource budgets.
why: It would turn numerical sampling designs into provably optimal configurations, replacing heuristic uniformity with guarantees.
key_works: Clément–Doerr–Klamroth–Paquete (2025), [*Searching permutations for constructing uniformly distributed point sets*](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12002279/).

title: Planted clique below the square-root scale
open: Can a planted clique of size \(n^{1/2-\delta}\), for some fixed \(\delta>0\), be detected or recovered in polynomial time — or is there a complexity-theoretic barrier showing no such algorithm exists?
status: The gap between the \(\sqrt n\) threshold and algorithmic reach has stood for decades. Kunisky–Mao (2026) give improved polynomial-time algorithms for detecting and recovering planted \(\Theta(\sqrt n)\)-cliques, improving constants at that scale but not breaking below it.
solved_when: Either a polynomial-time algorithm is given that detects or recovers planted cliques of size \(n^{1/2-\delta}\) for some fixed \(\delta>0\), or a suitable complexity barrier is proved ruling out such algorithms.
why: The planted clique model is a central testbed for computational-statistical separations; resolving the sub-\(\sqrt n\) regime would clarify whether detection there is fundamentally hard or merely lacking algorithmic ideas.
key_works: Kunisky–Mao (2026), [*Improved polynomial-time algorithms for detecting and recovering planted \(\Theta(\sqrt n)\)-cliques*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24780).

title: Versioned open-problem identity and status graph
subfield: Computational research, data, and sustaining infrastructure
open: Can we build a public registry that tracks the identity of open problems across their many versions — linking equivalent statements, stronger variants, special cases, counterexamples, and withdrawn proofs into evidence-backed status histories?
status: Proposed target. Existing problem databases and MaRDI provide components (Bloom, *Erdős Problems*; MaRDI [*Mission](https://mardi.imftr.de/about/mission)* and [*Portal](https://mardi.imftr.de/portal/portal)*), but combinatorics-wide reconciliation remains substantial work.
solved_when: A public registry exists that reconciles problem identities across combinatorics — including equivalent statements, variants, special cases, counterexamples, and withdrawn proofs — with evidence-backed status histories maintained at combinatorics-wide scale.
why: Without it, a million-entry census would multiply aliases and propagate obsolete claims; with it, the true status of any problem version is traceable to evidence.
key_works: Bloom, *Erdős Problems*; MaRDI, [*Mission*](https://mardi.imftr.de/about/mission) and [*Portal*](https://mardi.imftr.de/portal/portal).

bib.title: Versioned open-problem identity and status graph

title: Independently checkable extremal-witness archive
subfield: Computational research, data, and sustaining infrastructure
open: Can we build a public archive in which every claimed extremal combinatorial object — a record graph, design, code, coloring, or set system — is stored with a canonical encoding, full provenance, and a cryptographic hash, and can be verified by an independent checker that does not trust the source?
status: This is a proposed cross-resource target; existing repositories support parts of the workflow. Relevant infrastructure includes MaRDI's services and Heule's (2018) Schur Number Five certificates.
solved_when: A working archive accepts the listed object types (graphs, designs, codes, colorings, set systems), stores each with a canonical encoding, provenance, and hashes, and provides independent property checkers whose verification does not rely on the depositor's own computation.
why: It turns computational records into reusable mathematical evidence, so that a record-setting object, once deposited, can be trusted and reused without repeating the original computation.
key_works: MaRDI, [*Services*](https://portal.mardi4nfdi.de/wiki/MaRDI_Services); Heule (2018), [*Schur Number Five* certificates](https://www.cs.utexas.edu/~marijn/Schur/).

title: Tenfold cheaper combinatorial proof checking
subfield: Computational research, data, and sustaining infrastructure
open: Can we make independent checking of large combinatorial SAT proofs an order of magnitude cheaper than it is today — in storage, verification time, or measured energy — while preserving full certification? Concretely, this means at least \(10\times\) improvement on a preregistered combinatorial SAT-proof corpus under a frozen checker, corpus, hardware, and accounting protocol.
status: Proposed moonshot; no results yet. The motivating context is petabyte-scale certification such as the Schur number five proof (Heule, 2018, [Schur Number Five](https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v32i1.12209); [Brute trust](https://www.cs.utexas.edu/~mheule/publications/NAW18.pdf)). Related directions include proof compression and verified parallel SAT checking.
solved_when: A frozen competitive checker/version, proof corpus, hardware configuration, and accounting protocol are established before comparison, and a subsequent run achieves at least \(10\times\) lower storage, verification time, or measured energy on the preregistered corpus while retaining full certification.
why: A solution makes exhaustive computer-generated proofs independently auditable at far lower cost, so that massive certification efforts become practically checkable rather than trusted on faith.
key_works: Heule (2018), [*Schur Number Five*](https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v32i1.12209); [*Brute trust*](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~mheule/publications/NAW18.pdf).

title: Robust exactification of flag-algebra computations
subfield: Computational research, data, and sustaining infrastructure
open: Can a numerical flag-algebra solution — often large and badly ill-conditioned — be automatically converted into an exact rational certificate, including its nullspaces and any equality conditions?
status: Proposed extension of existing capability. Flagmatic (Vaughan, [*Flagmatic User’s Guide*](https://lidicky.name/flagmatic/UsersGuide.pdf); [repository](https://github.com/FordUniver/flagmatic)) already certifies supported cases; degenerate optima and scaling are the remaining targets.
solved_when: A tool takes such numerical solutions as input and outputs exact certificates covering degenerate optima, at a scale matching current flag-algebra practice.
why: It turns numerical extremal evidence into inspectable theorems, making large computations trustworthy rather than merely suggestive.
key_works: Vaughan, [*Flagmatic User’s Guide*](https://lidicky.name/flagmatic/UsersGuide.pdf); [Flagmatic repository](https://github.com/FordUniver/flagmatic).

title: Contamination-resistant research-combinatorics benchmark
subfield: Computational research, data, and sustaining infrastructure
open: Can we build a benchmark of research-level combinatorics tasks that reliably measures genuine mathematical progress rather than retrieval of known answers?
status: Proposed target, not yet built. CombiBench (Liu et al., 2025) supplies 100 formalized combinatorics problems, and construction-search systems such as PatternBoost (Charton–Ellenberg–Wagner–Williamson, 2024) demonstrate capabilities complementary to proof-oriented evaluation, but no time-stamped, contamination-resistant research benchmark with independent checking yet exists.
solved_when: A benchmark exists consisting of time-stamped, held-out research tasks with independent verification, reporting separate scores for novelty, correctness, and computational cost.
why: Without contamination-resistant design, evaluation systems may score highly by recalling training data instead of producing new mathematics; such a benchmark lets us measure actual research capability.
key_works: Liu et al. (2025), [*CombiBench*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.03171); Charton–Ellenberg–Wagner–Williamson (2024), [*PatternBoost: Constructions in Mathematics with a Little Help from AI*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00566).

title: Semantic audit of formalized conjectures
subfield: Computational research, data, and sustaining infrastructure
open: Can we build a workflow that audits formalized mathematical statements for faithfulness to the conjectures they are meant to encode — flagging missing hypotheses, incorrect quantifiers, convention mismatches, and vacuous formalizations — and validate it against examples adjudicated by experts?
status: Currently a proposed engineering target. Related resources include Liu et al. (2025), [*CombiBench*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.03171), and the [*Formal Conjectures* repository](https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures); the problem connects to specification validation and natural-language-to-logic alignment.
solved_when: The workflow exists, is validated against expert-adjudicated examples covering missing hypotheses, incorrect quantifiers, convention mismatches, and vacuous formalizations, and demonstrably detects these defects.
why: Proof checking alone does not establish that a formal statement matches the intended question; without such an audit, correct proofs of unintended statements can be reported as false solution claims.
key_works: Liu et al. (2025), [*CombiBench*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.03171); [*Formal Conjectures* repository](https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures).

title: Sustained funding and credit for mathematical data stewardship
subfield: Computational research, data, and sustaining infrastructure
open: How can the mathematical community secure durable funding, professional recognition, and service commitments for the ongoing stewardship of research data — the catalogs, certificates, and software dependencies on which independent replication depends?
status: This is a proposed policy target, not an allegation that any named project lacks funding. Published infrastructure programs, including MaRDI (2025) ([NFDI continuation-program letter](https://www.dfg.de/resource/blob/359426/nfdi-2025-mardi.pdf); [MaRDI consortium](https://www.nfdi.de/mardi/?lang=en)), identify sustainability and adoption as continuing needs.
solved_when: Standing funding lines and recognized service credit exist for maintaining catalogs, certificates, software dependencies, and independent replication infrastructure beyond individual grants.
why: Without sustained support, the evidence base of the field and the expertise of its curators are lost at the end of each grant; durable stewardship preserves both.
key_works: MaRDI (2025), [NFDI continuation-program letter](https://www.dfg.de/resource/blob/359426/nfdi-2025-mardi.pdf); NFDI, [MaRDI consortium](https://www.nfdi.de/mardi/?lang=en).
